Keynote 1: Pattie Maes + Ben Shneiderman
sessions.description:
Direct Manipulation vs. Interface Agents: The Debate Continues

In the late 1990s, Pattie Maes and Ben Shneiderman helped articulate two influential visions for the future of human-computer interaction. Maes advanced the case for interface agents: systems that could learn from users, personalize interaction, reduce information overload, and act on a user’s behalf when appropriate. Shneiderman championed direct manipulation: interfaces grounded in visible objects, rapid feedback, reversible actions, predictability, and a strong sense of user control. Their exchange helped define a lasting design question for HCI: how should interactive systems balance agency vs. control. Should good interfaces let people act directly on visible objects, or should they delegate work to systems that infer goals? That question now appears in recommender systems, intelligent assistants, notification filters, mixed-initiative tools, explainable AI, and modern AI agents.

The practical outcome was not that one side “won.” Direct manipulation remained foundational for GUIs, touch interfaces, creative tools, and dashboards. Maes’s agent vision also became real, but often under different names: personalization, collaborative filtering, recommender systems, context-aware assistance, and AI copilots. HCI absorbed the debate as a design constraint: automation is useful, but it needs transparency, controllability, calibration of trust, and graceful recovery from errors.

At UIST 2026 in Detroit, Maes and Shneiderman return to this conversation in a keynote debate moderated by Cliff Lampe. What was once a debate about software agents and graphical interfaces now sits at the center of contemporary interaction design, as generative AI systems, autonomous agents, copilots, recommender systems, and mixed-initiative tools reshape how people work with computers. Together, they will revisit the original arguments, reflect on how these ideas have evolved, and examine what today’s AI-infused interfaces demand from designers, researchers, and system builders. This keynote invites the UIST community to reconsider how we should balance automation with agency, personalization with transparency, and delegation with human control in the next generation of interactive systems.

Keynote 2: Mark Ackerman
sessions.description:
A Tentative Mea Culpa: A Look Backwards to Help the Next Generation of CSCW Researchers

In this talk, I will survey two research efforts of mine that began with best intentions, but slipped sideways into having problematic (if not downright negative) effects in the world. I will discuss my activities in the Platform for Privacy Preferences Project (P3P) as part of a World Wide Web effort and my activities in expertise sharing.

I do this partially as a mea culpa, but also to show the considerable caution that researchers must try to have. I will also briefly consider the role of regulation and governance in the United States as a way to solve some of the issues I raise. It has particular salience, given the recent debates about AI.

contents.title: SiMUSation: An Interactive Visitor Experience Simulation Framework to Support Museum Exhibition Design
contents.abstract:
Understanding how diverse audiences engage with narratives and content is central to exhibition design, yet designers often rely on intuition. Existing experience evaluation methods are typically retrospective, costly, and offer limited access to visitors' internal states, hindering early-stage iterative refinement.
Rather than relying only on post-implementation evaluation with real visitors, we explore LLM-driven persona simulation as a reference for early-stage design.
Following this idea, we present SiMUSation, an interactive framework designed to support early-stage exhibition design. SiMUSation models diverse visitor personas and simulates their exhibition experiences through a dual-layer representation that couples observable behaviors, such as movement and gaze, with corresponding internal responses, such as confusion and narrative engagement. Designers can steer simulations, inspect feedback from simulated visits, and iteratively revise layouts, content, and narrative flow to further examine how changes reshape visitor experience.
We implemented a prototype and evaluated it through a user study (N=12), showing that SiMUSation provides insights for reflection and refinement in early-stage exhibition design.
Our findings further highlight the potential of persona-driven simulation to support audience-informed evaluation and iterative decision-making across design tasks.

contents.title: HAPTCHA: Eyes-Free Haptic CAPTCHA in Mobile Environments: Design Principle, Security Evaluation, and User Experience
contents.abstract: Traditional visual CAPTCHAs face dual challenges: increasing vulnerability to automated solvers and maintaining usability without imposing excessive visual burden. We propose Haptic CAPTCHA (HAPTCHA), an eyes-free human-verification framework that leverages smartphone vibration as the primary information channel. HAPTCHA grounds security in a human closed-loop sensorimotor process that is inherently difficult for automated agents to emulate. We instantiate this framework through two complementary designs: tiltHAPTCHA, an efficiency-oriented spatial search task, and rhythmHAPTCHA, a robustness-oriented temporal reproduction task. Our security analysis against sophisticated imitation-learning bots shows that HAPTCHA's structured interaction traces provide a robust signal for discrimination, achieving up to 100% bot rejection rate in unseen attack scenarios. The usability evaluation across sitting, walking, and fast-walking scenarios demonstrates that HAPTCHA maintains high solvability (e.g., 96.7% success rate for tiltHAPTCHA while sitting) and offers superior usability with significantly lower cognitive workload than a visual reCAPTCHA mockup. These findings position HAPTCHA as an explicit haptic challenge layer that complements passive, risk-based verification by moving challenge information beyond the screen.

contents.title: Supporting The Many Lives of Personal Data with Rebite: LLM-Powered Goal-Directed Framing in Food Journaling
contents.abstract: People’s health and tracking goals frequently change, but most personal informatics systems struggle to adapt, leading people to abandon their data and start over. We propose goal-directed framing, an approach that repositions goals within personal informatics systems. Instead of fixing the meaning of data at capture time, the approach frames the collected data through the current goal and reframes it whenever the goal changes. We realize this in Rebite, a photo-based food journaling system that uses LLMs to read unstructured meal photos and produce goal-directed feedback. In a one-week deployment with 21 participants managing multiple dietary goals, we find that goal-directed framing shaped how participants engaged with their goals. Translating a goal into metrics helped them see what it meant in practice, confirming existing priorities, surfacing what they overlooked, and revealing where the metrics fell short. When goals changed, seeing past meals reframed under the new goal exposed overlaps and conflicts, prompting participants to negotiate trade-offs and refine priorities. We discuss how goal-directed framing both supports and complicates reflection as goals change, and offer design implications for personal informatics systems to support evolving goals.

contents.title: ShadAR: Real-time Prompting On-demand Visual Augmentation in Augmented Reality
contents.abstract: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough real-time via shader injection. When receiving a user’s prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user’s intent, analyzes the user’s view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage pattern, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how (“Highlight the book.”), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental/behavioral states (“Make me laugh.”). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., “Make me not miss my flight”) while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.

contents.title: Halftoning for 3D Printed Textile Nets
contents.abstract: 3D printed textile nets are fabric-like structures produced by printing a few layers of continuous, overlapping paths. These textiles can be fabricated with minimal post-processing and material waste on low-cost Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) 3D printers. Parametric design tools for generating toolpaths can be used to create a variety of textile structures and path patterns; however, the ability to control color patterns and transitions is limited by the continuity of the printed paths. We propose using halftoning to incorporate graphics patterns into the printed nets by dynamically controlling the printed path thickness during printing. Our workflow takes a grayscale input image and translates it into a two-color halftone pattern and a segmented toolpath. Line thickness is controlled by varying extrusion amount and printing speed, resulting in a colored pattern that matches the input image. We demonstrate our concept with a series of printed textile samples and a wearable corset.

contents.title: Codetations: Rich, Granular, and Maintainable Annotations for Evolving Code
contents.abstract: Developers accumulate rich contextual knowledge about their code (e.g., design rationales, edge cases, worked examples) that does not fit in source files and goes stale when kept in separate documents or in human memory. We present Codetations, a VSCode extension enabling persistent, interactive annotations on arbitrary code spans without modifying the underlying file. A novel hybrid annotation anchoring method combines editor tracking for local edits with LLM-based semantic matching for offline changes, keeping annotations stable as code evolves. Annotation tools are modules sharing a minimal API for document access and state management. We demonstrate that this API is expressive enough to support multimedia embedding,  automatic documentation maintenance, and external tool integration. In initial user studies with nine experienced developers, we found that attachment behavior matched their expectations. The diverse tools also enabled developers to imagine a variety of domain-specific use cases for annotations, particularly for validating and managing LLM-generated code. We discuss how a lightweight annotation layer can preserve contextual knowledge and  open up a novel design space of developer-defined annotations.

contents.title: Co-Annotator: Expert-Distilled ViT and VLM for Visual and Documentation Guidance in Age-Related Macular Degeneration
contents.abstract: Clinical AI often optimizes predictive performance without engaging how clinicians decide where to look and what to write. We present Co-Annotator, which distills expert gaze and dictation into two guidance components: a gaze-aligned Vision Transformer producing fixation-aligned areas of interest (AOIs), and an ontology-bounded vision-language model (VLM) that pre-fills editable biomarker summaries for retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT). We first collect expert gaze and dictations (US1) to train the models, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and biomarker generation. We then deploy the system with ophthalmology residents: a controlled resident study (US2) confirmed each modality is safe and independently beneficial, with AOI guidance producing lasting perceptual efficiency gains through post-guidance carryover and VLM guidance more than doubling bio\-marker documentation breadth. In a combined deployment across two academic institutions (US3), providing both modalities simultaneously produced efficiency gains that substantially exceeded either modality alone: correct diagnoses per minute increased by 40% and comment editing time fell by 67%, without compromising diagnostic accuracy. Notably, neither modality improved efficiency during guidance in US2, which makes the in-guidance efficiency gain under combined guidance in US3 the more striking result. Expert-distilled multimodal guidance can remove two distinct clinical workflow bottlenecks at once (visual search overhead and documentation burden) without compromising the diagnostic accuracy clinicians already achieve.

contents.title: TeethMark: Enabling Tongue-Tooth Interaction with Capacitive Sensing and Electrotactile Feedback using an Intraoral Wearable
contents.abstract: We present TeethMark, an intraoral interface that enables tongue–tooth interaction by leveraging the tongue as the active medium for gesture input and electro-tactile feedback, while utilizing teeth as positional cues for localization. By applying a flexible PCB on a 3D-printed brace, TeethMark can recognize tapping, sliding, and area-touch gestures, and deliver two forms of electrotactile feedback: co-located feedback when the tongue touches the inner side of the teeth, and always-available feedback on the lip-facing side. With our design tool, users can customize and generate their own flexible PCB layouts, selecting interaction locations at the level of individual teeth. We conducted a formative study examining the physical comfort and social acceptability of tongue gestures across different tooth locations. The validation study evaluates the perception of electrotactile feedback and the accuracy of tongue–tooth gesture recognition. Our results indicate that TeethMark provides a promising modality for discreet, hands-free interaction. We further demonstrate its versatility through a set of applications, including language education, VR sensory sharing, gamified myofunctional therapy, and fabrication tool support.

contents.title: Leadership in Human–Robot Teams: Effects of Proactive Agent Behavior on Group Cohesion
contents.abstract:
Hybrid teams of humans and embodied conversational agents (ECAs) are increasingly studied in human–computer interactions to support collaborative activities involving decision-making and coordination. In such settings, effective teamwork relies on positive group dynamics, particularly cohesion, a multidimensional construct reflecting both shared commitment to group tasks and interpersonal bonds among members. Given the established relationship between leadership and cohesion in human teams, this article investigates whether proactive, leader-like ECAs can foster cohesion in hybrid teams.
To this end, we design a proactive agent model and adapt a collaborative narration task to support multiple group configurations. We conduct a between-subjects Wizard-of-Oz experiment (N = 64) where teams of two humans and two robots collaborate as peers, comparing a condition where one robot is proactive with a condition where neither robot is.
Results validate our agent model and show that groups including  a proactive robot report significantly higher task cohesion. Behavioral analyses reveal increased participant involvement.
These findings suggest that proactive behaviors inspired by leadership strategies represent a promising design approach for ECAs aiming to foster cohesion in hybrid collaborative settings.

contents.title: ExtenString: Enhancing String-Based Interaction with Virtual Screens through Remapping
contents.abstract: Previous research has investigated string-based systems that bridge the fingertips and head-mounted displays (HMDs) to provide physical support when users reach out to click in virtual reality (VR). These systems rely only on a low-cost, simple passive string and have demonstrated exemplary performance. However, the limited hand movement range may restrict interaction space. We explored the use of remapping to overcome interaction in physical constraints, thereby supporting a wider range of scenarios. While users move on the spherical surface defined by the string, interactions can be mapped to virtual screens with positions and sizes different from the physical layout. We conducted studies to identify optimized designs that enhance user performance and satisfaction across various screen usage contexts, including physical interaction positions and cross-screen tasks. Finally, we demonstrate how the proposed method enables various scenarios in applications and discuss its potential use cases.

contents.title: Be My Ears: Enabling Semantic Alerting for Earphone Wearers with Pheme
contents.abstract:
Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) earphones provide immersive listening experiences but induce auditory isolation to earphone users, leaving them vulnerable to hazards and socially disconnected. We present Pheme, an agentic framework that transforms ANC earphones into context-aware auditory assistants. Informed by two user studies (N = 385
and N= 34) that reveal a high prevalence of missed critical sounds and significant linguistic ambiguity (73.6%) in user requests, Pheme employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) an LLM-based Query Understanding module to resolve intent and map ambiguous commands to acoustic targets; (2) Text-conditioned Audio Separation (via SAM Audio) to isolate target sounds from ambient noise; and (3) LALM-based Verification to validate detections against user intent, reducing false interruptions.

We evaluate Pheme against a baseline that directly feeds ambient audio into an audio language model for target event detection, using 1,584 audio samples across seven real-world scenarios. Our results show that Pheme achieves 82.2% detection accuracy for user-specified audio events at +5 dB SNR setup, outperforming the baseline by 9.5% while reducing the false positive rate by 11.9%. Moreover, Pheme significantly
reduces operational overhead, cutting API calls by 48.1% and LALM audio processing workload by 67.3%.

contents.title: Exhale to Execute: Transforming Commercial Microphone Arrays into Directional Airflow Sensors for Ubiquitous Interaction
contents.abstract: Ubiquitous computing environments frequently require hands-free input methods when users are physically occupied. Current exhalation detection approaches rely on dedicated airflow sensors or utilize standard microphones with basic volume thresholds. We introduce a software framework designed to repurpose commercial microphone arrays for directional airflow sensing. To address the limitations of simple amplitude thresholds, our system employs an absolute-energy gate, a cross-channel energy-uniformity ratio, and non-linear energy-weighted mapping. This acoustic pipeline enables standard microphones to estimate airflow direction under controlled conditions. Technical evaluations with a calibrated mechanical airflow source show that the framework distinguishes localized airflow impacts from the tested far-field background noise and separates coarse directional targets. This work includes no human-subject evaluation; the interactive demonstrations illustrate proof-of-concept mappings rather than validated interaction performance.

contents.title: LightShop: High-Precision Interactive Computational Light Painting
contents.abstract: Light painting is a photographic technique that integrates light cast by a handheld light source during the capture of a long-exposure photograph. This creates an image roughly equivalent to that of a static light source with geometry matching the captured motion of the light. Unfortunately, light painting is limited by the precision of hand motion, the inability to visualize progress during the painting process, and occlusions caused by the painter during capture. We introduce LightShop: an interactive system that helps users capture high-precision light paintings with a projector and real-time tracking from a head-mounted display (HMD). LightShop helps users compose, previsualize, and capture precise light paintings with guidance from augmented reality (AR) interfaces, using a novel computational exposure strategy to isolate light cast by the intended emitter on the scene. We demonstrate that LightShop lets users easily capture complex reflections and refractions among real objects illuminated by precisely constructed virtual light emitters.

contents.title: Revibing Code from Papers: Reimplementing HCI Artifacts
contents.abstract: Software artifacts for most technical HCI research projects are unavailable. The lack of access to these imposes limits on academic knowledge production. It is difficult to: extend or reuse research artifacts; use strong baselines in evaluating follow-up work; and perform replication or reproducibility research. In this work, we demonstrate the potential of new agentic AI technologies to revibe interactive software: reimplement systems directly from research papers. To measure the success of the approach, we describe a revibeability metric. By revibing recent research papers from UIST, and interviewing their original authors, we demonstrate the plausibility (and limitations) of revibed system. The results are encouraging. In many cases producing code suitable for strong baseline use. We argue that this may represent a fundamental shift in how we produce, use, and evaluate research artifacts in the technical HCI community.

contents.title: MetaBeads: Enabling Shape- and Stiffness-Changing Interfaces through Beaded Metamaterials
contents.abstract: As interactive systems increasingly extend into the physical world, designers need accessible ways to prototype interfaces that can change both shape and stiffness. In this paper, we investigate how simple, widely available materials—beads and string—can be used to construct shape- and stiffness-changing interfaces without specialized machinery. We introduce a set of reusable structural mechanisms that enable sturdy, wearable, and load-bearing structures from bead-based assemblies, each supporting a distinct mode of deformation and stiffness change, such as transforming from a flexible sheet into a jammed cuboid, a stiff tube, or a bistable curvature cell. To facilitate the creation of these structures, we provide an interactive design tool that guides craftspeople designing and fabricating their own MetaBead interfaces. We demonstrate the possibilities of MetaBeads through four application prototypes across wearable devices, educational tools, and adaptive furniture. Together, this work offers an accessible approach to prototyping shape- and stiffness-changing interfaces with everyday materials.

contents.title: Can You Say This for Me? Speaking Up by Proxy in Co-Located Discussion
contents.abstract: Equal participation in co-located discussion is important for effective collaboration, yet people often hold back when they anticipate negative interpersonal or professional consequences, especially when raising a point requires voicing it themselves. We present SecondVoice, a mixed-reality system that enables people to speak up through an embodied virtual proxy. By separating what is said from who says it, SecondVoice brings hesitant points into the live spoken discussion without putting the speaker on the spot. Using a private overlay, users specify their intent through a structured specification process rather than composing a full utterance. The system reformulates the input and voices it into the conversation through the proxy. We characterize a design space of participation channels under social risk. In a preliminary within-subject study (N=16), we compare the complete SecondVoice system with an anonymous text-board channel across two group discussion tasks. Half of participants reported using SecondVoice for a point they did not say aloud, compared with 18.8% for the text board. Proxy-delivered points entered the spoken floor and were followed by multi-turn group engagement, which we did not observe after text-board posts. Participants described the channel as situationally valuable but identified tradeoffs around timing, ownership, and trust in reformulation.

contents.title: PartInteractor: Intent-Driven Part-Aware 3D Authoring for Continuous Co-Creation in XR
contents.abstract: As Extended Reality (XR) evolves into an immersive computing medium, interactive 3D authoring becomes essential for creative and functional workflows. However, existing generative XR systems produce monolithic outputs lacking explicit semantic structure, limiting post-generation control. We introduce PartInteractor, a representation-to-interaction framework that investigates how semantic part hierarchies can be incorporated into generative XR authoring, and exposed as first-class, directly manipulable units, turning one-shot prompt-to-object generation into continuous component-level co-creation. PartInteractor supports speech, sketch, and image inputs, integrating an LLM interpreter with a retrieval-generation strategy to scaffold user intent prior to 3D generation. Instead of producing monolithic objects, our system generates semantically decomposed 3D assets with explicit part hierarchies, enabling rich component-level interaction over object structure and composition. Our evaluations suggest that part-aware representation increases post-generation control and reduces reliance on whole-object regeneration, while intent scaffolding mitigates ambiguity and improves intent-result alignment, together supporting more expressive and controllable human-AI co-creation workflows. These results highlight part-aware representation and intent scaffolding as promising design considerations for future generative XR authoring systems.

contents.title: Less Is More: Balancing Positive and Negative Space in Visual Concept Blending
contents.abstract: Graphic designers often blend visual concepts to communicate multiple ideas within a single image, leveraging positive and negative space to create balance, emphasis, and aesthetic appeal. While computational methods have begun to support automatic concept blending, they largely overlook the role of spatial composition in the design. To address this gap, we present an automatic pipeline that explicitly applies positive and negative space throughout the blending process. Our approach first identifies plausible regions for concept integration by combining semantic reasoning from vision–language models with geometric constraints derived from real-world examples. Conditioned on these regions, the system generates blended compositions using a hybrid pixel–vector pipeline: diffusion-based inpainting produces a fast, coarse initialization, which is then refined through vector-based optimization at the point level to ensure structural coherence and balanced semantic expression. A multimodal agent orchestrates this process as a planner and evaluator, enabling iterative improvement and interpretable control. Through an evaluation using both baseline comparisons and a user study, we demonstrate greater expressiveness, creativity, and concept recognizability by effectively leveraging positive and negative space. We further demonstrate the generalizability of our approach across diverse applications, including controllable image and infographic generation.

contents.title: HapTap: Ultrashort, Low Power Pulses for Localized Fingertip Haptics
contents.abstract: Linear-resonant actuators (LRAs) are typically designed for longer (100 ms) vibrations that feel spatially diffuse when coupled to the skin. In this work, we investigate ultrashort (1 ms) actuation signals using miniature (6 mm diameter) LRAs to create more focused fingertip sensations. To study the transition from diffuse vibrations to localized pulses, we first characterized actuator motion, then conducted a broad perceptual study followed by a targeted psychophysical evaluation. Physically, higher voltage (12 V vs 5 V) but shorter, quarter-cycle pulses produced slightly higher peak displacement (1.7X) and substantially higher estimated indentation force (4.9X) when compared to a baseline driving signal, though only for one polarity. Perceptually, shorter real and perceived durations increased the sense of pulse concentration and slightly improved valence. Finally, with 8 actuators arranged in a 2X4 array, our 1 ms pulses achieved higher localization accuracy than a 119 ms sinusoidal stimulus (71.6% vs. 61.9%) while using 9.6X less energy.

contents.title: TransfHAR: Self-Supervised Wrist Representations for On-Demand Activity Recognition
contents.abstract: Fine-grained wrist activity recognition can support applications such as procedural step guidance and context-aware assistance, yet acquiring labeled data for every new task, user, and activity granularity remains a bottleneck. We present TransfHAR, a self-supervised wrist IMU framework for on-demand, fine-grained activity recognition by learning transferable motion priors from global, unlabeled activities. We show that self-supervised pretraining on coarse wrist IMU activities (e.g., sitting, walking, exercise) learns motion structure rich enough to transfer to fine-grained manipulative, gestural, and procedural activities (e.g., snapping, stirring, waving) that are absent from pretraining. We implement TransfHAR as a real-time smartwatch application that lets users define and expand their own activity set for personalized recognition from only a few demonstrations. Across three offline cross-dataset evaluations, TransfHAR matches or exceeds fully supervised baselines that use complete label sets with equal or additional sensor channels, by 6.2 balanced-accuracy points on average. In an in-lab study with 10 participants each performing seven novel wrist activities, TransfHAR reaches 86.7% balanced accuracy across participants with five examples per class and 90.4% when updated from a single one-minute recording per class. These results indicate that broad self-supervised wrist pretraining provides an effective foundation for on-demand fine-grained activity recognition.

contents.title: EcoVibWood: Lower Impact Vibration Sensing in Plywood
contents.abstract: In this paper, we present EcoVibWood, an approach that combines alternative sensing materials with an automatic protective mechanism to support lower-impact plywood vibration sensing. We systematically explore commercially available alternatives for the triboelectric and electrode layers, including zinc, iron, gold leaf, graphite, paper, PBAT, and PLA, and evaluate whether they can retain the sensing performance of conventional copper and PTFE configurations. We further introduce a protective mechanism made from wood and bamboo that automatically isolates affected electrodes when screws penetrate the plywood, without requiring electronic components or manual intervention. Our experiments show that several alternative layer combinations achieve signal strength and SNRs comparable to, or exceeding, those of traditional copper--PTFE configurations. We integrate these materials into a working prototype and evaluate its performance across 26 everyday activities. EcoVibWood achieves an average recognition accuracy of 83.3\% using a Random Forest classifier and 94.7\% using a convolutional neural network, demonstrating that lower-impact material substitutions can support robust activity recognition.

contents.title: MAIC-UI: Making Interactive Courseware with Generative UI
contents.abstract: Creating interactive STEM courseware traditionally requires HTML/CSS/JavaScript expertise, leaving barriers for educators. While generative AI can produce HTML codes, existing tools generate static presentations rather than interactive simulations, struggle with long documents, and lack pedagogical accuracy mechanisms. Furthermore, full regeneration for modifications requires 200--600 seconds, disrupting creative flow. We present MAIC-UI, a zero-code authoring system that enables educators to create and rapidly edit interactive courseware from textbooks, PPTs, and PDFs. MAIC-UI employs: (1) structured knowledge analysis with multi-modal understanding to ensure pedagogical rigor; (2) a two-stage generate-verify-optimize pipeline separating content alignment from visual refinement; and (3) Click-to-Locate editing with Unified Diff-based incremental generation achieving sub-10-second iteration cycles. A controlled lab study with 40 participants shows MAIC-UI reduces editing iterations (4.9 vs. 7.0) and significantly improves learnability and controllability compared to direct Text-to-HTML generation. A three-month classroom deployment with 53 high school students demonstrates that MAIC-UI fosters learning agency and reduces outcome disparities---the pilot class achieved 9.21-point gains in STEM subjects compared to -2.32 points in control classes. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-MAIC/MAIC-UI

contents.title: Great Grave: Modeling Versioned Context Units for Longitudinal LLM Interaction
contents.abstract: Researchers use LLM chat for sustained intellectual work across long conversations—formulating problems, designing methods, and iterating on ideas. The resulting chat logs function as documents co-authored by the researcher and the model. Yet their linear structure turns them into a rich but practically unusable repository, a "great grave" where valuable decisions and rationale are buried in ever-growing scrolls of text. We present Great Grave, a system that transforms LLM chat logs into Research Workflow Graphs. Our approach segments conversations into intent-driven Context Units, groups them into decision-tracked Work Units, and extracts typed relations to form a navigable graph. An overlay interface provides a List View for hierarchical retrieval and a Graph View for relational exploration. A within-subjects study (N=12) showed that the overlay significantly improved performance on research comprehension tasks, with the largest gains in tasks requiring cross-temporal comparison and evolutionary reconstruction. While techniques such as context windows and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) help models leverage history, Great Grave enables users to do the same.

contents.title: Editrail: Understanding AI Usage by Visualizing Student-AI Interaction in Code
contents.abstract: Programming instructors have diverse philosophies about integrating generative AI into their classes. Some encourage students to use AI, while others restrict or forbid it. Regardless of their approach, all instructors benefit from understanding how their students actually use AI while writing code [1, 15, 26, 39]. Such insight helps instructors assess whether AI use aligns with their pedagogical goals, enables timely intervention when they find unproductive usage patterns, and establishes effective policies for AI use. However, our survey with programming instructors found that many instructors lack visibility into how students use AI in their code-writing processes. To address this challenge, we introduce Editrail, an interactive system that enables instructors to track students' AI usage, create personalized assessments, and provide timely interventions, all within the workflow of monitoring coding histories. We found that Editrail enables instructors to accurately detect AI use that conflicts with pedagogical goals and to determine when and which students require intervention.

contents.title: When and Where You Nudge Matters: Multi-Step Interface Interventions Against Address Poisoning in Crypto Wallets
contents.abstract: Crypto wallets are the primary applications through which users interact with Web3 ecosystems, and are subject to a range of attacks that lead to serious security consequences. Address poisoning is a prominent example: attackers exploit wallets' truncated address displays and users' habitual reliance on simplified transfer workflows to trick them into sending funds to fraudulent addresses. While prior work has quantified the prevalence and financial impact of such attacks, little is known about how to effectively defend against them. In this work, we take wallet interface design as a practical defense vector, introducing nudge interventions that help users resist these deceptions. This approach can be deployed through wallet updates without modifying underlying blockchain protocols, and directly targets the interaction point where the attack takes effect. We design nudges targeting three key stages of the transfer workflow where users are most vulnerable to this interface-induced threat. Through a between-subjects online experiment (n = 351) and semi-structured interviews (n = 20), we show that nudges can significantly reduce susceptibility to address poisoning attacks, but that their effectiveness varies depending on where and how they are placed within the transfer flow. Our findings offer design implications for building safer wallet interfaces, demonstrating how the placement and framing of interactive elements within a transaction workflow can meaningfully shape users' security-critical decisions.

contents.title: Prism-UX: Turning Evaluative Divergence into Traceable Design Evidence for LLM-Based Process-Level UX Evaluation
contents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly being integrated into interactive workflows, introducing new challenges for UX evaluation because user experience is becoming more context-dependent and more closely tied to process-level moments such as waiting, flicker, uncertainty, intermediate artifacts, and loss of control. However, existing AI-assisted evaluation methods often compress such process-level differences into a single decontextualized conclusion. Interviews with 10 practitioners revealed that reviewers often struggle to cite specific moments in an interaction, compare interpretations across stakeholders, or trace their judgments back to observable facts. We refer to this loss of perspective-specific evaluative distinctions as insight collapse. To address this problem, we propose Prism-UX, a traceable review system for short, visually observable UI workflows involving GenAI features. Prism-UX first transforms interaction screen recordings into citable storyboard evidence through a frame-difference algorithm, then supports side-by-side evaluation from configurable evaluative viewpoints over shared evidence, and finally applies a structured reasoning protocol that anchors review judgments in explicit Fact IDs. Through a technical ablation study and expert evaluation, Prism-UX reduced the logical conflict rate by 84%, increased grounding completeness from 0.38 to 0.82, and was rated more useful than automated baselines for trade-off inspection, discussion support, and decision confidence. The results suggest that preserving evidence-grounded evaluative disagreement, rather than forcing convergence, can support more traceable and disagreement-aware design review.

contents.title: Fold2Unfold: Screen Privacy Protection against Shoulder Surfing using Inter-Screen Reflection on Foldable Smartphones
contents.abstract: Smartphone use in crowded public spaces exposes users to shoulder surfing, allowing nearby bystanders to easily access privacy-sensitive information on the screen. We present Fold2Unfold, a screen privacy protection system for foldable smartphones that ensures screen content readable only from the user's viewpoint without additional hardware. Fold2Unfold decomposes the original content into two complementary, individually illegible shares displayed across screens, and leverages inter-screen reflection to reconstruct the content. By tracking the user's eye position and dynamically warping the content accordingly, the system ensures that the reconstructed content is readable only to the user. We implement Fold2Unfold on a commercial foldable device and evaluate its usability and security through controlled user studies involving a PIN entry task. Our results show that Fold2Unfold substantially reduces information leakage under shoulder surfing, with attackers inferring only 6.5% shown on a 10-digit keypad, while incurring a modest input time increase compared to our baseline keypad.

contents.title: Proxy3D: Interactive Spatial Proxies for Multi-View Consistent 3D Concept Design
contents.abstract: Generative AI shows great promise for accelerating 3D content creation in product design and game development. However, existing 3D generation pipelines still cannot effectively support the diverse 2D-to-3D requirements in design creation. To investigate this mismatch, we conducted a formative study that revealed two key challenges: (1) a 2D view edit provides the model with no explicit constraint for locating the intended change in 3D, and (2) generating 3D models from 2D plane edits often fails to maintain cross-view consistency. To address these gaps, we develop Proxy3D, an interactive, progressive editing system. It addresses the first challenge using an inferred spatial proxy as an interaction intermediary for spatial preview and precise local edits. To address the second, our system employs a video-to-3D generation approach conditioned on this proxy and explicit camera trajectories, producing a trajectory-linked sequence intended to support cross-view consistency. In a within-subjects comparative study, participants rated Proxy3D higher than representative baseline workflows in perceived controllability, target-design consistency, and overall satisfaction.

contents.title: The Rock Can Talk: Spatial AI and XR for Rock Climbing Navigation
contents.abstract:
We present RockXR, a mixed reality prototype that examines the potential for approaches like Worlds-in-Miniature (WiM), spatial route annotations, and conversational assistants to provide navigation cues and guidance during rock climbs. 

These three techniques mirror the combination of overview maps, situated overlays, and conversational turn-by-turn instructions that are increasingly common for pedestrian and car navigation. They also illustrate the growing potential for mixed reality visualization and guidance across technical sports and activities.

RockXR uses annotated digital \hlt{models} of climbing routes to render navigation information directly on the wall via a mixed-reality headset, while also providing persistent WiM overviews of the entire route. We also demonstrate how live 3rd person imagery generated from those digital \hlt{models} can support conversational interactions with route descriptions, allowing climbers to ``talk to the rock'' for guidance and feedback while climbing. To probe the potential of these approaches and gauge climbers’ receptiveness to them, we evaluated RockXR with 16 climbers in a controlled indoor study and complemented this with a field test on an outdoor multi-pitch climb. Our findings highlight the value of flexible guidance interfaces that span multiple reference frames and interaction modalities, and suggest that XR can meaningfully augment how climbers plan, interpret, and move through complex, high-risk terrain.

contents.title: Precise Duration Control for Video Editing via LLM Scoring and Constrained Optimization
contents.abstract: Editing videos calls for satisfying two fundamentally different kinds of requirements simultaneously. Editors often need to meet hard constraints, such as hitting a precise target duration, while also considering semantic objectives, such as preferring engaging content. These two requirements lend themselves to different computational tools, and combining them is non-trivial. Using video editing as a case study, we present a hybrid approach that combines using LLMs to provide semantically relevant labels for video clips with using mixed-integer linear programming to enforce hard constraints and select content. Our approach guarantees millisecond-precise output durations while optimizing for user-specified semantic objectives, such as informativity and topic relevance. Feedback from editors indicates that our tool supports interactive exploration across several video editing goals, including creating interview rough cuts and shortening edited videos for sharing across different platforms.

contents.title: Who's Keeping Score? Interactive Steering of LLM-Powered Scoring with Attune
contents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to score text records at scale (e.g., rating candidate resumes on a 1–5 scale). However, existing LLM-powered approaches do not account for the fact that effective scoring requires both holistic understanding of records and locally consistent judgments across similar ones. We present Attune, a mixed-initiative system for steerable LLM-powered scoring. Given a task description and scoring range, Attune performs pairwise comparisons across records to develop a global understanding first, and then resolves these comparisons into consistent score assignments—deriving scoring criteria and rules bottom-up in the process. These serve as shared representations of scoring logic that users can inspect and edit. Based on insights from a formative study (n = 12), Attune’s interface introduces novel steering interactions that allow users to deterministically refine scoring logic. Users can provide examples, directly edit criteria, rules, or target distributions, and give natural language feedback—with all refinements compiling into constraints that guide re-scoring. We validate our approach through a technical evaluation across three workloads and a user study with domain experts (n = 8) in healthcare, law, education, and AI evaluation.

contents.title: EITWatch: Smartwatch-Integrated Planar Electrical Impedance Tomography for Hand Gesture Recognition
contents.abstract: Wrist Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) senses hand gestures from muscle- and tendon-driven impedance changes, but prior wrist-EIT systems require electrode coverage beyond the watch-back contact patch and separate analog front ends. We present EITWatch, the first wrist-EIT system built around smartwatch case-back geometry, asking whether this contact patch alone can support gesture recognition: eight planar electrodes in a 31 mm ring acquire 35 impedance measurements at 48 Hz. Because a planar array cannot encircle the wrist, EITWatch uses multi-depth scanning to sample multiple source-sink distances and current paths; it beat matched adjacent injection by 15.1/10.4 percentage points (macro/micro) across all 12 participants. In a prompted study, within-session leave-one-round-out accuracy reached 91.4%/92.5% (window/trial) for six macro-gestures, and 90.1%/91.5% (window/segment) for five micro-gestures plus relax; window-level cross-session and leave-one-user-out transfer reached 73.2%/70.4% and 63.1%/55.3% (macro/micro).

contents.title: Armonii: Motion Design for Wearable Supernumerary Robotic Arms Toward Comfort and Embodiment
contents.abstract: Wearable supernumerary robotic arms (WRAs) can augment human capabilities, but their motions impose gravity- and actuation-induced torques that reduce comfort. Our formative study (n=10) shows that perceived burden scales differently across motion types and can exceed acceptable limits as intensity increases. We present Armonii, a threshold-aware motion design framework that uses inactive robotic arms to regulate motion-induced loads within perceptually acceptable bounds while preserving embodiment. Technical evaluation reveals a regime-dependent trade-off: gravity and actuation compensation align during vertical motion but conflict during horizontal motion. A user study (n=16) shows that prioritizing gravity compensation significantly reduces perceived burden vs. baseline (p<.05) without compromising embodiment, while prioritizing actuation compensation is less effective. A gravity-limited variant that balances both performs best, further improving comfort in a focused horizontal-reaching task (p<.01).

contents.title: CoNarrate: Computationally Modeling Information Prematureness to Scaffold the Co-Construction of Patient Narratives in Asynchronous Telehealth
contents.abstract:
Asynchronous telehealth requires patients to self-report their conditions, which serve as the critical basis for subsequent diagnosis and care.
However, patients often struggle to articulate all necessary details upfront.
This premature information delivery causes prolonged back-and-forth messaging, delayed clinical decisions, and increased physician burden.
Comparing 5,000+ initial self-reports with post-consultation logs, we identified five recurring patterns of information prematureness.
We model these patterns using the DIBH framework, mapping patient statements into a computable heterogeneous information space (Data, Information, Beliefs, Heuristics).
Leveraging this underlying architecture, we developed CoNarrate, an LLM-driven intake system that proactively detects prematureness and generates targeted scaffolding questions before doctor review.
A between-subjects study (N=46) demonstrated that CoNarrate significantly improved the clinical information richness of self-reports, reducing follow-up needs while maintaining high user satisfaction.
This work contributes a new lens for modeling information prematureness, and a novel algorithmic approach to scaffolding the co-construction of comprehensive medical narratives.

contents.title: “Live in the Editor”: Low-Tech In-Situ Feedback for Plain-Text Live Programming
contents.abstract: Live programming research has spent decades adding bespoke editors, custom file formats, and dedicated output surfaces. Yet the richest of these systems are often the least adoptable and the hardest to maintain, and few survive as platforms. We ask the question in the opposite direction: what is the least we need for live programming? We present Recho, whose entire mechanism is that a programmer marks a value with echo and saves the file; the runtime evaluates the program and writes each result back into the source as a generated comment beside the code that triggered it, replacing those comments in place on each run and leaving the rest of the file untouched. We do not claim probes, in-place evaluation, reactive execution, or inline widgets as new—these are the baseline we subtract from. Our contribution is subtractive: a file-mediated design point that removes the specialized editor, the notebook format, and the separate output surface while keeping feedback and liveness intact. Treating plain text as a constraint rather than a convenience changes what feedback is: output stops being a transient log and becomes a durable, local artifact that persists after execution, appears in diffs, travels with the file, and reopens in any editor. Incremental re-execution and inline widgets are optimizations layered on this core, not requirements. A formative study with eight programmers characterizes how the resulting save-and-inspect loop is used, and where its presentation falls short.

contents.title: CARVid: Content-Aware Retargeting of Videos with On-Screen Graphics
contents.abstract: Video editors routinely reframe landscape videos containing on-screen graphics, such as lower thirds or scoreboards, to portrait aspect ratios for sharing on social media. Existing methods often crop, shrink, or distort these graphics, reducing readability and disrupting their original design. Manual redesign is also slow and frustrating due to the difficulty of dealing with layered compositions or flattened videos with graphics that lack editable layers. We present CARVid, a content-aware retargeting tool for adapting on-screen graphics in videos to new aspect ratios while preserving readability and original design intent. CARVid leverages recent advances in foundation vision and segmentation models, together with a novel graphics-processing algorithm guided by a VLM critic, to detect graphical overlays, extract them from their underlying videos, and apply content-aware retargeting operations to adapt them to new aspect ratios. Our human-in-the-loop approach combines text-aware scaling, layout-aware horizontal and vertical segmentation, and content-aware space removal to support both automatic and user-directed retargeting of on-screen graphics. We conducted a technical evaluation using a custom dataset of 60 in-the-wild videos from popular internet sources that contain on-screen graphics. Results provide evidence of CARVid’s technical feasibility across a wide range of videos.

contents.title: StateScribe: Towards Accessible Change Awareness Across Real-World Revisits
contents.abstract: Real-world environments evolve continuously, yet blind and low-vision (BLV) individuals often have limited access to understanding how they change over time. Unexpected or relocated objects, layout modifications, and content updates (e.g., price changes) can introduce safety risks and cognitive burden. While existing visual assistive technologies can describe immediate surroundings, they operate as one-off interactions and lack mechanisms to surface meaningful changes across revisits. Informed by a survey of 33 BLV individuals, we develop StateScribe, a system that supports accessible awareness of real-world changes across revisits. StateScribe employs a dual-layer memory architecture that integrates episodic scene memory and object-centric temporal memory to enable scalable and structured change tracking. It provides both live descriptions of the current scene, and descriptions of what has changed, when and where it occurred across revisits, such as "The shop on your right has a 'CLOSED' sign; it was open at this time last week.'' Our evaluation shows that StateScribe maintains high accuracy (F1-score = 83.1%) across 11 revisits, while remaining low-latency (mean < 1.42s) and memory-efficient (< 55MB) across 110 revisits. A user study with nine BLV participants demonstrates that StateScribe improves change awareness across revisits in three real-world locations. Finally, we discuss implications for long-term AI-assisted companions that support broader change observation using multimodal sensing, extend beyond changes to other memory capabilities, and adapt to individual users, intents, and contexts.

contents.title: HueRistic: Optimizing Lighting for Live Video Color Design
contents.abstract: We present HueRistic, an interactive system that optimizes color in live video through physical lighting control. Our system integrates a camera with programmable LED lights, analyzing the colors in the live feed and measuring the effect of each light source.  HueRistic employs closed-loop optimization to find RGB lighting configurations that satisfy specific aesthetic objectives, such as enhancing color harmony or reproducing target colors in the scene. To support rapid exploration, HueRistic includes a design gallery that allows users to compare candidate lighting configurations before applying them to the scene. Our technical evaluation demonstrates that our system accurately simulates and produces high quality lighting solutions that satisfy aesthetic objectives. Our user study finds that HueRistic enables creators to discover lighting parameters that would be challenging to achieve through trial-and-error alone.

contents.title: IRIS: Navigating and Reflecting on Writing Traces Using Intelligent Document Histories
contents.abstract:
Much of the text produced throughout the lifetime of a document is impermanent. 
In this paper, we explore how writing activity traces can be made visible and interactive to help writers navigate their document histories and understand their writing processes. Using the Flower and Hayes cognitive process model of writing, IRIS infers writing process states from keystroke logs and presents them using an AI-enhanced version history. IRIS provides three primary interactions: revision highlighting that shows local process histories in-situ, conceptual filters that constrain the version history by process type or topic, and natural language inquiry that lets writers pose reflective questions about their writing and process. Following a formative and a longitudinal study, we find that writers use the interfaces to locate specific revisions and understand the progression of their writing. They use system outputs as interpretive material, relating them to pre-existing beliefs and confirming, challenging, and deepening their understanding of their writing.

contents.title: TypeRing: Ten-Finger Surface Typing with Dual IMU Rings
contents.abstract: Ten-finger surface typing promises a portable alternative to physical keyboards and touchscreens, making it well-suited for mobile scenarios, but remains challenging to balance sensing cost with input performance. We ask whether it can be enabled with two IMU rings, without relying on bulky wearables or continuous vision processing. We first present TypeRingIMU, which detects rapid ten-finger touches and identities with an F1-score of 98.4%, enabling efficient ten-finger typing on any flat surface using only two IMU rings. We further enhance it via optical-inertial fusion that opportunistically detects touch positions from IMU-triggered touch events, leveraging the front-facing camera already available on mobile devices, namely TypeRing. It removes fingering constraints, thus improving input naturalness and accuracy. Our method achieves 28.6 WPM input speed (63.5% of physical keyboards), with top-1 and top-12 accuracies of 88.5% and 98.1%, significantly outperforming current methods and demonstrating strong potential for efficient, convenient, and user-friendly mobile text input.

contents.title: SemanticSlider3D: Training-Free Continuous Semantic Editing for 3D Objects
contents.abstract: Fine-grained control over continuous semantic attributes of 3D objects is essential for 3D content creation, but is not well supported by conventional 3D modeling workflows or prompt-based interaction with existing generative AI tools. While slider-based methods have proven effective for fine-grained semantic control in 2D image generation, no equivalent approach exists for 3D. Extending these 2D methods to 3D is non-trivial due to challenges unique to 3D, including geometric integrity and cross-view coherence. We present SemanticSlider3D, a technique for continuous semantic attribute editing of 3D objects that requires no per-attribute training. Given a user-specified attribute, our pipeline constructs a semantic editing direction in the latent space of a state-of-the-art 3D generation model, presenting a diverse and coherent spectrum of 3D variations. A technical validation on a dataset of 50 3D object-attribute pairs shows our method was preferred by all five human assessors across variation range, consistency, 3D object quality, and attribute disentanglement, over a baseline combining a 2D slider with an image-to-3D model. An exploratory study with six participants demonstrates that SemanticSlider3D supported decision-making in 3D prototyping and was perceived as a valuable addition to existing workflows.

contents.title: SpatialBlend: Relational Reconstruction for Cross-Space Presence in Heterogeneous Spaces
contents.abstract:
Cross-space presence enables communication between people in different physical spaces as if they were in the same space. The central challenge is spatial heterogeneity: rooms differ in layout, geometry, and affordances, so directly replaying motion or relying on rigid shared layouts can make behavior invalid, unreachable, or hard to interpret. We present SpatialBlend, a runtime system for cross-space presence based on relational reconstruction: the system continuously describes how the user is interacting with nearby people and objects, then reconstructs avatar behavior in the viewer's room while respecting that room's geometry and affordances.

We implement SpatialBlend in Unity on Meta Quest 3 and evaluate it in the Freeform Collaboration prototype across an office and a living room with different layouts. In a deployment study with 26 participants (13 dyads), continuous shared presence throughout the room improved social presence, continuity, trackability, and spatial coherence over a zone-based baseline. We release SpatialBlend as open source at https://github.com/snuhcs/spatialblend.

contents.title: CineHaptic: Context-Aware Real-Time Audiovisual-to-Haptic Rendering System for In-Vehicle 4D Cinematic Experiences
contents.abstract: Haptic feedback significantly enriches cinematic experiences, but existing manual authoring and offline generation methods lack the scalability required for rapidly growing streaming media libraries. To address this, we present CineHaptic, a real-time system that automatically generates haptic effects for action-oriented cinematic content by estimating event salience and location for immersive in-vehicle 4D experiences. For each sound event, the system classifies its semantic salience into a four-level hierarchy, determining the necessity and intensity of haptic actuation. Concurrently, a cross-modal audiovisual analysis module estimates the sound’s spatial origin in the scene. CineHaptic then seamlessly synthesizes this semantic and spatial data into coherent spatiotemporal patterns, delivered through a custom six-actuator haptic seat. System-level evaluations confirm strict adherence to real-time processing and multisensory synchrony requirements over full-length cinematic content. Furthermore, an in-car user study shows that haptic feedback integrating audio salience, spatial location, and temporal dynamics significantly enhances user immersion and preference compared to baseline methods. Ultimately, our system provides a fully automated pipeline for multisensory rendering, tailored for next-generation in-car entertainment.

contents.title: CapFM: A Foundation Model for Capacitive Touch Sensing
contents.abstract:
Capacitive touch sensing supports rich interactive behavior, yet learning-based methods have been task-specific and rely on labeled datasets that are costly to collect and annotate.
We introduce CapFM, a foundation model for capacitive touch sensing that learns a shared representation across diverse touch understanding tasks.
We pretrain a Masked Autoencoder on a large corpus of unlabeled capacitive frames across seven datasets, through which our model captures a robust structure in the signal without task-specific supervision.
For downstream use, we keep CapFM's pretrained backbone fixed and attach lightweight task heads that use either global embeddings or spatial token features, depending on task output structure.
We evaluate CapFM's unified approach on eight diverse tasks, including finger identification, pitch and yaw estimation of the finger angle, 3D hand-pose estimation, high-resolution contact area segmentation, and input accuracy.
Across these settings, CapFM transfers effectively across datasets and hardware configurations.
Using the same training and validation regimen, CapFM pretrained without the respective dataset matches or beats all baselines and shows robust performance.
Our results show that foundation-model pretraining makes capacitive sensing models more data-efficient for downstream learning and transferable across tasks and hardware, which can support diverse applications based on CapFM's pretrained backbone rather than separate task-specific models.

contents.title: Dishplay: Edible Display Utilizing Magnetic Response of Iron in Cereal
contents.abstract:
This paper presents Dishplay, an edible display system that uses external permanent magnets to generate and animate visual patterns in liquid by actuating iron-fortified cereal.
Dishplay supports both static pattern formation through magnet placement and dynamic pattern transitions enabled by a linear actuator–driven magnet array.
Through technical evaluations, we examine how cereal quantity, liquid type and volume, and elapsed time affect display fidelity and characterize transition dynamics such as speed and precision.
Based on these results, we derive design considerations for visual fidelity and transition behavior and explore application scenarios.

contents.title: Maru: Information Architecture as a Shared Language for Generating Aligned and Persistent User Interfaces
contents.abstract: Generative user interfaces (GenUIs) promise on-demand components tailored to users’ needs. As users iterate on information tasks, they construct personal structures over information they encounter---how items are grouped, what gets prioritized, and what terms mean in their context. Yet, current systems leave these structural decisions to the model at each generation, ignoring the structural logic users have established. Without a persistent representational structure shared between user and system, GenUIs have no basis to remain aligned with what users have established. We draw on Information Architecture (IA), a design practice for organizing and structuring information, as a shared language to bridge user-constructed structure and system generation. We present a framework identifying four IA elements---partition, hierarchy, order, and vocabulary---and characterize how each maps to concrete UI generation decisions. We instantiate this framework in Maru, a conversational system that captures user prompts and interactions as IA preferences, persisting as rules both user and system draw on across generations. A user study revealed that IA persistence kept generated UIs aligned as sessions progressed, while alignment without it degraded, with diverse patterns emerging across users and contexts, pointing to the value of IA persistence in aligning GenUI to individual needs.

contents.title: TalkEase: A Multimodal Personalized Topic Guidance System for Long-distance Couples' Video Calls Driven by LLM
contents.abstract: Video-mediated communication (VMC) is vital for long-distance couples, yet the lack of shared context often leads to conversational stagnation. We present TalkEase, a real-time multimodal conversational support system that alleviates topic exhaustion through a sensing-understanding-action loop. TalkEase integrates multimodal interaction cues, including conversational rhythm, turn-taking dynamics, and affect-related signals, to estimate potential moments of interactional difficulty and provide contextualized topic suggestions. We introduce non-intrusive interaction techniques: ``Topic Bubbles'' provide shared peripheral visual anchors, while a ``Shuffle'' function empowers users with agency over AI suggestions. We further present Adaptive Fading, a theory-informed artifact mechanism inspired by scaffolding principles, which explores how AI assistance may gradually recede as users develop greater conversational autonomy. A mixed-methods study with 60 long-distance couples shows that TalkEase improves immediate Perceived Partner Responsiveness (PPR) and shifts cognitive demand from high-pressure topic generation toward low-stress suggestion evaluation. Our work offers an empirically grounded interaction approach for AI-assisted intimate communication while establishing design directions for future adaptive conversational support.

contents.title: Thin-Film Actuator Embedded Haptic Glove Supporting Thumb Kinematics for Displaying Volumetric Shape and Contact Indentation
contents.abstract: The dexterity of the human hand is fundamentally rooted in the coordination of the thumb’s opposition and adduction. Despite its significance, conventional haptic gloves often neglect these two degree-of-freedom (2-DOF) movements, typically providing only single-channel tactile or force feedback. This limitation severely diminishes realism and control during dexterous manipulation in virtual reality (VR) and teleoperation. In this paper, we present a compact, lightweight haptic glove capable of providing 2-DOF force (kinesthetic) and pressure (tactile) feedback specifically for the thumb. To achieve this, we developed a system that utilizes thin-film electrostatic clutches and a cross-tendon structure to effectively constrain thumb movements. Furthermore, to accommodate varying contact points on the thumb pad during diverse grasping tasks, we integrated two thin-film flexure actuators to deliver localized pressure feedback at two thumb-pad locations. A preliminary user study suggests that constraining 2-DOF thumb movements improves perceived realism and reduces visual--haptic discord during virtual grasping of a cylindrical object with self-selected postures. We further demonstrate the feasibility of the system for stabilizing grasping in the teleoperation of a humanoid hand.

contents.title: RampEMS: Onset Shaping for Stroke-Stable Pressure Modulation in Calligraphy
contents.abstract: Electrical muscle stimulation (EMS) can modulate force during ongoing voluntary action, but abrupt onset can evoke involuntary motion that perturbs fine motor control. We formalize pulse-width onset shaping as an EMS design dimension and implement it as RampEMS, which gradually increases pulse width to a target value instead of applying that value abruptly. Using brush calligraphy as an artifact-producing testbed, a formative study empirically characterized logarithmic onset curvatures and selected a 1-s profile as a task-specific balance between onset smoothing and timely force buildup. We then evaluated this selected profile in a controlled traced-calligraphy study with the characters Ei and San, comparing it with step-type EMS (StepEMS) at the same target pulse width and with noEMS. For Ei, RampEMS significantly increased brush pressure relative to noEMS; for San, RampEMS did not significantly decrease brush pressure relative to noEMS. For both characters, RampEMS produced significantly smaller noEMS-relative stroke error distances than StepEMS, indicating less EMS-associated positional perturbation rather than improvement over unassisted writing. RampEMS also yielded significantly higher SUS scores and lower Raw NASA-TLX scores than StepEMS. Together, these results support pulse-width onset shaping as a task-specific strategy for reducing trajectory disruption during ongoing fine-motor action.

contents.title: MagToTheFuture: Transforming Passive Objects into Circuit-Free Haptic Devices via Magnetic Fields
contents.abstract: We present MagToTheFuture, a tabletop system that uniquely integrates co-located force, vibration, and thermal feedback to passive objects via magnetic fields, without any onboard electronics. Prior magnetic approaches faced a physical limitation in that coil designs optimized for strong magnetic force inherently conflict with the conditions required for efficient induction heating, thereby restricting the use of multiple co-located modalities. MagToTheFuture accommodates this electromagnetic characteristic by placing a force–vibration coil and a thermal coil together within a single actuator structure while driving the two coils independently. A hall-sensor array estimates patch position and identity, while a linear motion system positions the actuator to deliver force, vibration, and localized heating at a single site. Technical evaluations validate reliable sensing accuracy and haptic outputs across materials, demonstrating the feasibility of augmenting everyday objects into interactive interfaces. User studies showed that multimodal feedback improved four dimensions of the haptic experience in Content Augmentation and Object-Embedded Augmentation, while improving two dimensions in Informational Augmentation. These results highlight the potential of our approach to support more expressive, scalable, and accessible interactive systems.

contents.title: GazeTune: Facilitating Precise Gaze-Driven Interactions with Cascaded Touch Input
contents.abstract: Eye gaze has become an essential input for spatial computing, but its coarse targeting and saccadic nature limit precision and complicate continuous interactions such as dragging, especially under user motion. Gaze+pinch has also become standard in XR for its convenience, yet mid-air gestures remain imprecise, fatiguing, and socially unacceptable. These limitations underscore the need for an approach that preserves the speed of gaze while enabling stable, fine control. We present GazeTune, a cascaded multimodal interaction technique combining gaze and touch to refine gaze-based selection and manipulation. Touch serves as a refinement channel within gaze pointing, allowing precise cursor and target control. Our work investigates how gaze-and-touch enhances dragging and mitigates Motion-Induced instability. In a study (N=20), we compared GazeTune against gaze-only and gaze-pinch methods in 2D dragging. Results show that GazeTune achieves significantly lower error with comparable execution time, validating its effectiveness and balanced trade-off between time and accuracy.

contents.title: Eliciting Empathetic Expression Through Robot-Initiated Touch in Companion Scenarios
contents.abstract: Companion robots are becoming increasingly integrated into everyday life, making the ability to express empathy a critical aspect of their design. However, prior research has focused primarily on verbal and visual cues, leaving robot-initiated touch largely underexplored. To address this gap, we first conducted a pilot study to identify six representative robots whose proactive touch was most acceptable across three morphology types (Human-like, Animal-like, and Machine-like). We then conducted an elicitation study to examine users’ expectations for robot-initiated touch across four emotional states (Happy, Depressed, Tense, and Relaxed). The results showed that both emotional states and robot morphology shaped preferred touch locations and touch behaviors, yielding a set of 24 user-preferred touch gestures. Finally, a Wizard-of-Oz study in a virtual environment demonstrated that a balanced subset of these gestures effectively conveyed empathic intent and improved both users’ affective states and their perceptions of the robots. These findings provide design implications for robot-initiated touch in future companion robots.

contents.title: IntentLint: Supporting Intent Scaffolding and Prompt-time Linting in Human-AI Collaborative Data Analysis
contents.abstract: In human-AI collaborative data analysis, as analyses rapidly evolve, the artifacts meant to capture shared understanding often become incomplete or difficult to interpret, leading to undocumented assumptions, cross-user misaligned intent, context-poor prompts, and unwanted agent behaviors. To address these challenges, we introduce a rule-based coordination layer with two interaction mechanisms, intent scaffolding and prompt-time linting, that make analytic intent explicit and actionable during human–AI collaborative data analysis. We implement them in IntentLint, a proof-of-concept system that infers analytic intent from shared notebooks, represents it as structured, editable rules, and checks users' prompts against shared rules. IntentLint helps analysts externalize and refine their intent and proactively checks prompts for potential conflicts. A study with 16 data analysts shows that IntentLint improves awareness of collaborators’ intent and encourages reflection on analytic strategies, and provides design implications for supporting more aligned and transparent human-AI collaborative data analysis.

contents.title: Earmony: Orchestrating Adaptive Auditory Cardio-Respiratory Biofeedback on Commodity Earables
contents.abstract: Commodity earbuds are becoming an increasingly promising platform for everyday health and wellness support. Building on their wearability and ubiquity, we present Earmony, an adaptive auditory cardio-respiratory biofeedback system that runs on off-the-shelf earbuds. Using only the built-in in-ear microphone, Earmony unobtrusively senses cardio-respiratory signals without requiring additional sensors. To support simultaneous sensing and audio playback, we develop a robust detection framework that preserves signal quality under concurrent audio output. Building on this capability, we implement a closed-loop system in which auditory feedback is dynamically modulated by the user’s real-time physiological state rather than following a fixed pace. Specifically, musical chords guide breathing and adapt continuously to both breathing dynamics and heart rate variability (HRV), enabling responsive and personalized regulation. A user study (N=20) shows that Earmony maintains significantly elevated HRV for longer durations than static systems, demonstrating the potential of seamless, earbud-based adaptive biofeedback.

contents.title: Penquiry: A Pen-based Interactive In-situ Q&A System Leveraging LLMs
contents.abstract: Pen-based digital devices remain a preferred medium for active, cognitively engaging study. Concurrently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have become indispensable for self-directed learning, enabling students to clarify concepts. However, a fundamental interaction gap exists between the fluid, spatial nature of pen-based workflows and the discrete, keyboard-heavy requirements of LLMs. We present Penquiry, an in-situ question-and-answer system that bridges this gap by enabling learners to pose questions directly on digital study materials via a pen. We characterize two primary interaction challenges in this multimodal transition: a Referential Barrier, which hinders grounding fine-grained visual elements into the query context, and an Expressive Barrier, which forces learners to translate diverse, non-textual intents---such as equations and diagrams---into rigid, typed sentences. To resolve these, Penquiry introduces a mediation layer featuring Content Snapping for unambiguous referencing and Question Autocompletion to expand sparse ink keywords into rich semantic queries. Through two iterative user studies (N=16 per study), we demonstrate that Penquiry significantly reduces the cognitive and physical overhead of inquiry compared to traditional interfaces, providing a new blueprint for pen-based, in-situ AI interaction.
