contents.title: Sensorimotor Stickies: A Reconfigurable On-Body Platform for Closed-Loop Sensorimotor Training
contents.abstract: Closed-loop sensorimotor training systems can improve learning by sensing movement and delivering real-time feedback, yet most are built as fixed implementations tied to a single task, even though the core technology (inertial and tactile sensing, vibrotactile cueing, rule-based logic) remains the same. We present Sensorimotor Stickies, a reconfigurable on-body platform that treats sensing and vibrotactile feedback as modular stickies that can be patched onto the body as needed. The platform includes miniaturized adhesive modules for IMU sensing, optional tactile sensing, and vibrotactile actuation; low-power firmware and BLE infrastructure for raw streaming and motor control without task-specific rewrites; and a companion mobile app that provides a shared body-centered model for placement, calibration, and feedback authoring. Together, these components enable reconfiguration across training scenarios, user needs, and feedback setups. We evaluate the platform through technical characterization, configured application demonstration, practitioner-mediated configuration sessions, and an end-user study, demonstrating technical feasibility, reconfiguration breadth, and end-user configurability for first-time setup, calibration, and within-task feedback reconfiguration.

contents.title: Relative-Motion-Aware Color Presentation with High-Speed Projection
contents.abstract:
This paper proposes a color image display method where the perceived image changes according to the viewer's direction of movement relative to the display surface. 
Conventional motion-responsive displays require camera-based tracking, which poses challenges for privacy and scalability in public spaces. 
To address this, we propose a display method that leverages the relative motion between the viewer and the display surface without any sensors. 
The system can present different images for two arbitrary directions of the viewer's movement. This is achieved by temporally decomposing target images and reintegrating them through high-speed projection, enabling motion-contingent display without external sensors. 
We describe the mechanism for inducing specific color perception during movement and evaluate image fidelity through experiments. 
Furthermore, we implement a digital signage application and conduct user studies to discuss its effectiveness. 
Our approach enables adaptive signage that responds to movement direction without the need for complex tracking systems.

contents.title: EvoMaestro: Toward Interpretable and Steerable LLM-Driven Program Evolution
contents.abstract: Recent program evolution systems use large language models (LLMs) to generate and iteratively improve populations of programs, producing striking advances in mathematics, algorithm design, and scientific computing. Yet these systems largely operate as fully automated black boxes. As populations grow, domain experts must make sense of the scores, code changes, reasoning, and algorithmic ideas across many programs, while current interfaces provide limited support for understanding or redirecting the evolution. We characterize this need to understand and steer populations of evolving algorithmic ideas as semantic oversight. A formative study with 8 domain experts yields six design requirements for this emerging human-computer interaction problem. We then propose a steerable program evolution framework that lets expert judgments shape subsequent evolution. Built on this framework, EvoMaestro is an interactive visual analytics system that organizes evolution information from population overview to source code. It helps experts locate and compare noteworthy programs, guide evolution with natural language, combine promising ideas, and prune unproductive directions. A seven-day system demonstration illustrates how an expert applied these capabilities throughout a long-running evolution process. A within-subjects study with 12 participants shows that EvoMaestro improves users’ understanding of evolution processes, reduces cognitive workload, and supports expert steering. These findings suggest that preserving expert agency in open-ended LLM-driven search requires support for both informed judgment and the ability to shape subsequent automation.

contents.title: AtmoSteer: Personalized Scene Control with Reusable Atmospheric Recipes
contents.abstract: Generating scenes that convey atmospheres such as “cozy” or “contemplative” is difficult because people interpret them subjectively and often struggle to express them concretely. We present AtmoSteer, a human-in-the-loop approach that captures a user’s personal interpretation of an atmosphere as an atmospheric recipe: a weighted set of descriptive tags that can be reused across scenes for tasks such as image generation and image search. AtmoSteer supports users in discovering their own atmospheric recipes by exploring diverse interpretations with images and constructing a personalized vocabulary of visually grounded tags that describe style, layout, objects, and lighting. The system then supports preference refinement through two modes: slider-based weight adjustment of tags and visual example-based elicitation. In a user study on image generation (N=20), images generated from recipes produced by AtmoSteer were significantly more preferred and better aligned with participants’ subjective interpretations than those generated using generic descriptors or style transfer techniques.

contents.title: 4DOrthosis: Therapist-in-the-Loop Design and Fabrication of Force-Customized Hand Orthoses via 4D Printing
contents.abstract: Hand orthoses play an important role in rehabilitation by stabilizing joints and facilitating movement, with progressive resistance training being particularly critical for muscle function recovery. Yet existing fabrication workflows rarely support patient-specific fit, force customization, and workflow-compatible monitoring simultaneously. We developed 4DOrthosis through a therapist-in-the-loop process that elicited three design requirements: personalized force, efficient fabrication, and support for monitoring-enabled rehabilitation workflows. 4DOrthosis combines FDM-based 4D printing, a force-structure characterization pipeline, and a parametric design tool that generates orthoses from patient hand dimensions and target force requirements, achieving customized rehabilitative force within an experimentally characterized range of 1–20 N. Studies with five rehabilitation-related evaluators and six users indicate feasibility, workflow compatibility, positioning 4DOrthosis as a practical human-centered fabrication approach for rehabilitation devices.

contents.title: Avatar Cloak: Protecting Behavioral Privacy with State-Aware Motion Substitution in Immersive MR Telepresence
contents.abstract:
Immersive telepresence in Mixed Reality (MR) allows users to communicate through embodied avatars driven by live-tracked motion.
While this supports embodied interaction, it can also expose privacy-sensitive behaviors. 
This creates a gap between protecting behavioral privacy and maintaining interaction quality.
To address this, we present Avatar Cloak, a motion substitution concept that replaces live-tracked motion with appropriate animations to conceal sensitive behaviors.
Through a formative study, we implemented a State-Aware Substitution that substitute avatar motion based on conversational states when users choose to conceal behaviors.
A user study (N=36) showed that State-Aware Substitution increased users’ sense of control over privacy, reduced concerns about misinterpretation, and enhanced  engagement and message understanding.
These findings inform the future designs of motion substitution systems that balance privacy protection with embodied interaction in MR telepresence.

contents.title: MBits: Multi-modality 3D-printed objects via resonance-tunable spring-mass units
contents.abstract: The geometric customization possible using digital fabrication has unlocked various explorations into objects' static properties: their shape, texture, materials, and embedded mechanisms. Less-explored is how geometry can enable new modes of interactivity through customizing object dynamics---how an object responds to forces and motions. We contribute MBits : programmable, simulatable, and reconfigurable spring-mass units which react to mechanical waves and enable controllable dynamical outputs in the form of haptics, motion, display, and audio. Objects with MBits can be printed from scratch using our toolkit or can include off-the-shelf springs, with geometry or mass modification pre- or post-manufacture to tune their responses. Each MBit responds strongly to a single vibrational frequency, and collections of multiple MBits can, with a single actuator input, create mechanical filters, cascading sequences, or individually targetable vibration regions. We contribute a collection of characterization experiments, embedded in a CAD design tool, along with sample applications showing the possibilities of MBits.

contents.title: Print & Place: Using a 3D Printer for the Assembly of Electronic Devices
contents.abstract: Print & Place is a novel process that appropriates unmodified commodity FDM 3D printers to enable in-situ pick-and-place of electronic components. Traditionally, producing functional 3D-printed electronics has required manual assembly, extensive post-processing, or compromises using high-resistance filaments. Our approach overcomes these barriers by automating the continuous positioning, electrical connection, and encapsulation of parts throughout the print process, broadening the range of devices that can be additively manufactured. Our method leverages adhesion from cooled beads of extruded thermoplastic to pick up and place elements within an evolving 3D structure. We present a workflow that integrates mechanical and electronics design with job preparation, generating a part-placement tray and custom pick-and-place movements. We characterise the adhesive performance, electrical reliability, and operational limits of the technique. Finally, we demonstrate how Print & Place enables the fabrication of fully encapsulated electronic devices, advancing additive manufacturing from geometric fabrication toward the production of functionally integrated, bespoke devices.

contents.title: MemCanvas: A Structured Memory Canvas for Evolving Intent Alignment in LLM Dialogues
contents.abstract: Aligning user intent in complex, evolving dialogues with Large Language Models (LLMs) is a significant challenge. We attribute this to a cognitive divergence between LLM's linear reasoning based on context and statistical semantic representations, and the exploratory, non-linear, and personalized nature of human intent. These gaps not only cause progressive misalignment but also leave users without a clear understanding of model's perception or means to control its trajectory. To bridge this gap, we introduce MemCanvas, an interactive system that organizes dialogue history into shared, editable memory structures to complement outcome-based approaches. By scaffolding intent via three interaction primitives—Trees (for thematic directions), Relations (for logical connections), and Tags (for personalized semantics)—MemCanvas enables users to externalize evolving intent and proactively steer the LLM’s reasoning. Our technical evaluation and user study (N=28) demonstrate that MemCanvas effectively aligns user intents and enhances users’ sense of control, transparency and collaboration. Ultimately, this work illustrates how intent scaffolding can serve as a practical supplement to standard linear interfaces, fostering more process-aligned human-AI collaboration.

contents.title: PÅCKER: Modularizing Large Laser-Cut Objects for Easy Transport and Storage
contents.abstract: We present PÅCKER, a software tool that makes large, laser-cut 3D objects efficient to pack and ship. Inspired by modern flat-pack furniture, PÅCKER achieves this by de-composing 3D models into multiple 3D components. Components are pre-assembled at the vendor’s site, shipped efficiently (since components tend to be convex, they pack well), and post-assembled IKEA-style at the receiver’s site. PÅCKER users decompose models using our custom split tool, which requires them to specify only where to split the model; the tool then automatically selects the most suitable split plane and connector type. Models componentized using PÅCKER are robust: in our technical evaluation, they withstood 94Nm+ of torque. In our user study, participants assembled decomposed chair models about 3.6x faster than the control group and rated them as requiring less demand to assemble.

contents.title: Attribution Gradients: Incrementally Unfolding Citations for Critical Examination of Attributed AI Answers
contents.abstract: AI answer engines are a relatively new kind of information search tool: rather than returning a ranked list of documents, they generate an answer to a search question with inline citations to sources. But reading the cited sources is costly, and citation links themselves offer little guidance about what evidence they contain. We present attribution gradients, a technique to boost the informativeness of citations by consolidating scent and information prey in place. Its first feature is bringing evidence counts, supporting/contradictory excerpts, links to sources, and contextual explanations into one place. Its second feature is the ability to unravel second-degree citations in place. In a lab study, we demonstrate usage of the full gradient in a critical reading task and its support for deep engagement that increased the depth of what readers took away from the sources versus a standard citation and document QA design.

contents.title: Veriscope: Provenance-Aware Verification of LLM Reasoning Artifacts in Conversational Data Analysis
contents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted by data analysts to perform various analytical tasks within conversational interfaces, owing to their capabilities in code generation and analytical reasoning. Conversational LLMs generate diverse artifacts through multiple reasoning steps and summarize analytical results into insights. Verifying such analysis remains essential yet challenging, as it requires examining both diverse artifacts and the underlying complex reasoning logic, which is not fully addressed by previous work. To facilitate validating LLM-generated results, we present a claim-centered view of analytic provenance and introduce Veriscope, an interactive system that supports fine-grained verification across interconnected artifacts, on-demand tracing of analytic provenance, and modification of analytical results. We formulated our design considerations based on findings derived from a formative study conducted with data analysts (N=6) who have prior experience in verification. We evaluated the effectiveness and usability of our method through a user study (N=18), which demonstrated that Veriscope substantially improves the efficiency of verifying analytical results produced by LLMs. The reliability of LLM-based features was assessed through a technical evaluation.

contents.title: DOBI: Dynamic Opportunistic Body Input via Spare Joint Recruitment for Hands-Free XR
contents.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) systems are often most useful when users are engaged in ongoing physical tasks, yet current interaction techniques still largely assume the hands are available. We present opportunistic body input, an interaction paradigm that redirects continuous XR control to whichever available body region remains free in the moment. To investigate how users naturally coordinate these spare-body movements, we conducted an elicitation study across six hand-busy scenarios. We found that while users' preferred spare body regions shift dynamically based on physical constraints, the resulting spontaneous movements share a consistent, low-dimensional kinematic structure organized around a dominant principal axis. Building on these findings, we present DOBI (Dynamic Opportunistic Body Input), a real-time XR technique that uses gaze to target a UI element, a brief trigger gesture to identify the recruited spare body region, and the region's subsequent motion to drive continuous 1D control. A 1D Fitts' law study establishes the baseline motor performance of this paradigm across four distinct body regions, achieving throughputs up to 2.62 bits/s with an overall 5.0% error rate, and a dual-task usability study shows that DOBI supports reliable, low-effort control (SUS = 84.2) while users remain engaged in realistic hand-busy activities.

contents.title: Reference-Based Manipulation: A Framework and Pipeline for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning
contents.abstract: When manipulating objects in immersive platforms through speech and gesture, users naturally construct spatial references—referring to scene entities, their bodies, or the environment. Leveraging spatial cognition theories, this work systematically examines how users construct and communicate spatial intent. Using a custom toolkit, we conducted a Wizard-of-Oz study to observe unconstrained multimodal (speech + gesture) input patterns in Virtual Reality for scene construction. Based on these findings, we formalize a framework that decomposes spatial references into three core components—Source, Anchor, and Frame—while characterizing their compositional strategies and explicitness. We demonstrate the utility of this Reference-based Manipulation framework by implementing an LLM-based pipeline featuring a set of example interaction techniques with a preliminary technical evaluation. Finally, we discuss key lessons learned for supporting reference-based spatial interaction.

contents.title: Beyond Dense Sensing: Biomechanically-Guided Hand Pose Reconstruction from Reduced Observations
contents.abstract:
Accurate full-hand dynamic capture in XR remains challenging because existing approaches largely depend on dense and layout-specific observations, including optical keypoints and high-density wearable sensing. Although such dense inputs can provide rich motion evidence under favorable conditions, they also introduce important practical limitations. Vision-based tracking becomes unreliable under self-occlusion, tool manipulation, and challenging illumination, while dense gloves increase hardware burden and often require reconstruction models tightly coupled to a specific sensing layout. As a result, existing hand-pose reconstruction pipelines remain strongly dependent on increasingly dense input observations.
In this paper, we present PIRO-Pose, a biomechanically-guided sensing-model co-design framework for full-hand pose reconstruction from sparse wearable measurements. Instead of directly mapping sensor signals to poses, PIRO-Pose first transforms heterogeneous sensing inputs into a canonical anatomy-anchored sparse representation, where sensor reduction is guided by hand kinematic topology and inter-joint dependencies. Based on this structured representation, PIRO-Pose reconstructs dense hand articulation through anatomically structured graph expansion, multi-scale temporal modeling, and kinematic decoding with physiological constraints.
Experiments show that PIRO-Pose achieves accurate real-time reconstruction on our in-house sparse-sensing dataset, remains competitive on a public high-density glove benchmark after compressing the original dense sensor streams into the same reduced interface, and maintains robust continuous tracking under severe visual degradation. Together, these results show that reliable full-hand reconstruction can be achieved not only through dense sensing itself, but also through structured reduction and reconstruction on a normalized sparse observation space.

contents.title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
contents.abstract: In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character’s reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

contents.title: MatComposer: Structural-Semantic Retrieval and Iterative Exploration for Procedural Material Graph Authoring
contents.abstract: Procedural materials are essential for resolution-independent surface appearance design, yet authoring remains expertise-intensive because users must translate high-level visual intent into complex node-based logic. While generative models can automate synthesis, they often produce static rasterized outputs that bypass the structured, editable representations required for professional iteration and asset reuse. We present MatComposer, an interactive system for authoring editable procedural material graphs through retrieval, exploration, and composition. MatComposer introduces a slot-based representation that decomposes material descriptions into functional modules, supported by intent parsing with Large Language Models (LLMs) and a dual-space retrieval pipeline that jointly considers semantic relevance and structural suitability for recomposition. The system enables users to perform slot-wise iterative refinement from intermediate previews and automatically composes selected sub-graphs into functional, editable procedural graphs. A within-subjects user study (N=20) shows that, for non-expert users, MatComposer improves exploration efficiency, follow-up editing efficiency, and perceived editability over baseline retrieval workflows.

contents.title: MorphoChrome: Interactive, Handheld Fabrication of Programmable Structural Color
contents.abstract:
Surfaces that change color with viewing angle—from select butterfly wings and hummingbird feathers to passport holograms—communicate, authenticate, and display information without power or pigment. This is possible through structural color: vivid, view-dependent color produced by nanoscale geometry rather than pigment. However, existing methods for producing structural color are highly complex, lab-bound, and offer no direct user control over color output, color mixing, or angular encoding. We present
MorphoChrome, a novel handheld optical system and workflow for interactive, programmable structural color fabrication. By exposing a holographic photopolymer film to user-controlled wavelengths and angles of coherent light, MorphoChrome directly inscribes the nanostructures required to produce iridescent color. Within the
device, red, green, and blue laser diodes mix via optical beam combining to generate mixed color outputs. The device can be controlled either independently or through a digital twin user interface that provides physics-informed, live iridescent preview, and precise
color selection for RGB color mixing. We evaluate MorphoChrome’s color gamut, color quality, resolution, and sub-second fabrication speed. We introduce a new resin-based adhesion process for integrating holographic films with 2D and 3D objects of diverse material composition (from PLA to fabric), and demonstrate a range of designs produced by our system through applications for colorimetric sensing, security, and biomimetic design.

contents.title: MultiVerse: A Creator-Centered Approach for Authoring Context-Adaptive Lyrics
contents.abstract: Generative AI may enable new forms of context-aware creative expression by dynamically tailoring media content to its consumption context. For instance, AI systems could adapt song lyrics to the listener and their current activity. However, existing media adaptation systems primarily optimize for audience experience, often neglecting artists’ intent, style, and preference. We address this challenge by introducing a novel creator-centered approach to adaptive media authoring and present MultiVerse, a system that instantiates this approach for steering adaptive lyrics. Our approach allows creators to explicitly author controls based on their intent, lyric structure, and audience context, and uses rule-based validations to ensure controls are followed. We conducted a study with 10 songwriters, comparing MultiVerse with a prompting-based workflow for composing adaptive lyrics. The comparison revealed that creators preferred to author how lyrics adapt by explicitly specifying relevant context and adaptation constraints, while recognizing trade-offs in flexibility and iteration speed. Interviews further revealed that creators viewed adaptive media as enabling new forms of audience connection, introducing a distinct creative process, favoring new compositional strategies, and reshaping notions of authorship.

contents.title: Programming by Teaching: Authoring Agent Workflows through Voice Conversation
contents.abstract: Agent workflow automation is increasingly accessible to users without programming experience, but much of the knowledge needed to author workflows is implicit. Programming by Demonstration captures what users do on screen but not the rules behind their actions. We propose Programming by Teaching, where users teach a task to an AI through real-time voice conversation while navigating the application, as they would teach a colleague. The AI listens, takes notes, and generates an agent workflow. We implemented both modes in the same Chrome extension and compared them in a within-subjects study with 28 participants, primarily non-programmers. Teaching passed held-out edge-case tests at 87.2% compared to 46.7% for demonstration (p=.002). Teaching reduced cognitive load (p=.04), scored higher on both pragmatic and hedonic quality (p≤.001), and made it easier to incorporate rules not visible in the UI (p=.003). The hardest part of demonstration was not building the workflow but editing it afterward; teaching sidesteps this by front-loading specification into conversation.

contents.title: PATHWiSE: Empowering Teachers with a Generative AI Authoring System for Personalized Robot-Assisted Learning
contents.abstract: Homework assignments often lack the personalized guidance and social interaction crucial for learning. Social robots offer a promising way to bring personalization and interactive support into learning activities; however, teachers rarely have the technical expertise needed to operate robots, let alone create or customize robot-assisted learning (RAL) lessons. To address this challenge, we introduce 	extit{PATHWiSE}, a robust, no-code authoring system designed to empower teachers to create custom RAL activities. Developed through participatory co-design activities with middle school science teachers and students and iteratively refined through multiple user studies, PATHWiSE enables educators to author, preview, and personalize RAL activities that can be tailored to different robot platforms and delivered with either in-person or on-screen robots. The system maintains a flexible trigger-action programming model to define robot expressions contextually related to lesson materials. Through integrated teacher- and student-facing portals, teachers can deploy RAL lessons using a lightweight and portable browser-based approach that affords integration with a wide range of systems. AI-assisted comment and emotion-expression generation tools augment teacher lesson creation while preserving teacher autonomy and expertise in content design. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of PATHWiSE, including its authoring workflow, interface architecture, backend integration, and representative use cases drawn from iterative studies to illustrate the capabilities of the full system.

contents.title: HALO: Interactive Co-abductive Reasoning in Scientific Hypothesis Generation
contents.abstract: Scientific discovery is essential yet inefficient, primarily because generating hypotheses within a vast search space hinders breakthroughs. While current AI systems assist in generating new hypothesis candidates, they lack interactive support for the reasoning process by which users develop these outputs into promising hypotheses, resulting in surface-level hypotheses. To address this issue, we present a co-abduction, a human-AI collaborative framework for abductive reasoning in scientific hypothesis generation. To operationalize co-abduction, we build HALO, a human–AI collaborative system for molecular hypothesis generation in drug discovery, enabling improved candidate clustering, strategy identification, and multi-strategy synthesis. In expert studies involving 10 medicinal chemists, HALO significantly facilitated abductive reasoning for hypothesis generation—efficient candidate observation, systematic strategy identification, and coherent multi-strategy composition—and enabled participants to produce higher-quality, more diverse candidate molecules.

contents.title: Social.Wiki: A Web Held in Common
contents.abstract:
Many of the websites people depend on have owners whose interests are not fully aligned with their users. We address the root of this problem by presenting a reimagining of the web where sites are not owned at all but are instead collaboratively produced like Wikipedia articles. We call the system Social.Wiki because it supports the co-creation of interactive social sites, such as those for microblogging, messaging, dating, gaming, ride sharing, and so on. With off-the-shelf AI tools, people with little or no programming experience can edit these sites to better reflect the needs and preferences of their communities.

Social.Wiki builds on ideas from collaborative malleable software systems such as Webstrates, but is designed for public participation rather than use only within small, trusted groups. To this end, we present a model of plural governance: rather than replacing the web's ownership with another governance model that may not suit every community, Social.Wiki allows individuals to choose the rules that determine which edits to a site they see. Additionally, we present a granular security model for protecting personal data in a malleable environment.

Complementing the decentralized design and governance of Social.Wiki sites, both site edits and within-site data are stored on Graffiti, a decentralized infrastructure, decoupling the ownership of underlying servers from the ownership of sites.

We evaluate Social.Wiki through case studies that demonstrate the range of sociotechnical structures it supports, as well as through deployments at a hackathon and in the wild.

contents.title: ATOM: Geometry-Aware Microgesture towards Object-Agnostic Tangible Interaction
contents.abstract: This paper presents ATOM, an integrated framework towards agnostic and tangible object interactions with microgestures. Our goal is to support microgesture interactions across different everyday objects, with the capability to automatically leverage the geometric affordance of each object. We formulate a fingertip-aware detection pipeline to leverage generative 2D and 3D models for geometry enhancement and refinement. We then introduce a usability-based method to prioritize the detected elements based on their ergonomic suitability for interactions. Building on this foundation, we further develop an AR system to transform everyday handheld objects into tangible user interfaces with 0D, 1D, and 2D microgesture interactions. Across transitions among everyday cooking objects of varying shapes and sizes, ATOM outperformed ablation baselines in task completion, usability (SUS), and workload (NASA-TLX). A further study with 10 objects demonstrates ATOM’s generalizability across objects and grasps, highlighting its potential towards fluid, object-agnostic tangible interaction in real-world AR scenarios.

contents.title: RingIO: An Eyes-Free Smart Ring with Inputs via Touch and Outputs via Touch
contents.abstract: In many interactive domains, output modalities are added to assist users with their inputs (e.g., gestural animations or vibrations to confirm inputs on touchscreens). While smart rings gained immense popularity for their wearable form factor, their compact size and constrained power budget limit the use of traditional output modalities (e.g., displays or large vibration motors). In this paper, we explore how an extremely low-powered form of haptic feedback—electrotactile stimulation—can be applied to smart rings to enable eyes-free IO. To explore and validate this, we devised a smart ring prototype incorporating an array of double-sided electrodes for collocated capacitive touch input and electrotactile output, enabling a variety of electrotactile animations—given its unique input & output (IO) capabilities, we refer to it as RingIO. In a user study, we found that users recognize ring-based electrotactile animations with up to ~89% accuracy and with average localization errors less than 30 degrees. We demonstrate how haptics can support eyes-free interaction on smart rings in a series of applications.

contents.title: Sonic Stage: Auto-Generating Interactive Spatial Soundscapes to Facilitate Dialogue Video Comprehension for Blind Viewers
contents.abstract: Audio description (AD) makes film and television accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) audiences by narrating characters’ actions. However, in scenes with lots of dialogue, AD often omits important actions because it is constrained not to overlap with speech. It is not yet known how to convey characters’ actions during dialogue. We present Sonic Stage, a system that transforms dialogue videos into interactive spatial soundscapes, enabling BLV audiences to intuitively understand characters’ actions and movements through immersive auditory cues. Sonic Stage conveys essential visual information during dialogue through three auditory techniques: (1) spatialized dialogue to represent spatial layout, (2) diegetic sound to convey character actions, and (3) interactive descriptions to provide context-specific visual details. Evaluation with 12 BLV viewers showed that Sonic Stage significantly improved video comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement. We highlight opportunities for enhancing video accessibility across diverse genres through immersive, interactive audio representations.

contents.title: SHRIMP: Iterative Refinement of Robot Task Plans
contents.abstract: As collaborative robots have entered domains such as manufacturing, agriculture, and healthcare, programming or adapting robot behavior typically requires robotic expertise that most end users lack. Natural language lowers this barrier. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have made it feasible to translate natural language into robot task plans. However, language-based task specification suffers from semantic ambiguity, and generative models lack transparency for how language instructions become robot actions, making it difficult for users to validate the plan before execution. To address these issues, we introduce SHRIMP, a system that allows users to automatically generate a hierarchical robot primitive plan using natural language and iteratively revise their plan through re-prompting and explicit correction. At each revision, SHRIMP allows users to validate their plan in simulation, and once satisfied, execute it on the physical robot. Through a user study involving participants planning tabletop kitchen tasks (n=35), we validate that SHRIMP improves perceived control and enhances robot transparency. System videos and source code are available at https://wisc-hci.github.io/SHRIMP.

contents.title: GuitarFins: Skillful Input Triggering with a Guitar Pick
contents.abstract:
Having a guitar strapped on inevitably restricts physical movement when it comes to using digital interfaces (e.g., via mouse and keyboard) or adjusting equipment settings in between. Furthermore, guitarists typically use a guitar pick, which is often an additional hindrance---the pick often needs to be tucked or put down whenever having to operate an interface, which incurs additional context switching costs. However, we believe that the guitar pick can be turned from a hindrance into an opportunity by utilizing the guitarists' dexterity with a pick for fast and convenient user input.
We introduce GuitarFins---physical input elements, with which the pick becomes the end-effector for physical user input. To test the performance and subjective experience of using guitar-embedded input while holding a pick, we conducted a user study with 16 guitarists for which we augmented two guitars---one with GuitarFins and one with buttons. We found a variety of nuanced differences in terms of performance and individual preferences.

contents.title: Multiverse Architecture for Desired Realities
contents.abstract:
Many previous works that deal with uncertainty, such as touch or text input, resolve imprecise or ambiguous input via probabilistic models, aiming to hide ambiguities or letting users explicitly select from a number of suggestions. In this paper, we introduce a multiverse architecture for Desired Realities, a new type of reality that, instead of hiding ambiguities and uncertainty, makes them a central part of immersive experiences and interactions. Our multiverse architecture is a generalization of conventional universe systems and enables applications to seamlessly split into a multiverse at runtime whenever needed, to later collapse into a universe again. Undesired universes are removed implicitly---users simply interact with their desired universe without resorting to explicit disambiguation.
This tech-concept paper forms the foundation for technical as well as user-centered multiverse research, while inviting readers to rethink conventional (universe) application logic.

contents.title: Treellis: Exposing Editable Assembly Structures for Progressive Human-AI Co-Creation of 3D Models
contents.abstract: Generative AI lowers the barriers to 3D modeling but offers limited control over outcomes. We present Treellis, a human-AI co-creation tool for 3D modeling. Given a text prompt, Treellis produces a 3D object along with a user interface that reveals its component-level assembly structure and in-situ editable parameters. This enables users to inspect and iteratively refine problematic regions of the model at multiple levels of granularity using both AI-assisted operations and direct manual edits, while preserving usable substructures unaffected. Across a between-subject controlled study and a multi-session open-ended study, we found that Treellis helped users develop efficient hybrid strategies between AI and manual to create complex 3D designs. Results also show that exposing AI-generated 3D artifacts as editable assembly structures can support localized repair and reduce refinement friction in human-AI 3D co-creation.

contents.title: Training Under Pressure: Designing and Evaluating a Multi-Stressor VR Environment for Public Speaking Training
contents.abstract: Effective public speaking requires performing under stress, yet prior VR training systems have primarily focused on reducing anxiety rather than building the resilience to withstand it. In this paper, we introduce a multi-stressor VR public speaking training system that combines audience non-verbal behavior, crowd size, and AI-generated contextual Q&A, each designed across manipulable levels of stress. In an exploratory within-subjects study (N=12), we characterize how combined stressor intensity relates to speaking performance and the contribution of individual stressors. Results show that our parameterized stressor design successfully induced distinct anxiety levels, with negative non-verbal animations serving as a stronger source of stress than either crowd size or AI-generated adversarial interruptions. In addition, AI interruptions forced a cognitive context switch during speech, prompting speakers to adopt coping strategies such as adjusting eye gaze and pacing to regain composure. Finally, participants identified the high-stress negative audience condition as the most valuable for training. Together, these findings suggest that rather than minimizing stress, VR systems for public speaking should calibrate challenges to a productive zone and incorporate cognitive scaffolds that help users sustain performance under high-pressure interruptions.

contents.title: SwapSense: Reusable Vision-Based Contact Force Sensing Across Swappable Passive Haptic Modules
contents.abstract:
The haptic qualities of physical interfaces---such as key-click sensations and stylus-tip stiffness---strongly shape user experience beyond functional performance. Prior work has explored reconfigurable passive structures to diversify such haptic experiences, but existing solutions typically sacrifice rich sensing capabilities or require dedicated sensing modules for each configuration.
In this paper, we present SwapSense, a modular vision-based haptic I/O framework that physically decouples a shared sensing module from interchangeable haptic augmentation modules. A camera captures sequential deformation of a shared sensing substrate, and an encoder--decoder network estimates contact forces, while each attached augmentation module independently modulates force--displacement characteristics. Our results show that a model trained for pressing force estimation can generalize across users and support effective adaptation to previously unseen augmentation components. Across leave-one-augmentation-out evaluations, adaptation to unseen target components required at most 25% of target-component data, with fine-tuning completed within 15 minutes. A complementary perceptual study further shows that the five haptic augmentations span a perceptually diverse two-dimensional perceptual space. Together, these results demonstrate that SwapSense enables reusable contact force sensing and perceptually expressive passive haptic reconfiguration within a single framework.

contents.title: Gridlock: Plain Text with Guides
contents.abstract:
Plain text documents are pervasive in software development for code files, documentation, as well as human-readable data serialization formats. They can be diffed, checked in to version control systems, easily searched, and manipulated by countless other tools which understand this universal format. Although unstructured, plain text documents typically conform to a formal syntax, such as in a programming language, or visual conventions, such as the alignment of columns in a table. Maintaining such documents often requires tedious secondary edits to keep the formatting in sync.

We present Gridlock, a text editor with guides, which users manipulate to align, group, or hide parts of their plain text documents. Vertical and horizontal guides in Gridlock form a kind of cellular structure, in which the underlying data is partitioned into semantic fragments while retaining raw text-editing capabilities. Our design adapts familiar notions from spreadsheets---such as rows, columns, and cell resizing and clipping---into a user interface that is fundamentally centered around a plain-text editing experience. We evaluate our design through several small but suggestive examples, involving code, tabular data, and ASCII diagrams.

contents.title: Programmable Machine-Knitted Sensors for Deformable Interfaces
contents.abstract: Knitted textiles are well suited to wearable sensing because they are soft, conform to the body, and remain comfortable during wear. Industrial knitting also allows sensing layouts to be defined digitally. We present a programmable machine-knitted capacitive sensing substrate for wearable deformation sensing. The substrate realizes five functional layers through three physical knitted layers, with conductive yarn stripes and dielectric regions formed directly during knitting. The same sensing structure can be adapted to different wearable forms by modifying the knit pattern, which we demonstrate with elbow and shoulder prototypes. To evaluate how well the fabric captures deformation, we reconstruct the deforming fabric surface from spatial capacitance patterns using synchronized motion capture as supervision. We compare five model families under a six-fold leave-one-session-out protocol, with a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) representing the field-based family. FNO and ConvLSTM achieve the lowest elbow reconstruction errors; on the shoulder, FNO has the lowest fabric-only mean and median error, while ConvLSTM does not improve over the single-frame baselines. These comparisons show that the relative value of spatial, temporal, and auxiliary pose representations depends on the wearable form. Surface reconstruction provides a shared geometric basis for evaluating programmable knitted deformation sensors across body regions.

contents.title: Generative Experiences for Digital Mental Health Interventions: Evidence from a Randomized Study
contents.abstract: Digital mental health (DMH) tools have extensively explored personalization of interventions to users’ needs and contexts. However, this personalization often targets what support is provided, not how it is experienced. Even well-matched content can fail when the interaction format misaligns with how someone can engage. We introduce generative experience as an approach to DMH support, where the intervention experience is composed at runtime. We instantiate this in GUIDE, a system that generates personalized intervention content and multimodal interaction structure through rubric-guided generation of modular components. In a preregistered study with N=237 participants, GUIDE significantly reduced stress (p=.02) and improved user experience (p=.04) compared to an LLM-based cognitive restructuring control. GUIDE also supported diverse forms of reflection and action through varied interaction flows, while revealing tensions around personalization across the interaction sequence. This work lays the foundation for interventions that dynamically shape how support is experienced and enacted in digital settings.

contents.title: MagicPen: Enabling Dynamic Physical Scaffolding through Haptic Feedback for 3D Content Creation in VR with a Variable-length Stylus
contents.abstract: Stylus interaction is widely used for 3D content creation. In VR, it is typically mid-air, offering spatial freedom while lacking the grounded haptic feedback required for both shape perception and active geometric editing. To address this, we present MagicPen, a variable-length stylus that delivers grounded haptic feedback and enables active 3D editing through on-surface interaction. MagicPen operates through dynamic physical scaffolding, an interaction approach that adjusts the length to the interaction context: compliantly rendering geometry the user is actively creating, or resistively rendering predefined virtual geometry as a rigid constraint. We conducted three user studies comparing MagicPen with mid-air interaction in terms of accuracy, task load, and user preference: (1) single-axis positioning for depth precision; (2) freeform 3D planar drawing in compliant mode; and (3) drawing on rendered geometry in rigid mode. Results show MagicPen improves depth positioning. MagicPen better supports 3D content creation by enabling grounded shape perception.

contents.title: TapTwice: Rich Offline Interfaces Between NFC-Enabled Devices
contents.abstract: Applications that rely on the Internet are subject to latency and unstable connectivity. To ensure reliability, applications such as contactless payment are designed to accept offline devices: interfaces are rendered on public terminals, and authorization is completed through simple NFC taps. However, interacting with public devices raises security concerns (i.e. shoulder surfing) and constrains user input. To address these limitations, we present TapTwice, a new interaction technique that relocates the entire process to the user’s smartphone and relies solely on NFC, hence preserving the reliability of offline interaction and providing the ability to render complex interfaces. Users first tap to download an interactive interface via NFC, complete the interaction on their personal device, and then tap again to transmit the results back for finalization. To achieve this design, we modified the NFC software stack on two Google Pixel 6 Pro phones to unlock higher transmission throughput, achieving a link nine times faster than the default. This improvement allows self-contained interfaces to be transferred within seconds. We further demonstrate how leveraging personal smartphones enhances privacy and convenience — for example, by enabling biometric authentication in place of PIN entry and supporting autofill in place of repetitive input across different terminals.

contents.title: InstructMesh: Selective Refinement of Generative 3D Models for Fabrication
contents.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI allow users to create 3D models from text or images. However, these models prioritize visual plausibility over geometric accuracy, often generating results with flaws that compromise their intended use post-fabrication. We present InstructMesh, an interactive post-generation refinement tool that enables selective repair of generative 3D models through region selection and targeted operations, such as opening or sealing voids, or adjusting local thickness. Users can invoke edit operations via natural language prompts or slider controls. By operating directly on the intermediate latent representation, InstructMesh allows users to apply robust geometric corrections without requiring expert modeling skills. To inform our design, we first analyze common fabrication-related failure modes in outputs from state-of-the-art generative tools. We then conduct two user studies, demonstrating that novices can identify and perform fabrication-relevant repairs on generative outputs using InstructMesh, and revealing user preference for hybrid interfaces that combine slider controls with natural language input.

contents.title: CapAura: A Proxemic Interactive Infrastructure on Everyday Furniture through Capacitive Architecture Unit
contents.abstract: We propose CapAura, a proxemic infrastructure that enables users to interact with the living space. We achieve this by deploying a ceiling-to-floor capacitive space and utilizing conductive furniture in between as passive electric-field extenders, transforming surface-limited floor sensing into volumetric, whole-body awareness with zero instrumentation on the user and no modification to the furniture itself. We develop CapAura into a prototype that enables room-scale proxemic sensing across multiple scales, detecting people's Position, Identity, Movement, and Orientation—without cameras or worn devices. From a sparse 3×5 capacitive grid, our prototype achieves 29.7 cm MPJPE (Mean Per Joint Position Error) across 32 body joints, 99.61% within-session user-identity recognition, 66.1% activity recognition, and 73.61% hand-orientation recognition. Beyond passive sensing, our user study (N=16) shows that furniture proximity and touch can serve as ambient interaction triggers—perceived as functionally effective (M=4.44, p=.002) and novel and exciting (M=4.79, p<.001)—turning the living space into a spatial interface that reaches beyond the user to their immediate, touchable surroundings.

contents.title: Integrating Visual and Acoustic Modalities for Near-Eye Gaze Tracking
contents.abstract: Near-eye gaze tracking underpins gaze-based interaction on head-mounted displays, yet the dominant vision-based approach incurs substantial power consumption and computational overhead. Acoustic sensing has recently emerged as a low-power, high-rate alternative, but lacks user-friendly calibration and loses accuracy after device slippage and re-wearing. To address these complementary limitations, we present a dual-modal gaze tracking system that integrates an acoustic module and a visual module on a single eyewear platform. Visual predictions implicitly calibrate and continuously correct the acoustic modality through a state-machine-based coordination strategy, eliminating dedicated acoustic calibration and providing system-level robustness to device slippage and re-wearing. An error-state Kalman filter fuses the two asynchronous modalities to produce the final gaze estimate. When the visual modality operates at 1 Hz, the fused system achieves 1.40° within-session and 2.13° across re-wearing sessions at 83 Hz output rate, close to the sparse visual baseline. When needed, the system allows the visual modality to operate at up to 30 Hz and the acoustic modality at up to 750 Hz, contributing to improvements in overall accuracy and output frame rate.

contents.title: Attune: A Self-Annotation Tool for Understanding Robot Operator Attention Profiles
contents.abstract: Deploying robot fleets in complex, real-world environments requires human operators to supervise multiple robots simultaneously. Managing operator attention is a fundamental challenge of designing multi-robot supervision interfaces, encompassing both feed layout and feed content (i.e., robot behavior design). Thus far, designers lack empirical guidance on the latter—how to change a robot’s behavior to capture, sustain, or relinquish operator attention during multi-robot supervision. In our vision of the future, designers should be able to use this guidance to calibrate robot behavior to different operator attention profiles. Treating operator eye gaze as a robot behavior design clue, we created a pre-deployment elicitation tool called Attune. Attune automatically identifies when meaningful gaze shifts occur, provides AI assistance for annotating why shifts occurred, and outputs a summary of operator gaze patterns for operator review. We evaluated Attune through a user study in which participants annotated the visual triggers that drew their attention. Our findings unveil variation in observed gaze patterns and reveal how Attune helps characterize operator attention.

contents.title: WhatIf: Interactive Exploration of Large-Scale LLM Agent Simulations for Policy Reasoning
contents.abstract: Policymakers in domains such as emergency management, public health, and urban planning must make decisions under deep uncertainty, where outcomes depend on how large populations interpret information, coordinate, and adopt over time. Existing tools only partially support this process: tabletop exercises enable collaborative discussion but lack dynamic feedback, while computational simulations capture population dynamics but are designed for offline analysis. We present WhatIf, an interactive system that enables policymakers to steer, inspect, and compare LLM-powered social simulations in real time. Informed by a formative study in emergency preparedness planning, we derive four design requirements for interactive policy simulations: fluid steering, real-time scale, collaborative exploration, and multi-level interpretability. We developed WhatIf guided by these requirements and evaluated it with five preparedness professionals across three disaster evacuation scenarios. Our findings show that participants used the system as a space for iterative branching and comparison rather than evaluating fixed plans; reflected on tacit planning assumptions when agent behavior violated expectations; surfaced previously unrecognized planning vulnerabilities; and grounded their reasoning in inspectable agent-level cases rather than aggregate outputs alone. These findings suggest broader design implications for LLM-powered social simulation systems: designing such systems as interactive, shared reasoning environments—rather than offline predictive tools—can better support expert decision-making under deep uncertainty.

contents.title: ProConte: Supporting Progressive Authoring of Anime Storyboards through Partial and Exceptional Representations
contents.abstract:
Creative practice is rarely fully formal. Even in highly structured production settings, professionals routinely rely on incomplete entries, deferred decisions, and exceptions to standard formats in order to think, explore, and communicate. In storyboard authoring, such deviations are not edge cases but part of the work itself.

We present ProConte, a user interface for Japanese animation (anime) storyboarding that accommodates partialness and exceptions through a malleable substrate and a set of coordinated interfaces. Developed in close collaboration with a professional anime director, ProConte supports unspecified timings, exceptionally sized frames for expressive camera work, and unordered free-canvas frames for tentative externalization.

The director used ProConte to author the complete storyboard for a 25-minute television anime episode, and we conducted six two-hour lecture sessions in which he created storyboards while explaining his process aloud. Together, the episode production and lecture sessions provided complementary qualitative evidence: the former situated ProConte in real-world production, while the latter made the director’s authoring process more inspectable. These materials showed that, in this case, our design supported progressive authoring in practice: ideas could be externalized before they were fully specified, revisited later, and developed across multiple semantically distinct stages without premature commitment to a formal structure.

contents.title: Generating Personalized Games with Sensing Data to Support Self-Reported Data Collection
contents.abstract: Collecting in-situ behavioral data to support research studies often involves prompting repeated ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) on smartphones and wearables. Sustained engagement, however, remains a major challenge because study participants often experience survey fatigue and declining motivation over time. To address this challenge, we introduce Personalized Adaptive Games for Engagement (PAGE): a novel LLM-powered approach that integrates data collection with a personalized game experience. PAGE uses a participant's previously collected data to dynamically generate personalized puzzles, embedding behavioral data collection within engaging gameplay. We deployed a prototype using a variant of a word wheel puzzle game in a two-week feasibility study (N=15); while participants responded to EMAs in both weeks of the study, they also received sensor-based personalized puzzles in one of those weeks. We found that most participants (80%) preferred the week with personalized puzzles. Participants also contributed richer EMA data (72 additional unique contextual tags) and 1,188 additional uncompensated responses via a feasible in-game data collection channel during the puzzle week. We discuss design guidelines for developing context-aware personalized games to support engagement, potentially for use in longitudinal studies.

contents.title: Sighted by Default: Addressing Implicit Vision Assumptions in Real-Time VLM Assistance for BLV Users
contents.abstract: Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based assistance is reshaping independence for blind and low-vision (BLV) users, yet current tools fail in dynamic settings. While request-response architectures like BeMyAI impose prohibitive latencies, our formative study (N = 15) reveals that even real-time alternatives like Doubao fail due to a deeper structural problem: sighted-default bias—the implicit assumption that users possess parallel visual access to their surroundings. This bias manifests as verbose, vision-centric narratives that overlook the serial nature of auditory perception, flooding the user's limited cognitive bandwidth with information that is neither timely nor actionable. To address this, we derive three design principles: Continuity, Conciseness, and Calibrated Honesty. We present VIA-Agent, which co-optimizes a specialized cognitive core with a low-latency Real-Time Communication (RTC) architecture for continuous bidirectional streaming. In a within-subjects evaluation (N = 9), VIA-Agent matched Doubao's success rate, significantly reducing mean task time by 21.4% (91.7s vs. 116.7s) and conversational turns from 5.9 to 4.3 while achieving higher trust.

contents.title: StitchSwitch: Programmable Surface Deformation and Bistability in Embroidered Textiles
contents.abstract:
Programming 3D surface deformation has been widely explored in rigid and semi-rigid materials, but achieving predictable shape change in wearable textiles remains challenging. We present StitchSwitch, a computational design and fabrication system for programming surface deformation and bistability into embroidered textiles through a continuous parametric tessellation design space. Embroidering triangle-tessellated patches onto pre-stretched elastic fabric encodes out-of-plane deformation and passive bistability directly into the textile.
 
We characterize how patch diameter and embroidery fill percentage govern deformation, revealing varied deformation outcomes and a saturation regime where increasing density shifts deformation from vertical height to lateral distribution. We develop a reduced-space simulation model predicting this relationship in real time, integrated into a garment-scale design tool supporting live 3D preview, inverse design, and fabrication-aware export.
 
We demonstrate StitchSwitch through two garment-integrated applications, a tactile garment interface and a deformation-based storage pocket, showing how programmable bistable deformation enables functional structures directly within textiles.

contents.title: ElectroPad: Extending Gamepad Haptics for Hand Movements in Video Games with Electrotactile Feedback
contents.abstract: Gamepads are among the most widely used haptic devices, yet their haptic feedback remains limited in supporting hand-movement scenarios in video games that require precise tactile sensations at specific hand locations. Electrotactile feedback offers a promising alternative, providing high-resolution, precisely mapped stimulation that can be seamlessly integrated onto controller surfaces. We present ElectroPad, an electrotactile gamepad cover embedding 190 electrodes per handle, delivering rich texture and shape feedback to hand regions in contact with virtual objects. Two user studies demonstrate that our system reliably conveys tactile cues, achieving mid-to-high levels of realism, while significantly enhancing enjoyment and immersion compared to visual-only conditions. Participants also expressed strong willingness to adopt the system and offered concrete suggestions for refinement. These findings highlight electrotactile stimulation as a powerful complement to gamepad haptics, expanding the design space for game interactions and enabling more expressive user experiences.

contents.title: AquaWeave: Weaving Liquid-Activated Morphing Bio-Textiles
contents.abstract: In Human–Computer Interaction (HCI), weaving has been used to fabricate soft, interactive interfaces through complex structures and functional wefts. Recent work introduces biomaterials with dynamic behaviors into weaving. AquaWeave systematically investigates and compares how weave parameters mediate liquid-activated morphing behaviors across multiple bioyarn systems. We contribute fabrication and characterization of morphing bioyarns-- alginate, chitosan, gelatin--that enable swelling and dissolving properties, and a design menu of weaving structures to investigate how float length, weft density, yarn placement, and compound structures mediate and control these transformations. Through a workshop study, we capture textile practitioners’ perspectives on designing with morphing bio-textiles, highlighting the role of sampling in conveying material behavior and the importance of tactile engagement in shaping design decisions. Our findings show how weaving can shift material transformation from a failure mode to programmable deformation, while designing with morphing bio-textiles relies on embodied interaction with materials, where making, activation, and evaluation are closely intertwined.

contents.title: Do Simulated Users Steer Like Humans? A Biomechanical Reinforcement Learning Testbed for Systematic Steering Law Evaluation
contents.abstract: In interface research, obtaining human performance data remains a persistent bottleneck, which simulated users promise to break. While biomechanical simulation has made significant progress for discrete target acquisition, continuous steering represents a fundamentally harder problem: every UI path geometry imposes different kinematic demands. We present a computational testbed that generates steering trajectories across arbitrary UI paths using a muscle-actuated upper-limb model driven by reinforcement learning, without human reference data and without path-specific redesign. Instantiated across six geometries and six Steering Law formulations, the testbed enables a systematic evaluation of steering performance not just in terms of time, but behavior. Our simulated users adhere to most Steering Law formulations for curved and narrowing path geometries, while L-shaped paths yield weaker fits. A targeted user study (N=12) shows that simulated and human trajectories match in shape on linear, narrowing, circular, and spiral paths, but diverge on L-shaped and sinusoidal paths. These findings establish biomechanical simulation as a robust computational instrument to study HCI tasks beyond discrete target selections, surfacing conditions that most warrant human investigation.

contents.title: TherMosaic: Accelerating Perceived Thermal Transitions Through Spatiotemporal Thermal Feedback
contents.abstract: Thermal feedback can enrich immersive interaction, but thermoelectric devices often change temperature too slowly to match interactive timing. We present TherMosaic, a spatiotemporal thermal feedback approach that accelerates perceived temperature transitions by leveraging two perceptual mechanisms: spatial summation and thermal adaptation. Focusing on the fingertip, we first investigate this approach using a custom 2x2 array of independently controlled Peltier modules. Across three controlled perceptual studies, we show that distributed thermal stimulation can preserve stable hot and cold percepts despite local deviations, that adaptation helps maintain these percepts during changing stimulation, and that combining these effects reduces perceived transition time by about 30%-40% for transitions originating from hot or cold states.  We then translate the same design principles into a standalone wearable implementation of TherMosaic and evaluate it in virtual reality. Our results show that this approach reduces perceived thermal lag and improves temporal alignment between thermal and visual events in interactive use.

contents.title: Present Drawing: Exploring Avatar-Mediated Drawing Events with Physical Traces
contents.abstract: We introduce Present Drawing, an approach for staging an avatar-mediated drawing event that leaves physical traces in the real world. Present Drawing aims to reconfigure conventional drawing events by relaxing their physical constraints. We describe an organizer-oriented design space for such an event along four elements: Time, Site, Control Source, and Avatar Embodiment. To ground this concept, we developed a proof-of-concept prototype in which an observer wears a head-mounted display to view an avatar. The avatar's motion is synchronized with a customized pen plotter whose mechanical parts are hidden from the observer. We also developed five application examples spanning live, playback, multi-site, mascot, and system-controlled configurations. We conducted an initial evaluation of one representative playback autograph configuration, showing the basic plausibility of the core Present Drawing experience as an avatar-mediated drawing event and highlighting factors associated with perceiving the avatar as the drawer.

contents.title: AdaptaFace: Adversarial Assistance for Inclusive Facial Gesture Interaction
contents.abstract: Facial gestures can enable access for people with motor impairments (PwM), yet recognizers may not reliably interpret individual facial movement patterns. Existing approaches either constrain agency by requiring predefined templates or impose repeated calibration, data collection, and computation through user-specific retraining. We present AdaptaFace, an input-level compatibility layer using bounded, proxy-dependent adversarial perturbations to translate user-compatible gestures into inputs for an unchanged facial action unit (AU)-based recognizer. Designed around six personalization principles informed by interviews with 12 PwM, AdaptaFace supports both recognition enhancement and gesture vocabulary extension. In a within-subject study with 16 participants, AdaptaFace increased task completion from 59.7% to 90.5% and reduced workload from 5.61 to 4.21. Offline validation showed strong steering with aligned perturbation generation and evaluation but weaker cross-recognizer transfer, defining the approach’s boundary. These findings frame adversarial assistance as input-side accessibility mediation for personalized facial-gesture interaction.

contents.title: Projective Walls, Floors, and Windows: Aligned Plane Interactions for Interior Architectural Design in VR
contents.abstract: In interior architecture, fundamental elements, such as walls, floors, and windows, profoundly shape the spatial experience through their dimensions and arrangement. In this study, we present a novel VR interaction technique that allows interior architectural designers to experience a space at full scale while precisely creating these elements. Our technique achieves this by projectively aligning an on-demand, virtual handheld plane with remote surfaces. By first analyzing a renowned architectural textbook, we found that all fundamental interior elements can be created through a unified three-step procedure of  defining a plane, sketching a profile, and extruding a volume. Through physical prototyping, we then established that a single virtual handheld plane can seamlessly integrate all three steps into a continuous workflow. Finally, we implemented this concept as a set of VR interactions and reproduced three iconic interior spaces that collectively encompass all 13 fundamental element types. These reproductions demonstrate that our concise interaction technique is sufficiently expressive to construct complex, real-world interior spaces.

contents.title: PersonaTeaming: Supporting Persona-Driven Red-Teaming for Generative AI
contents.abstract: Recent developments in AI safety research have called for red-teaming methods---the practice of probing an AI system with adversarial inputs in order to surface harmful, biased, or otherwise problematic behaviors before deployment---that effectively surface potential risks posed by generative AI models, with growing emphasis on how red-teamers' backgrounds and perspectives shape their strategies and the risks they uncover. While automated red-teaming approaches promise to complement human red-teaming through larger-scale exploration, existing automated approaches do not account for human identities and rarely incorporate human inputs. In this work, we explore persona-driven red-teaming to advance both automated red-teaming and human-AI collaboration. We first develop PersonaTeaming, which incorporates personas into the adversarial prompt generation process to explore a wider spectrum of adversarial strategies. Compared to RainbowPlus, a state-of-the-art automated red-teaming method, PersonaTeaming achieves higher attack success rates while maintaining prompt diversity. However, since automated personas only approximate real human perspectives, we further instantiate PersonaTeaming as PersonaTeaming Playground, a user-facing interface that enables red-teamers to author their own personas and collaborate with AI to mutate and refine prompts. In a user study with 11 industry practitioners, we found that PersonaTeaming Playground enabled diverse red-teaming strategies and outputs that practitioners perceived as useful, and that AI-generated suggestions in the PersonaTeaming Playground encouraged out-of-the-box thinking even when practitioners did not follow them strictly. Together, our work advances both automated and human-in-the-loop approaches to red-teaming, while shedding light on interaction patterns and design insights for supporting human-AI collaboration in generative AI red-teaming.

contents.title: Dramarrator: Object-Based Audio Editing for Audio Drama Production from Books
contents.abstract: Audio dramas weave dialogue, sound effects, and music into immersive stories. Creators often adapt books into audio dramas, but this process remains labor-intensive, requiring them to interpret source material, author scripts, generate audio assets, and assemble them on a timeline. Because story elements like characters and scenes manifest across many interdependent assets, a single change can ripple into manual updates across the entire project. We present Dramarrator, an audio drama authoring tool built around object-based audio editing, where these story elements are represented as editable objects. Dramarrator extracts these objects from a book, generates linked audio assets (speech, sound effects, and music), and composes a multi-track audio drama. Edits to any object (e.g., a character’s voice) automatically propagate to all dependent assets. In a user study with professionals (N=8), Dramarrator significantly lowered task load when creating audio dramas. A listener study (N=300) shows that creator-refined output from Dramarrator approaches the quality of productions made with existing professional tools, and an exploratory study (N=3) suggests object-based editing lowers entry barriers and generalizes beyond audio dramas.

contents.title: MUSE: An Interactive Meta-Agent for Understanding and Steering LLM-powered Data Science Systems
contents.abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled a new class of agentic data science systems that allow users to complete complex data science workflows through natural language. Although these systems can significantly reduce manual effort, it remains difficult to diagnose their behavior and steer the reasoning process when failures or unexpected outputs occur. We present MUSE, an interactive meta-agent that enhances user understanding and control of agentic data science systems by (1) dynamically restructuring low-level execution traces into multiple semantic levels that support navigation from high-level overviews to low-level implementation details; (2) enabling users to reference specific workflow steps in context to ask grounded questions, provide feedback, and revise problematic steps without manually locating relevant execution history; and (3) supporting mixed-initiative steering by surfacing suspicious steps for inspection, scaffolding the repair process, and translating user repair intent into contextualized instructions for the underlying agent. In a between-subjects study (n=15), MUSE improved task efficiency and increased users' confidence in understanding and steering agentic data science workflows.

contents.title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
contents.abstract: Great fiction earns its verisimilitude through precise details, from how a longsword is gripped to pierce armor gaps to why a bleeding corpse cannot yet smell of decay, weaving domain expertise into the fabric of invented worlds. Current AI writing tools offer limited support for discovering and integrating unfamiliar domain knowledge into narrative. They require explicit queries that authors cannot formulate, generate finished prose that risks homogenizing voice, or assist only within the boundaries of what authors already know. We argue that AI should reveal latent knowledge gaps to writers while preserving their agency to transform discovered knowledge into authentic prose. Grounded in formative interviews with 9 fiction writers, we present VeriForge, a mixed-initiative writing system that divides cognitive labor so that the system assumes initiative over domain discovery while the author retains full initiative over narrative synthesis. VeriForge realizes this through three complementary mechanisms. Proactive inline highlighting flags potential knowledge gaps as authors draft. Dual-stream querying pairs conversational responses with source-anchored Knowledge Cards for direct fact extraction. A spatial Knowledge Canvas allows authors to organize and connect discovered knowledge across their writing. These mechanisms are powered by a graph-based retrieval-augmented generation pipeline grounded in domain-specific source materials. A within-subjects user study (N=12) provides preliminary evidence that this paradigm helps authors recognize previously overlooked knowledge gaps, supports creative exploration, and is perceived by expert raters to produce passages with stronger domain grounding in a controlled cold-start writing task.
