contents.title: Co-opting Mobile Device Cellular RF Front Ends for HCI Sensing
contents.abstract: Modern smartphones contain sophisticated cellular modems that can tune their antennas. We show how this latent internal capability, intended to minimize power consumption while maximizing antenna performance, can be co-opted as a sensing capability in already ubiquitous mobile devices. For example, we can sense electromagnetic loading from a user’s hand, surrounding objects, and nearby materials, enabling diverse applications such as detecting grip pose, worn device placement, and passive interactive widgets. As a proof of concept, we selected five example use cases from the HCI literature, created with different and specialized sensors, and re-implemented them with a commercial off-the-shelf smartphone. We use these examples to evaluate sensing performance, comparing to prior work, the results of which underscore the promise and generalizability of smartphone RF hardware as a future sensing modality.

contents.title: Boosting WiFi-based Gesture Recognition via High-fidelity and Behaviorally Diverse Data Synthesis
contents.abstract: Artificial-intelligence–driven WiFi-based human gesture recognition (HGR) critically depends on high-quality, well-labeled real-world datasets. However, collecting real WiFi data is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Data augmentation (DA) has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance the value of limited real data and improve system generalization. Existing wireless DA methods, however, either cannot generate samples for new gesture classes or fail to capture behavioral diversity sufficiently, fundamentally limiting their scalability to new sensing tasks and augmentation effectiveness. In this work, we propose SynthFi, a novel DA framework capable of synthesizing high-fidelity and diverse WiFi data, even for unseen classes with very few real samples. SynthFi incorporates two key components: a diversity-inducing factor quantification method that extracts rich behavioral variation cues from limited data, and a diffusion-based generative model that produces realistic samples conditioned on diverse behavioral features. Extensive real-world experiments show that SynthFi can improve recognition accuracy by 40% through DA, even when only two real samples of unseen classes are available, outperforming existing solutions.

contents.title: AreaCode: Encoding Conductive Tags through Coverage Modulation for Inductive Sensing
contents.abstract: Contact-based object recognition enables interactive systems to infer how users engage with physical objects. However, existing inductive sensing approaches are limited to conductive materials or rely on geometric tag patterns that require sensor arrays, restricting their use on small or irregular objects. We present AreaCode, a method that expands the design space of conductive tags by encoding identity through conductive coverage within the sensing region. This approach enables tags with identical shapes and materials to produce distinct and reliable signatures, even when sensed using a single inductive coil. Through a series of experiments, we characterize material choices, pattern designs, and encoding capacity, demonstrating up to 17 distinguishable tag levels with high recognition accuracy. We further demonstrate applications on everyday objects and surfaces, including small items that cannot accommodate conventional sensor grids. Our results highlight how modulating conductive coverage enables expressive, passive tagging and extends inductive sensing to a broader range of interactive scenarios.

contents.title: FlexiFab: Laser-Cutting Volumetric Compliant Structures with Tunable-Stiffness
contents.abstract: Laser cutting is a powerful fabrication tool for rapidly creating 3D objects from 2D sheet materials. While most research has focused on making these constructions robust and rigid, we expand this area by introducing robust yet compliant laser-cut structures. We present FlexiFab, a method for fabricating load-bearing volumetric objects with tunable stiffness. The core of our approach is to utilize planar lattice structures for programmable compliance, integrated into a robust framework via an orthogonal interlocking assembly. By interlocking these elements, the planar sheets provide mutual lateral support that prevents out-of-plane buckling and structural failure. We also incorporate standard threaded nuts into the assembly, which not only provide structural reinforcement but also allow users to customize local or global stiffness post-fabrication. We demonstrate these benefits through applications such as an adjustable bike seat and provide a parametric design tool to facilitate the end-to-end design process.

contents.title: Camera-Free Object Discovery and Interaction with GazeTags
contents.abstract: We present GazeTags, a camera- and computer-vision-free approach for worn head-gaze object awareness. Our small electronic tags cost roughly $2 each and can operate for more than a year on a coin cell battery. They work in concert with a user-worn device (smartglasses, hearables, etc.) that periodically emits a focused infrared signal aligned with the user’s head direction. Only GazeTags within that narrow head-oriented beam wake and respond, providing their identity and optional payloads such as object state or live sensor readings. By avoiding cameras and computer vision pipelines, our approach is very energy efficient, able to operate continuously even in battery-constrained wearables, and sidesteps non-trivial privacy issues. We describe our hardware design, characterize our system performance and operating tradeoffs, and demonstrate how GazeTags can enable practical gaze-aware environments.

contents.title: LandmarkLens: Predicting and Presenting Effective Landmarks for Mixed-Reality Urban Exploration
contents.abstract:
People with a poor sense of direction (SOD) struggle to build cognitive maps for effective spatial navigation, and existing navigation tools prioritize efficiency over spatial learning. 
We present LandmarkLens, a mixed-reality navigation system that highlights landmarks informed by empirical navigation strategies of skilled navigators, layered on top of turn-by-turn directions.To inform LandmarkLens, we conducted a landmark attention study with 20 participants (ten good SOD, ten poor SOD) who navigated across four Tokyo neighborhoods in virtual reality (VR). We found systematic group differences in where they look, what they verbally identify as navigation cues, and what types of landmarks they consider effective. We then used these formative study insights to instruct a vision-language model (VLM) to identify navigation-relevant landmarks in LandmarkLens and conducted a follow-up study with eight poor-SOD participants against a turn-by-turn baseline. Participants showed improved performance in scene recognition, suggesting that guided landmark attention can support landmark-level spatial knowledge acquisition for people with poor SOD, a first step toward broader spatial learning.

contents.title: Surprise2Refine: Axis-Centered Exploration-To-Refinement for Agent-Assisted Creative Scaffolding
contents.abstract: Designers require different design spaces across creative stages: broad during exploration, and targeted during refinement. Yet existing agent-driven tools assume a fixed or continuously expanding space, leaving designers to manage and navigate it themselves. Informed by a formative study with five designers, we propose an axis-centered workflow that adaptively broadens and narrows the design space to support structured exploration and refinement. We implemented this workflow in Surprise2Refine, a prototype that allows users to build and reshape an 𝑛×𝑛 design space through a set of axis-centered interactions as their creative intent evolves. A within-subjects study with 14 designers shows that Surprise2Refine enhances users’ sense of control, supports tracking of scaffolding paths, and improves the perceived creativity of design outcomes. We further distill design insights to guide future agent-assisted tools for creative scaffolding.

contents.title: Reperceiving Everyday Sounds with Hidden Texture
contents.abstract: Ubiquitous hearable devices often prioritize digital immersion by suppressing real-world sounds, distancing users from their physical surroundings. Conversely, noticing rich acoustic details in everyday sounds brings benefits such as supporting mindfulness and fostering musical appreciation. We explore how hearables can scaffold users to hear “more” of their everyday soundscapes. We present a wearable system that identifies hidden textures in everyday sounds, specifically overtones that shape timbre but are often perceptually hidden. Grounded in prior literature in auditory cueing, the system amplifies these overlooked textures in real time to produce a short-term attentional shift, enabling users to continue noticing these details after device use. We evaluated the system through two studies. A psychoacoustic study (n = 32) showed that the overtone textures detected by our system could be effectively cued. Across 10 sounds, participants showed a 13% improvement in detecting the overtone texture immediately after one-time cueing. These results were further validated by an in-lab user study (n = 12), where participants wore the system while interacting with everyday objects. In 69% of trials, participants reported that cued texture became more perceptually salient after using the device than before. Qualitative accounts further suggested that the device use can encourage participants to form new mental associations with familiar sounds.

contents.title: MetaCanvas: A Toolkit for Prototyping Tessellation-Based Shape-Changing Structures by Cut-and-Configure Authoring
contents.abstract: Origami tessellation offers a promising substrate for shape-changing interfaces, yet prototyping such structures remains labor-intensive: users often need to assemble modular parts or rebuild structures to explore alternative forms and motions. This limits rapid iteration, especially when motion behavior needs to be revised after fabrication. We present MetaCanvas, a prototyping toolkit that supports the design of tessellation-based shape-changing structures through a reusable active canvas and a cut-and-configure workflow. The toolkit combines a pre-fabricated tessellation substrate with embedded actuation, a digital interface for specifying cut patterns and motion regions, and a tangible controller for adjusting actuation parameters without re-fabrication. This workflow enables users to customize shape and iteratively tune motion on the same canvas. We evaluate MetaCanvas through technical characterization, five demonstration artifacts, and a design study with 12 participants. The results show that MetaCanvas supports rapid customization of tessellation structures, localized motion design, and post-fabrication exploration of shape-changing behaviors. Based on these findings, we discuss how reusable and reconfigurable substrates can broaden the design space of shape-changing interface prototyping.

contents.title: ArtScape: Detecting, Characterizing, and Interactively Exploring Urban Art at Scale Using Vision Language Models
contents.abstract: Urban art brings cultural expression, community identity, and aesthetic enrichment to cities. Currently, there are no systematic ways of exploring urban art at scale. We introduce ArtScape, a VLM-based interactive tool that lets users view, search, filter, and tour four categories of art (murals, mosaics, sculptures, graffiti). To comprehensively and automatically detect urban artwork throughout a region, we designed a custom five-stage pipeline that uses VLMs to detect and describe urban artwork within 360° panoramic Street View images, achieving a micro-F1 of 0.83 on an urban art dataset we labeled. ArtScape categorizes, describes, and scores the reachability and interestingness of each artwork while deduplicating based on proximity and similarity. We evaluated this tool with 12 participants spanning urban planners, artists, sighted users, and blind and low vision users. Our findings show that ArtScape’s at-scale AI artwork curation enables granular and aggregate urban art discovery, thereby helping people learn about their communities and city-wide trends, motivating in-person urban exploration, and expanding perceptions of what constitutes urban art.

contents.title: Electrotactile Improves Thermal Referral
contents.abstract: Thermal referral enables thermal sensations in locations lacking thermal actuators—this is achieved using vibrotactile actuators to redirect a nearby thermal sensation to where a tactile sensation is applied. However, we found that its reliance on vibration introduces critical limitations: it struggles to produce cold referral, and the inherent strong tactile “buzz” makes it unsuitable for simulating non-contact thermal events, such as the chill of an open freezer in VR (in contrast to contact-based thermal events like touching the freezer’s cold handle). To improve this, we propose a shift from vibrotactile to electrotactile-based thermal referral. We evaluated in two user studies—a psychophysics experiment (N=22) and a VR deployment (N=20)—where we contrasted electrotactile with vibrotactile-based thermal referral. Our results reveal key advantages of the electrotactile-based thermal referral: (1) increases the referral rate for cold sensations; (2) increases thermal perception while minimizing tactile; and (3) improves realism across a range of VR thermal scenarios, specifically distinguishing between contactbased and non-contact thermal events. Finally, we provide design guidelines for choosing tactile cues to create immersive multi-modal thermal experiences in VR.

contents.title: Granular I/O: Enabling Bi-directional Malleable Interaction for Actuated TUIs with Magnetic Particles
contents.abstract: Granular materials — clusters of small discrete particles — afford a uniquely malleable form of physical interaction, enabling intuitive shaping, splitting, and merging through natural hand gestures. Despite their rich interaction potential, granular materials remain largely unexplored as a form factor for actuated, bi-directional Tangible User Interfaces (TUIs). We present Granular I/O, an approach that employs millimeter-scale passive magnetic particle clusters, actuated by external magnetic field controllers, to enable malleable input and output interactions for granular-based actuated TUIs. We describe a comprehensive design space for malleable granular interaction, alongside a full hardware and software implementation covering particle cluster fabrication, two actuation platforms, and authoring software. We further report technical characterization and evaluation to validate the system, and demonstrate a range of applications that harness malleable I/O for interactive use.

contents.title: SketchAloud: Combining Time-Aligned Sketch & Speech for Multimodal Specification of 3D Designs
contents.abstract: Sketching enables users to quickly express visual ideas. Describing what they are trying to sketch can give generative models additional context for interpreting user intent, but understanding how to combine the sketch and speech data effectively is challenging, particularly when user intent depends on temporal context and deictic references (e.g., "this pillar"). We present SketchAloud, a technique that captures this temporal context by constructing a mapping between speech segments and sketch strokes. We evaluate SketchAloud through two user studies. A controlled experiment (N=12) examines user interaction, showing that sketch with speech is easier to use and more effective at capturing user intent compared to either modality alone. A follow-up study (N=700) involving over 35,000 pairwise comparisons assesses output quality, demonstrating that while sketch and speech each offer distinct strengths for specifying structure and semantics, their combination improves both output quality and consistency by reducing failure cases.

contents.title: Data-Oriented Debugging Across Place and Time
contents.abstract: Programmers routinely instrument and run their code with tools such as print statements or breakpoints in order to understand how their programs behave at runtime. When multiple tools are available to programmers, how should we think about their strengths and weaknesses? In this paper, we provide one lens for comparison called data-oriented debugging. In this lens, a programmer has data needs and expresses them as queries to their debugging tools. Queries reach into clusters of program data organized by place and time. Tools differ in which of these queries they make easy. We develop this lens through formative interviews with professional programmers, a comparative tool-use study, and an analysis of existing debugging tools. We offer the lens as a reflective aid for tool designers and researchers to assess the capabilities of a debugging tool of interest.

contents.title: Bifur-circuits: Interactive and Modular Metamaterial Building Blocks Via Bifurcated Geometries
contents.abstract:
Mechanical metamaterials have gained traction in the HCI community for enabling interactive applications, including shape-changing displays and novel sensing paradigms. However, these structures typically support a limited set of stable geometric configurations, constraining the range of geometric expressions they can support through modularity. To overcome this constraint, we present Bifur-circuits, a mechanically and electrically modular, fully 3D metamaterial assembly toolkit. Bifur-circuits enables interactive geometries capable of exhibiting an exponentially increasing number of configurations as a function of units in an assembly. It accomplishes this through two layers of mechanical reconfiguration: at the assembly level, where modules can be added or removed, and at the configuration level via mechanical bifurcation, where structures split into new stable configurations upon reaching a critical geometric threshold. All units are internally routed such that electrical modularity produces a valid and unique circuit per configuration. 

We contribute a Fusion 360-based construction tool, a Java-C++ simulation tool for real-time shape recognition, and a multi-material 3D printing fabrication pipeline. Our technical evaluation shows that Bifur-circuits maintain electrical connectivity after 10k cyclic compressions, and that shape recognition latency scales linearly with unit count (20 units maps to a 5-second detection time). Finally, we contribute two applications demonstrating Bifur-circuits' potential, across scales, for reconfigurable spatial environments and adaptive tangible user interfaces.

contents.title: A Benchmarking Framework for Context-aware XR Interfaces
contents.abstract: Everyday Extended Reality (XR) systems aim to provide context-aware access to the right functionalities at the right time and place, with minimal manual reconfiguration as users switch context. Yet these interfaces are hard to evaluate: current prototyping and user-study workflows offer no systematic, repeatable way to compare adaptation methods across users and scenarios. We present ContextXR, a novel benchmarking framework for context-aware XR interfaces. ContextXR represents an XR application as a connected graph of functional facets, each a semantically coherent group of related capabilities that together support a shared user intent. On this representation, we build MineXR++, a dataset augmenting prior XR interface data with facet-level annotations, and formulate three canonical tasks of context-aware suggestion: context factor analysis, initial facet suggestion, and next facet suggestion. Our evaluation protocol scores suggestion methods by a simulated interaction metric, the navigation and search cost of reaching the desired functionality. Through experiments benchmarking global popularity, relational retrieval, and LLM-based methods, we demonstrate that ContextXR enables the systematic, reproducible evaluation of context-aware XR interfaces.

contents.title: X-Hinges: 3D Printing Self-Sensing Compliant Mechanisms for Continuous and Multi-DOF Motion Sensing
contents.abstract: We present X-Hinges, a design and fabrication method for self-sensing compliant mechanisms based on multi-material FDM 3D printing. By co-printing two conductive filaments of different conductivities within a compliant body, resistive sensing elements are embedded directly during fabrication without post-assembly, enabling continuous motion sensing across multiple degrees of freedom in a single print. The structure supports three degrees of freedom, each equipped with a dedicated sensing element configuration for multi-DOF motion estimation. We develop a precision data acquisition system and data-driven regression models that enable continuous, real-time motion sensing. We also introduce an interactive design tool for customizing the geometry, mechanical properties, degrees of freedom, and sensing configurations of X-Hinges. The tool also supports augmenting existing 3D models with self-sensing structures, endowing ordinary objects with continuous multi-DOF sensing capabilities. Finally, we present a set of application examples demonstrating the capability of X-Hinges for fabricating personalized interactive interfaces.

contents.title: LinkHydro: Design and Rapid Fabrication of Soft Self-Pumping Tubes for Prototyping Hydraulic Interface
contents.abstract: Liquid-based interfaces offer rich expressive capabilities but are often constrained by bulky and noisy hydraulic systems, limiting their use in interactive applications. Recent fiber-based pumps integrate actuation into tubes, enabling silent and compact fluid control, yet they remain difficult to fabricate, design, and deploy in rapid prototyping scenarios. To address these challenges, we present LinkHydro, a method for designing and rapidly fabricating soft self-pumping tubes based on electrohydrodynamics (EHD). By leveraging heat-shrink tubing and a simple fabrication process, LinkHydro enables on-demand production of pumps in approximately 10 minutes. We further introduce a design support tool that allows users to parametrize pump characteristics such as pressure without requiring specialized knowledge. LinkHydro supports modular reconfiguration of tubes, enabling intuitive and tangible control of liquid behavior. We evaluate fabrication time, design support, pumping performance, and silent operation, and demonstrate application scenarios that highlight its potential for prototyping hydraulic interfaces.

contents.title: SpeLL: A Generative Framework for Synthesizing 3D Visual Effects from Text Prompts with Large Language Models
contents.abstract: Creating visual effects (VFX) for 3D content requires specialized design knowledge and technical expertise. Existing methods focus on creating VFX for videos or exploring designs for novices, while professional workflows need frameworks producing complete parameterized 3D assets. This study presents SpeLL, a generative framework that produces editable 3D VFX drafts from text prompts using large language models and retrieval-based asset assembly. A formative study with professional VFX designers identified three design requirements: preference for simplified prompting, need for VFX-specialized assets, and manual spatial-temporal coordination. SpeLL addresses these through prompt enhancement, a spatial design module for component retrieval and layout arrangement, and a temporal design module for activation sequencing. A user study with twenty professional designers evaluated SpeLL against ablated frameworks, 3D generation baselines, and manual workflows. Results showed SpeLL scored higher on intention alignment, spatial-temporal layout quality, and editability, and reduced the effort needed to reach editable VFX structures. Participants valued parameterized outputs over visual complexity, emphasizing workflow integration and manual refinement. These findings indicate that combining LLM reasoning with retrieval-based asset assembly can support early exploration and drafting in professional VFX workflows, while leaving final expressive control to designers.

contents.title: Delta: A DSL for Enlivening Typeset Formulas with Interactive Explanations
contents.abstract:
Many important mathematical ideas are described with formulas, but formulas can be difficult to understand. This has prompted some authors to embed formulas in interactive explanations that relate symbols to text, computation, and visualizations.
However, implementing such designs with standard tools is difficult and time-consuming. To lower the threshold and raise the ceiling of formula explanations, we design and implement Delta, a TypeScript-embedded domain-specific language for creating interactive formula explanations. Delta gives authors the ability to turn formulas into calculators, explain them with step-by-step walkthroughs, and link symbols to nearby text and visual descriptions. It is designed to integrate with LaTeX math in web-based writing contexts, with a React-based runtime that handles necessary state management. In a controlled study, participants edited a simple interactive formula spec more quickly and easily with Delta than with a custom React baseline. In an observational study, participants largely found the language's constructs intuitive after an hour of continuous use.

contents.title: KeepOut: An Embodied Intervention Using The Posture to Reduce Habitual Smartphone Overuse
contents.abstract: Existing interventions for smartphone overuse mainly focus on mitigating the behavior, with limited attention to the conditions that sustain it, which may lead to the recurrence of overuse. Habit theory frames these conditions as contextual cues, and we hypothesize that slumped posture may function as one such cue, which we explore as a design opportunity for intervention. We present KeepOut, a continuous embodied intervention that nudges the users towards upright postures. The system links screen luminance to posture, dimming it during slumped posture and restoring it upon upright posture. We evaluated KeepOut in a 4-week field study (N=38), comparing it with a common periodic notification-based method. Results showed that KeepOut significantly reduced both the usage time (-16.5%) and launch frequency (-25.9%) compared with the pre-intervention condition. Drawing on interviews and daily reports, we inspect the reason for KeepOut’s effectiveness, as well as its influence on phone-use behaviors, posture, and broader daily well-being. Our work demonstrates how behavioral states can be incorporated into intervention design, and suggests posture as a potential direction for understanding smartphone overuse.

contents.title: ShiftLens: Mechanically Actuated Optical Surfaces for Switchable Appearances on 3D Objects
contents.abstract:
Interactive objects often rely on embedded electronics for dynamic surface appearance, which can increase fabrication complexity and reduce robustness in everyday settings. We present ShiftLens, a design and fabrication system for creating 3D objects with mechanically switchable surface appearances, enabling dynamic visual output without electronics. ShiftLens combines a lenticular lens layer with a patterned backplane to create an optomechanical surface that changes appearance through small, controlled shifts between the two layers. This allows objects to display distinct, high-resolution appearances that are discrete. To make these transitions reliable, we introduce actuation mechanisms that translate inputs such as pressing, sliding, and rotating into repeatable surface changes. We also contribute a computational design tool that takes 3D geometry, desired appearances, and actuation types as input, and automatically generates the lenses, patterns, and actuation mechanism geometry for single-pass multi-material 3D printing. Finally, we analyze the geometric constraints for supporting 
ame{} on curved surfaces, the lens design trade-offs that affect viewing range and pattern quality, and demonstrate ShiftLens through a range of applications.

contents.title: MoTUI: Personalization of In-Vehicle Tactile Interfaces for People With Vision Impairments and the Blind
contents.abstract: Configuring in-vehicle interfaces for people with vision impairments (VIPs) requires jointly tuning buttons, feedback modalities, layout, and speech parameters. This defines a design space too large for manual exploration, with inherently conflicting objectives such as maximizing situation awareness while minimizing cognitive load. Prior work recognizes personalization as critical but offers no systematic method to achieve it. We contribute MoTUI, an open-source Modular Tactile User Interface with reconfigurable hardware and software for runtime exploration of this design space and replication of existing designs. MoTUI is configuration-agnostic and supports multiple personalization strategies; we instantiate and evaluate one, pairing it with Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (HITL-MOBO) to navigate the space efficiently. In a within-subject study (N = 12 VIPs), HITL-optimized configurations outperformed a static baseline and an LLM-generated design on situation awareness, perceived workload, and satisfaction, with significant gains over the LLM-based approach. For psychological ownership, optimized configurations were rated significantly higher than both baselines. Importantly, optimization converged on substantially different configurations across participants, indicating strong individual differences; qualitative findings further explain these personalized outcomes.

contents.title: ImageDirector: Expressing Spatial Intent via 3D Direct Manipulation for Generative Image Editing
contents.abstract: Generative image editing through text prompting suffers from two fundamental limitations: text is imprecise for specifying spatial changes, and iterative edits often introduce unwanted visual drift. In contrast, people naturally approach image editing with a compositor's intuition: manipulating individual objects while expecting the rest of the scene to remain intact. We present ImageDirector, a generative image editing system that supports this intuition by enabling users to manipulate objects in a 2D generated image as if they exist in 3D space. Given a generated image, our system segments a selected object, turns it into a manipulable high-fidelity 3D proxy via image-to-3D lifting, and lets users reposition, rotate, and scale it through direct manipulation. The system then re-composites and harmonizes the result with background regions preserved. In a within-subjects study (N = 12), ImageDirector significantly outperformed a text-only prompting baseline in spatial accuracy and visual consistency across iterative edits; participants also reported substantially greater perceived control and expressiveness over the editing process. Finally, we discuss how this approach extends to broader content creation workflows, opening new possibilities for intuitive, precise, and controllable human-AI co-creation.

contents.title: BridgeScope: Interactive Analysis of Cross-Modal SAE Features in Multimodal Large Language Models
contents.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have become a key tool for mechanistic interpretability, decomposing entangled model representations into sparse, human-interpretable features. However, existing SAE analysis workflows target language models and do not address a fundamental question in multimodal settings: does a given feature genuinely bridge shared semantics across text and image, or does it merely reflect modality-specific biases and spurious co-activation patterns?We present BridgeScope, a visual analytics system for retrieving, diagnosing, and validating cross-modal SAE features in multimodal large language models. BridgeScope integrates three capabilities: (1) input-driven feature retrieval that identifies features specifically activated by text, image, or joint input while filtering out globally frequent features; (2) multi-dimensional cross-modal diagnosis that evaluates features along cross-modal alignment, modality balance, intra-modal cohesion, and semantic consistency; and (3) steering-oriented intervention assessment that enables users to manipulate features and examine both intended output changes and unintended side effects. Through case studies, a retrieval effectiveness ablation study, and a user study with interpretability researchers, we show that BridgeScope helps discover genuinely shared cross-modal features, identify modality conflicts and biases, and conduct targeted intervention analysis for multimodal hallucinations—extending SAE-based visual analytics from language models to the multimodal regime.

contents.title: Contexty: Capturing and Organizing In-situ Thoughts for Context-Aware AI Support
contents.abstract: During complex knowledge work, people engage in iterative sensemaking: interpreting information, connecting ideas, and refining their understanding. Yet in current human-AI collaboration, users struggle to externalize and manage this evolving thinking, while AI systems---relying on explicit prompts or passive computer-use observation---cannot access it, creating a gap between users’ thinking and what AI knows. We explore how to bridge this gap by designing affordances for easy sharing of in-situ thoughts and collaborative context management with AI. A probe study (N=10) of a desktop LLM application with snippet memoing revealed both the value of in-situ context capture and the need to organize accumulating context. We then present Contexty, which extends the probe with a canvas-based collaborative space where users can organize, inspect, and refine their accumulated task context with AI. Our evaluation (N=12) showed that Contexty significantly improved users' perceived task awareness, thought structuring, and sense of authorship and control, with participants preferring snippet-grounded AI responses over non-grounded ones (78.1%). We discuss how capturing and organizing users' cognitive context enables AI as a context-aware collaborator while preserving user agency.

contents.title: Predicting Tool Extension in VR Interactions Using Gaze Features
contents.abstract: The ability for virtual reality (VR) systems to create a sense of presence in users has long captured the attention of HCI researchers. One aspect of presence during interaction is tool extension - the experience of integrating a tool into one's body schema. Prior research shows that features of visual attention correlate with experiencing tool extension in VR, but no previous methods provide an ability to predict a user’s tool extension state in real-time. We investigate building this predictor through a study with 18 participants. Participants used virtual tools designed to either promote or inhibit tool extension (a simple hammer vs. an unpredictable linkage-driven hammer). VR gaze-tracking data reliably distinguished these conditions based on the distribution of gaze across areas of interest such as tool, task, and elsewhere. We also found that perspective (first vs. third person) did not affect tool extension. Our results suggest a straightforward gaze-based predictor for tool extension. We conclude by providing a design space demonstrating the practical value of this predictor and several applications enabled by it.

contents.title: MuscleJockey: Motor Initiation via Electrical Muscle Stimulation While Preserving User Control
contents.abstract: In body-actuation interfaces, due to the difficulty predicting user intention in real time, it is challenging to induce movements while preserving user control. We propose MuscleJockey, a body-actuation interface concept in which the system controls the initiation of a movement, while the user controls the direction of the movement. MuscleJockey is based on the division of roles between machine and human: electrical muscle stimulation applied to the shoulder initiates the movement, while the user handles this initiated movement to reach toward a prepared direction. We conducted a user study in which cues were presented at random times, and participants performed reaching movements toward the direction that had been presented beforehand. Consequently, MuscleJockey resulted in a significantly shorter time from cue to movement onset (63.0 ms shorter than the control condition), while maintaining comparable directional accuracy across conditions. These results provide evidence that the time between cue and movement onset can be reduced while preserving user control. Future work should evaluate user control in precise direction, force, and pointing tasks. We believe this study opens up an alternative design direction for body-actuation interfaces.

contents.title: From Style Replication to Style Exploration: Enabling Art Style Exploration with Analyze-Experiment-Resituate Framework
contents.abstract: Art style is a signature of professional digital artists that develops through repeated experimentation, reflection, and adaptation. While generative AI (GenAI) can reproduce styles with high fidelity, current tools provide limited support for exploring new stylistic directions and may encourage style replication over exploration. To address this gap, we propose Analyze-Experiment-Resituate (AER), a framework for AI-assisted style exploration derived from interviews with 10 professional digital artists. Rather than prioritizing visually appealing outputs alone, AER supports three core practices of style exploration, including interpreting references, trying out stylistic possibilities, and reflecting on how emerging styles may be received. Specifically, AER enabled artists to (1) analyze artworks into interpretable stylistic elements, (2) have controllable experimentation guided by their own choices, and (3) resituate emerging styles through simulated social perspectives. We implemented AER in a prototype system and evaluated it in a controlled study with 16 artists. Compared with a direct style-transfer workflow, AER increased artists' agency and reflection as they pursued new stylistic directions. A two-week field study with four artists revealed how the AER framework influenced daily style exploration, such as reflection, experimentation, and stylistic decision-making at each stage. We discuss opportunities and challenges in designing AI-assisted style-exploration workflows, and outline implications for future artistic support tools.

contents.title: Sketch, Edit, Flatten: Bridging the Gap in Fashion Design
contents.abstract: Translating a creative vision into a tangible garment traditionally requires technical designers to interpret a fashion designer's 2D concept sketches into functional 3D mockups and 2D patterns. We propose a novel workflow that empowers fashion designers to generate 3D simulated garments directly from their 2D sketches. Our interface supports multi-stage refinement through a trio of tools: a Sketching tool for drafting ideas on an avatar’s front and back views, a 3D Pen tool for manipulating complex curve networks in 3D space, and a Flattening tool that converts enclosed areas into 2D patterns. By automatically consolidating 2D strokes into a cohesive 3D geometry, the system bridges the gap between conceptual drawing and technical simulation. Evaluations with professional designers indicate the system is both intuitive and effective, allowing for the creation of 3D garment shapes and patterns without specialized technical or pattern-making expertise.

contents.title: Generative Proxy: Synthesizing Proxy-Based Interfaces for Real-World Interaction Across AR Glasses
contents.abstract: Interacting with real-world objects in AR is difficult, especially when targets are distant, cluttered, or occluded. These challenges are amplified on emerging lightweight AR glasses, which often lack binocular or large field of view on display, but also continuous inputs, such as hand or eye tracking. Proxy-based interfaces offer an alternative by allowing users to interact with virtual abstractions of physical objects that can be repositioned, reorganized, and adapted to the task and device. However, designing such interfaces is currently manual and highly device-specific. We present Generative Proxy, a method for automatically generating proxy-based interfaces from three specifications: scene, intent, and device capabilities. We formulate generation as a constrained synthesis problem that first produces valid interfaces for the target device and task, then ranks candidates using semantic and articulatory distance inspired by direct manipulation theory. We demonstrate Generative Proxy across diverse scenes, device profiles, and user intents. Expert evaluation shows initial evidence that generated proxy UIs are useful and usable, highlighting proxy-based abstraction as a promising interaction paradigm for future AR glasses.

contents.title: MaterialVellum: Steering Generative AI by Leveraging Expressive Material Affordances to Form Design Constraints
contents.abstract: We present MaterialVellum, an interaction approach for steering generative AI through material-inspired manipulation of design constraints. In urban design, for instance, zoning bounds can be defined by the stretch of elastic bands, building density redistributed by molding clay, and functional relationships organized by the pull of magnets. MaterialVellum departs from current interfaces that rely on natural language prompts, and instead leverages users' existing knowledge of physical materials to represent and manipulate design constraints. We introduce a framework that maps material affordances, such as elasticity, malleability, or attraction, to spatial, relational, and proportional constraints that underpin design. These mappings are operationalized in user interfaces through familiar direct manipulation multi-touch gestures, including stretching, sculpting, and clustering, whose effects feed as control parameters into generative AI pipelines. We demonstrate this approach through technology probes, including an urban design, a floral design, and a graphical design scenario. A qualitative study (N=10) shows that material-based interactions improve accessibility of constraint expression, support exploratory workflows, and lower barriers for non-experts, while effectiveness depends on alignment with users' mental models.

contents.title: Before You Say It: Anticipating Verbal Behavior from Longitudinal Everyday Conversations with LLMs
contents.abstract: Knowing someone deeply means not just understanding what they say or do but also how they will likely think, react, and engage across situations. Such predictions could eventually inform systems to anticipate when the individual is about to deviate from their goal, catch regrettable behaviors before they are made, and surface blind spots before they take hold. While many interactive systems model users to enable more personalized interactions, most cannot make such behavioral predictions, as this often requires longitudinal observation and inference of how the individual's behaviors unfold across various everyday situations. In this work, we introduce a novel LLM-based predictive behavioral modeling approach that anticipates a user's likely behavior across everyday conversational situations. We (1) collect a longitudinal dataset of over 1,000 hours of naturalistic conversations from 14 participants using a wearable smartwatch; (2) evaluate LLM-based predictions against ground truth behaviors; and (3) use semi-structured interviews to explore participants’ perceptions of behavioral predictions and their views on possible forms of future behavioral support. Altogether, our findings provide evidence that person-specific verbal behavior can be predicted from longitudinal conversational data. This opens up new possibilities for potential future context-aware, anticipatory, proactive and personalized AI systems.

contents.title: Body Sublimation: Designing State-Changing Extended Hand for Embodied Out-of-Reach Interaction
contents.abstract:
Recent research in extended reality (XR) and robotics has explored approaches for extending human reach beyond the inert physical body. 
XR enables embodied interaction with distant targets but lacks physical manipulation. In contrast, robot-mediated systems enable real-world interaction but often disrupt embodiment due to physical constraints such as latency, limited workspace, kinematic mismatch, and collision avoidance. 
Therefore, reconciling physical manipulation with perceptual embodiment remains an open challenge.
In this paper, we present Body Sublimation, an interaction concept that integrates the perceptual flexibility of XR with the physical capabilities of robotic systems. 
A virtual hand in XR serves as the user's extended body while both the original hand and robotic manipulator are hidden using diminished reality. 
A hidden robotic hand then performs physical manipulation, offloading the physical constraints from the user's perception, thereby maintaining embodiment continuity.
We validate the Body Sublimation approach through a user study against a pass-through baseline, where the robot body is always visible, and application scenarios. Compared with a pass-through baseline in which the robot remains visible, our approach maintains task performance while improving trajectory efficiency in obstacle-reaching scenarios, and contributes to a stronger sense of embodiment.

contents.title: Understanding the Role of AI-Enabled Live Tables in Scholarly Sensemaking
contents.abstract:
AI-assisted tools are increasingly used to support information extraction and multi-document reading in research workflows. However, conventional conversational LLM interfaces often mismatch researchers' specific needs, potentially inducing unnecessary cognitive load. To explore more effective interaction paradigms, we developed Lignin, an academic literature reading tool centered on tabular information representation and real-time AI querying. Building on existing table-based reading tools, Lignin combines dynamically configurable query columns, per-cell regeneration and editing, and source-level traceability. This design allows users to revise query dimensions as their questions evolve and supports cross-document comparison during scholarly sensemaking.

 

A controlled experiment was conducted to examine the impact of this tool versus traditional AI interaction modes on cognitive activities during exploratory tasks in unfamiliar domains. Through observations and interviews, we identified instances in which participants appeared to benefit from particular design features, clarifying how different information formats and interaction styles influence such tasks. These findings offer valuable insights for the design of future AI-assisted reading tools and the optimization of AI-mediated research practices.

contents.title: Cardinal Pressure Pulses Rendered by a Wristband Can Elicit Phantom Directional Cues
contents.abstract: Extended reality systems are moving toward camera-based hand tracking, abandoning controllers and the helpful haptic feedback they commonly provide. While many wrist-worn devices can output vibrations, pressure pulse cues offer a promising alternative: they operate silently and deliver comfortable, focal percepts distinct from the buzzing of vibrotactile motors. We present SuperCUTE, a 15-gram wristband with four soft cutaneous electrohydraulic actuators that apply pressure at cardinal wrist positions. Phantom tactile sensations, created by co-activating adjacent actuators, can expand the directional vocabulary of sparse haptic arrays beyond their physical sites. Building on this idea, we characterize the directional cueing capabilities of SuperCUTE in a study with twenty participants. Single-actuator 2-Hz pressure pulses were localized with high precision (~71% of responses within ±22.5° of the target), adjacent pairs usually produced phantom percepts at intermediate directions, and intensity imbalance steered perceived direction toward the stronger actuator, expanding the wristband's four actuators into sixteen directional cues spanning 360°. During haptic-only VR guidance, hand movement directions matched cue geometry across all cue types. Demonstrations of closed-loop haptic guidance and orbiting pressure animations illustrate how spatially distributed pressure pulse cues can enrich extended reality interactions.

contents.title: InsightToast: Proactive Information Retrieval & Glanceable Visualization in the Side Channel of Data-Rich Meetings
contents.abstract: Missing institutional context during meetings can impede effective participation. Retrieving relevant information, often scattered across heterogeneous internal and external sources, requires costly task-switching that disrupts both individual focus and collective conversational flow, particularly detrimental during cognitively demanding tasks such as decision-making. We introduce InsightToast, a mixed-initiative application that monitors verbal discourse in real time, identifies topics and informational needs as they emerge, and proactively retrieves relevant information through a multi-agent large language model (LLM)-based pipeline integrating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to produce source-grounded insights as succinct text and glanceable interactive charts, delivered through a peripheral interface as ephemeral toasts in the conversation's side channel. To demonstrate the potential for yielding serendipitous insights, we showcase a usage scenario involving a knowledge base of legislative documents as the meeting's context. We then report on a comparative study (N=16), in which participants arrived at informed policy decisions while maintaining natural conversation flow.

contents.title: What If You Could Call Your Future Self? NicoCall as a Personalized Future-Self Video Call for Nicotine Cessation
contents.abstract: Interacting with one's future self may support nicotine cessation, but effective design requires balancing trust, emotional impact, and user acceptance. We present NicoCall, a personalized future-self video call system that supports Hoped-for and Feared framings, grounded in Possible Selves theory. We ran a three-condition between-subjects experiment (N=51) comparing the Hoped-for Self, Feared Self, and Control conditions on post-session Future Self-Continuity Questionnaire (FSCQ) scores, smoking urge, and smoking cessation self-efficacy. The findings suggest that NicoCall was associated with higher post-session FSCQ scores and self-efficacy, and with lower smoking urge overall. Hoped-for framing showed more consistent gains in FSCQ scores and self-efficacy, whereas framing differences in urge reduction remained directional. Qualitative findings further suggest that personal fit and social presence may shape uptake of future-self interaction, with identical visual and interactional elements interpreted differently across framing conditions.

contents.title: LitPivot: Developing Well-Situated Research Ideas Through Dynamic Contextualization and Critique within the Literature Landscape
contents.abstract: Developing a novel research idea is hard. It must be distinct enough from prior work to claim a contribution while also building on it. This requires iteratively reviewing literature and refining an idea based on what a researcher reads; yet when an idea changes, the literature that matters often changes with it. Most tools offer limited support for this interplay: literature tools help researchers understand a fixed body of work, while ideation tools evaluate ideas against a static, pre-curated set of papers. We introduce literature-initiated pivots, a mechanism where engagement with literature prompts revision to a developing idea, and where that revision changes which literature is relevant. We operationalize this in LitPivot, where researchers concurrently draft and vet an idea. LitPivot dynamically retrieves clusters of papers relevant to a selected part of the idea and proposes literature-informed critiques for how to revise it. A user study (n=17) shows researchers produced ideas rated by experts as better grounded, perceived their ideas as more novel and useful, and reported stronger understanding of the literature space. An open-ended study (n=5) reveals how researchers use LitPivot to iteratively evolve their own ideas.

contents.title: Kneadix: A Multi-Process Loom with Dynamic Warp-Weft Role Assignment
contents.abstract: Current weaving technology permanently sets the role of the warp and weft yarns during the setup phase of production. This limitation is inherent to the structure of modern looms in which the warp actuation mechanism (heddle) commits the layout before fabrication starts. In this paper, we propose a heddle-less loom architecture in which yarn carriers are manipulated by a set of horn gears, an actuation mechanism adapted from braiding machines. By re-interpreting weaving, knitting, and braiding as yarn-twisting processes, we demonstrate that our design can create fabrics combining these processes without seams. We present a proof-of-concept implementation illustrating actuation, yarn tension management, and combing. We used this implementation to validate our design by fabricating fabrics that combine all three processes, manage yarn insertion, and handle complex edge management. We conclude with a discussion of the limitations of the current prototype and its potential beyond a flat sheet of fabric.

contents.title: Narrative Keyframing for Generative Creative Writing
contents.abstract: We introduce narrative keyframing, an interaction technique for AI-assisted creative writing that lets writers specify different types of narrative constraints at selected moments in a story, then use AI to generate intervening prose. Inspired by the use of keyframing in animation, narrative keyframing offers a flexible way to connect story planning with adaptive control over generated text. We explore three types of keyframes: plot keyframes define significant events in a story, character keyframes represent how individual characters change over the narrative, and perspective keyframes capture how individual characters experience different events through first-person narratives. Plot and character keyframes offer a flexible way to adapt the type of high-level conditioning explored in previous AI writing tools to more customizable, iterative, and fine-scale control, while perspective keyframes add a new way to control characterization and focalization by using first-person narratives as an intermediary. Through a user study, we show that narrative keyframing supports a more controllable, transparent, and engaging way to use generative AI in creative writing.

contents.title: FleetScape: A Mixed Reality Sandtable for Spatial Supervision and Control of Scalable Drone Fleets
contents.abstract: As autonomous drone deployments scale from individual units to coordinated swarms, the human operator’s role shifts from direct piloting to high-level supervision. Current interfaces often treat multi-drone control as a scaled-up version of single-drone operation. We instead investigate how reframing fleet supervision as spatial interaction can better support the spatial, temporal, and safety demands of complex missions. We present FleetScape, a Mixed Reality (MR) sandtable system that externalizes layered real-time mission, safety, and environmental data while enabling fluid transitions between manual intervention and autonomous supervision. We developed a high-fidelity building inspection simulation that generates and streams synchronized multi-drone and environmental data for MR visualizations. We used this prototype to conduct a user study with six experienced drone pilots managing fleets of up to 15 drones. Our findings show that FleetScape supports situational awareness through layered spatial representations and clarifies control mode transitions. However, a limit to situational awareness was observed as fleet size increases, leading to different supervisory strategies. Finally, we derive design implications for supporting scalable drone fleet supervision.

contents.title: HIDAgent: A Platform-Agnostic Hardware Bridge for Personal Computer Use Agents
contents.abstract: Computer Use Agents powered by performant VLMs are increasingly capable of visually interpreting GUIs and executing actions like humans do. However, their method of controlling UIs remains tethered to system-specific APIs or VNC connections, limiting agents to specific platforms and open OS environments. This paper introduces HIDAgent, a platform-agnostic hardware bridge that allows agents to observe any device via HDMI capture and control it via emulated HID mouse and keyboard events—all over a single physical connection. Built for less than $30 using off-the-shelf components, HIDAgent enables agents to operate across mobile, desktop, and even legacy or “closed” systems without local software installation. We demonstrate the flexibility of this approach through six diverse use case prototypes, ranging from cross-device automation to accessibility. By decoupling the agent from the host OS, HIDAgent facilitates research into a future where personal agents are mobile and independent of the devices they control.

contents.title: CinemaWorld: Generative Augmented Reality with LLMs and 3D Scene Generation for Movie Augmentation
contents.abstract: We introduce CinemaWorld, a generative augmented reality system that augments the viewer’s physical surroundings with automatically generated mixed reality 3D content extracted from and synchronized with 2D movie scenes. Our system preprocesses films to extract key features using multimodal large language models (LLMs), generates dynamic 3D augmentations with generative AI, and embeds them spatially into the viewer’s physical environment on the Meta Quest 3. To identify key augmentation techniques for CinemaWorld, we conducted an elicitation study with eight film students, which led us to identify several key augmentation types, including particle effects, surrounding objects, textural overlays, character-driven augmentation, and lighting effects. We evaluated our system through a technical evaluation (N=100 video clips), a user evaluation (comparison study: N=12 and in-the-wild study: N=8), and expert interviews with film creators (N=8). Results indicate that CinemaWorld enhances immersion and enjoyment, suggesting its potential to enrich the film-viewing experience.

contents.title: TeachUp: Facilitating Early-Stage Teachers to Learn Instructional Strategies from Classroom Videos with Reflective Support
contents.abstract: Recorded videos of offline open classes provide good examples for early-stage teachers to learn instructional strategies, e.g., how to organize cooperative learning. However, learning by watching these videos is challenging, as these strategies are implicitly performed, and it lacks in-situ reflective support. In this paper, via a formative study (N=9), we design TeachUp to support the learning of instructional strategies from classroom teaching videos. TeachUp adopts an LLM-powered pipeline to detect nine instructional strategies in videos (precision = 63.4%), provides reflective questions and hints while watching, and generates customized practices with reflective feedback. A within-subjects study (N=16) shows that compared to a traditional video-playing and self-practicing baseline, early-stage teachers with TeachUp are more engaged in learning and perform better in applying learned strategies to new tasks. Interviews with four in-service teachers further generalize our findings and TeachUp's use cases. We discuss practical implications for fostering video-based learning of instructional strategies.

contents.title: Elsewise: Authoring Open-ended Interactive Narrative with Possibility Space Visualization
contents.abstract: Interactive narrative (IN) authors craft spaces of divergent narrative possibilities for players to explore, with the player's input determining which narrative possibilities they actually experience. Generative AI can enable new forms of IN by improvisationally expanding on pre-authored content in response to open-ended player input. However, this extrapolation risks widening the gap between author-envisioned and player-experienced stories, potentially limiting the strength of plot progression and the communication of the author's narrative intent. To bridge the gap, we introduce Elsewise: an authoring tool for LLM-based INs that implements a novel Bundled Storyline concept to enhance authors' perception and understanding of the narrative possibility space, allowing authors to explore similarities and differences between possible playthroughs of their IN in terms of open-ended, user-configurable narrative dimensions. A user study (n=12) shows that our approach improves author anticipation of player-experienced narrative, leading to more effective control and exploration of narrative possibility spaces.

contents.title: Seeing Beyond the Chart: Behaviour-Aware Self-Directed Visual Acuity Screening with Multimodal Interaction
contents.abstract: Early detection of vision deterioration is critical for timely intervention, particularly for myopia, which is increasing rapidly worldwide. Yet existing digital visual acuity tests remain limited, where many depend on another person to operate the interface and enter responses, making self-screening inconvenient and difficult to perform independently. They are also behaviour-blind, ignoring cues clinicians use to judge response reliability, such as hesitation, forward head movement, or effortful focusing, which can compromise measurement precision. We present a behaviours-aware interactive system for self-directed visual acuity screening on laptops and other smart devices with a camera and a screen. Our system combines finger-pointing recognition for natural response entry, multimodal behaviours detection for identifying signs of struggle during testing, and intelligent usage guidance that helps users complete setup and testing correctly. Together, these features improve ease of use, independence, and reliability. The approach supports practical self-checking at home and may broaden access in under-resourced settings where shortages of eye care professionals can delay detection, especially for children at risk of missing the critical window for early intervention. \hl{ Results shows the approach reduced falsely reassuring outcomes while maintaining close agreement with clinician-administered visual acuity assessment, alongside improved user-rated usability and trust.

contents.title: Augmenting Human Performance with an XR Agent Learning from Online Behavior and BCI Evidence
contents.abstract: We present OLIVE, a framework for adapting a foundation model to provide real-time assistance in temporally demanding, high-stakes, and dynamic tasks. We show that passive EEG, fused online with behavioral evidence, can meaningfully extend the number of targets users detect and engage beyond their unaided action bandwidth. OLIVE learns from both explicit behavioral signals (the targets the user shoots down in an XR first-person shooter game) and implicit physiological signals (fixation-locked EEG) to provide timely guidance, continuously adapting a frozen vision-language model's inference on which items are task-relevant by jointly estimating per-source reliability without manual labels or offline training. Through three user studies deploying an assistive agent driven by OLIVE in XR, we show that OLIVE outperforms prior test-time adaptation frameworks in convergence speed and likelihood. Combining implicit physiological and explicit behavioral signals, the OLIVE agent produces the largest and most reliable within-session improvement to a user's ability to detect and engage targets, largely independent of the individual's skill. When the target switches silently, the agent that uses both behavioral and physiological signals reconverges significantly faster than the behavior-only agent (1.27 times faster on average, p = 0.008), restoring trustworthy guidance at the moment the task changes, precisely when reliable assistance matters most.

contents.title: ASIDE: From Conflict Participants to Co-Observers Through Dyadic Spectator Reflection
contents.abstract: When people argue over text, they share a record of what was said but may hold different accounts of what it meant. Existing AI reflection tools typically work from one person's account, while dyadic tools support co-expression without making interpretation gaps inspectable. We present ASIDE, a system for Dyadic Spectator Reflection (DSR). DSR follows the sequence externalize independently, then encounter together. From a past chat conflict, ASIDE creates a pixel-art theatrical replay with revisable AI-generated inner-state hypotheses. Partners first confirm hypotheses about themselves and separately edit their interpretations of the other. After both finish, they view the co-annotated scene together and review Divergence Cards that pair a confirmed account with the partner's reading at a specific conversational beat. In an exploratory study with 10 couples who revisited real text-based conflicts, participants described the theatrical replay as helping them step out of their roles and observe the conflict together. We contribute DSR as a reusable interaction structure for dyadic reflection and an exploratory account of how partners used it to revisit past text-based conflicts from a shared observer position.

contents.title: OpenGut: An Open-Source Platform for Gut-Computer Interaction Research
contents.abstract: Researchers are increasingly exploring the gut as a human-computer interface due to its gut-brain axis, linking physiological states with emotion and cognition. Despite its potential, the gut research space remains highly fragmented and underexplored. This is largely due to the absence of open and accessible hardware and software tools that could enable systematic investigation across disciplines and communities. To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with six experts to identify pain points in using existing platforms. Based on the themes identified, we formulated a set of requirements, and developed OpenGut, a rapid prototyping platform for gut research. Our open source platform consists of three main components: a wearable hardware platform for data capture and playback, a graphical user interface for visualization and analysis, as well as accompanying documentation for platform setup and customization. We perform technical evaluation of OpenGut for its signal quality, noise suppression, as well as outline potential usage scenarios for gut research.

contents.title: ProtoCall: Preemptive Physical Feedback for Sequential Skill Augmentation
contents.abstract: Mastering sequential skills is essential for everyday and professional tasks such as cooking and assembly. However, executing actions in the correct order and with appropriate timing remains challenging, particularly during transitions between consecutive steps. Existing approaches, including haptic guidance, error-based feedback, or post-error correction, either increase cognitive load, reduce users' agency, or intervene too late to prevent errors. We developed ProtoCall, a custom wearable physical feedback system, combined with a Vision–Language Model (VLM) for interaction inference, and designed three feedback strategies targeting different stages of the error process: 1) preemptive attentional nudging (attention-level guidance by head actuation), 2) preemptive reaching nudging (action-level prevention of reaching), and 3) post-error nudging. We conducted a user study with 16 participants on a sequential step-transition task, revealing trade-offs between physical feedback strategies across augmentation, retention, and user experience.

contents.title: From Gaze to Guidance: Interpreting and Adapting to Users’ Cognitive Needs with Multimodal Gaze-Aware AI Assistants
contents.abstract: Current LLM assistants are powerful at answering questions, but they have limited access to the behavioral context that reveals when and where a user is struggling. We present a gaze-grounded multimodal LLM assistant that uses egocentric video with gaze overlays to identify likely points of difficulty and target follow-up retrospective assistance. We instantiate this vision in a controlled study (n=36) comparing the gaze-aware AI assistant to a text-only LLM assistant. The gaze-aware assistant was rated as more accurate and personalized in its assessments of users' reading behavior, and users spoke fewer words during the interaction. We also observed a preliminary condition difference on a short recall measure. Qualitative results underscored both perceived benefits and failures when gaze behaviors were misinterpreted. Our findings suggest that gaze-aware LLM assistants can better target retrospective assistance while highlighting the need to confirm gaze-derived hypotheses with users.

contents.title: NaturalEdit: Code Modification through Direct Interaction with Adaptive Natural Language Representation
contents.abstract: Code modification requires developers to comprehend code, plan changes, articulate intent, and validate outcomes, making it cognitively demanding. While natural language (NL) code summaries offer a promising external representation of this process, existing approaches remain limited. Systems grounded in exploratory data analysis are restricted to narrow domains, while general-purpose systems enforce fixed NL representations and assume that developers can directly translate vague intent into precise textual edits. We present NaturalEdit, which treats code summaries as interactive representations tightly linked to source code. Grounded in the Cognitive Dimensions of Notations, NaturalEdit introduces three key features: (1) adaptive, multi-faceted code summaries with a flexible Abstraction Gradient; (2) interactive mapping mechanisms between summaries and code that ensure tight, structurally stable Closeness of Mapping; and (3) intent-driven bidirectional synchronization that reduces Viscosity during editing while preserving Visibility and Consistency through incremental diffs. A technical evaluation confirms NaturalEdit's viability, and a user study with 20 developers shows that it improves comprehension, intent articulation, and validation while increasing developers' perceived confidence and control.

contents.title: StitchOver: Technical Embroidery on Seamed Fabrics
contents.abstract:
Smart textiles embed interactivity into everyday garments, supporting use cases like always-available sensing for medical applications or sports. Machine embroidery allows integrating functionalities into existing textiles. However, embroidering onto real-world textile goods remains challenging. Textile goods are rarely made of a single homogeneous substrate of fabric, and embroidery with functional materials such as conductive threads requires machines to be more tightly calibrated than for decorative embroidery. In particular, seams, which bring together different substrates, along with machine variability, cause shifts in tension and friction between the functional thread and the textile substrate that frequently lead to defects (70% of samples in our evaluation).
We present a technique to reliably embroider on seamed fabric even when using functional threads. Our software tool automatically digitizes user-defined stitch patterns by introducing what we call “JumpStitches” to bypass seam interference.
We evaluated our approach under varying machine states (under-tensioned, calibrated, and over-tensioned), and across multiple seam and pattern configurations. Our results show that the JumpStitch mechanism eliminates defects, while maintaining conductivity compared to 70% defects without JumpStitches, and even in poorly calibrated machine-states continues to work well.

contents.title: HeadRoom: Lightweight, Edge-deployable Pipeline for Adaptive Notification Routing
contents.abstract: Emerging wearables, such as smart glasses, can deliver notifications through multiple sensory channels, but there is still a limited understanding of how to choose the right channel at the right moment. We propose HeadRoom, a lightweight, edge-deployable pipeline that estimates the availability of visual and auditory channels in real time from egocentric video and audio. Our controlled user study (N=25) shows that, under high perceptual load, routing notifications to the more available channel reduces response time relative to routing them to the less available channel. This work opens up a new possibility for adaptive routing of notifications in wearable and immersive systems.

contents.title: InvisIto: Weaving Unobtrusive Infrared Markers for Ubiquitous Textile Interaction
contents.abstract:
Textiles are increasingly explored as media for interacting with digital information. However, many of the existing approaches rely on visible tags, printed overlays, or electronic modules that compromise the fabric’s aesthetic and tactile qualities. To address this, we present InvisIto, a method for weaving visually unobtrusive yet machine-readable infrared markers directly into fabrics using near-infrared (NIR)-absorbing yarns. Although these yarns look similar to standard fibers in ambient light, they produce strong contrast in NIR imaging. Our method includes: (1) a design tool that helps users easily embed infrared markers into weaving drafts, (2) five disguising strategies that further reduce marker visibility under ambient light, and (3) a camera-based detection pipeline for decoding and tracking the woven markers. InvisIto supports both woven QR codes for data encoding and woven ArUco markers for binary input and deformation tracking.
We demonstrate applications across hand weaving, Jacquard weaving, and industrial fabrication, showing that InvisIto supports scalable interaction and fabrication from bespoke artifacts to mass production.

contents.title: Sidekick: Designing Communication for Effective Multitasking with Computer Use Agents
contents.abstract: Computer Use Agents (CUAs) can autonomously execute complex, multi-step tasks within GUIs, enhancing efficiency through parallel multitasking. However, our formative studies with CUA experts and GenAI users indicated that current feedback is primarily text-based, requiring sustained attention to monitor progress and offering limited visibility to trace past GUI interactions. Based on the findings, we developed a prototype system, Sidekick, for communicating CUAs’ status with multimodal feedback across different stages of interaction: (i) When CUAs run in the background, Sidekick signals its execution state through ambient cues. (ii) Upon resuming interaction with CUAs, Sidekick provides multimodal summaries of completed actions to support rapid context resumption. (iii) When CUAs operate in the foreground, Sidekick enhances transparency by verbalizing and visualizing the agent’s reasoning. A study with 30 participants demonstrated that Sidekick significantly improved multitasking performance with CUAs compared to baseline systems that presented textual feedback either in a typical chat or in an ambient display. Sidekick supported progress awareness, and error and action traceability more effectively. Finally, we demonstrate the promise of Sidekick through several example applications, and discuss implications for long-horizon human-agent collaboration.

contents.title: Steerable Chatbots: Exploring Personalization Control Interfaces via LLM Activation Steering
contents.abstract: Personalizing LLM responses typically requires users to articulate their preferences through prompting, which can be burdensome at cold start and difficult to articulate in natural language. We introduce an alternative paradigm, steerable chatbots: rather than asking users to describe what they want, let them directly manipulate it via a linear factor. We implement this through activation steering, leveraging a linear scalar to control how strongly a preference is expressed in the LLM's output. We first assess the computational viability of activation steering as a method to control granular preference expression, then we explore how the factor can be exposed to users. We prototype three activation steering interface designs that vary on the axes of agency (user-led vs. system-driven) and fluidity (static vs. adaptive). A within-subjects user study (n=14) in cold-start personalization tasks shows the potential for steerable chatbots to align better with underlying user preferences than prompting alone, while revealing heterogeneous values around control, persistence, and transparency in LLM personalization.

contents.title: AgentLens: Adaptive Visual Modalities for Human–Agent Interaction in Mobile GUI Agents
contents.abstract: Mobile GUI agents can automate smartphone tasks by interacting directly with app interfaces, but how they should communicate with users during execution remains underexplored. Existing systems rely on two extremes: foreground execution, which maximizes transparency but prevents multitasking, and background execution, which supports multitasking but provides little visual awareness. Through iterative formative studies, we found that users prefer a hybrid model with minimally invasive, just-in-time visual interaction, but the most effective visualization modality depends on the task. Motivated by this, we present AgentLens, a mobile GUI agent that adaptively uses three visual modalities during human--agent interaction: Full UI, Partial UI, and GenUI. AgentLens extends a standard mobile agent with adaptive communication actions and uses Virtual Display to enable background execution with selective visual overlays. In a controlled study with 21 participants, AgentLens was preferred by 85.7\% of participants and achieved the highest usability (1.94 Overall PSSUQ; lower is better) and adoption intent (6.43/7).
