contents.title: User Attention Is All chatLLMs Need: Proactive Intervention Against Attention Drift While Waiting for chatLLMs
contents.abstract: In chat-based large language model (chatLLM) interaction, users repeatedly wait for responses to be generated after submitting prompts, and this waiting period can trigger attention drift to off-task activities. We first characterize this vulnerability in everyday chatLLM use (Study 1, N=16). Drift episodes were disproportionately concentrated in generation intervals, emerged early after query submission, and were predominantly self-initiated. Based on these findings, we present Q2Focus, a proactive sidebar intervention that delivers lightweight, task-relevant micro-questions immediately after query submission to keep users cognitively anchored during waiting. Beyond sustaining attention, users' answers can be reused in subsequent dialogue to improve downstream task performance. Because disengagement can be intentional, Q2Focus is designed as an optional aid that appears quickly, remains low-friction, and withdraws once model output arrives. In a 14-day mixed-design study (N=36), Q2Focus outperformed no-intervention and reactive baselines: overall drift decreased by 50%, self-initiated drift by 83%, and task performance improved across writing, coding, and research without increased reported cognitive demand. In a no-intervention follow-up on Day 14, prior Q2Focus users remained more focused than baseline users, providing preliminary evidence of possible carryover beyond in-the-moment prompting.

contents.title: NailBender: Exploring Nail Flexion for Haptic Input and Output
contents.abstract: We introduce NailBender, a lightweight (<1 g) nail-mounted device that uses a single piezoelectric plate with segmented electrodes for both sensing and actuation. At ±90 V, the piezo produces 50 μm of deflection across 1–100 Hz, requiring just 40 mW at 20 Hz. Actuation remains detectable down to ±20 V. The piezo can also sense forces from 0.1 to 24 N applied to the bare fingerpad, as well as heartbeat and environmentally coupled vibrations. Using NailBender, we demonstrate single and multiple input/output configurations: variable-force pinch buttons (3 levels, 90.7% accuracy), spatially differentiated left/right tactile actuation (5 patterns, 83.2% recognition), and ML-based micro-gesture classification (5 gestures, 98% accuracy after per-user calibration). These results show that NailBender can enable expressive, bidirectional haptic interaction in a compact, wearable form factor without blocking the fingerpad.

contents.title: iRing: Rich Interaction on Smart Ring with Multi-point Capacitive Touch Screen
contents.abstract:
Rising interest in smart rings reflects a growing demand for immediate, lightweight interaction. However, prior designs have largely treated rings as input-only interfaces or provided only limited on-device visualization, falling short of supporting tightly coupled, direct, and expressive co-located interaction.
To bridge this gap, we present iRing, a lightweight (6.4 g), low-cost ($46.43), open-source, and reproducible smart ring platform centered on a capacitive multitouch display. We design a compact multitouch interface using accessible components that accommodate the ring’s constrained form factor. The platform further integrates a flexible OLED display, a BLE microcontroller, an IMU, and a PPG sensor, supporting both local and remote interaction.
To translate hardware-level touch sensing into interaction events, we introduce nano interactions—a compact vocabulary that adapts familiar touch primitives for direct, co-located input and visual output on ultra-small, curved surfaces. Nano interactions enable interactions to be completed within a single glance–touch cycle and are designed to support one-handed, low-attention use while in motion.
We implement a set of applications to explore the design space enabled by multitouch interaction on a ring. A user study with 12 participants demonstrates reliable touch interaction and yields positive short-term assessments of usability, comfort, and social acceptability, highlighting opportunities for compact interfaces that support glanceable and on-the-go interaction.

contents.title: TagTutor: Restoring Practice Visibility for Guitar Tutoring in Private Listening Settings
contents.abstract: Electric guitar practice often takes place in private listening settings, such as practicing through headphones at night or on an unplugged solid-body guitar. In these settings, the learner can still hear or feel the instrument, but a tutoring system has little usable airborne sound to capture, creating a visibility gap for feedback. We present TagTutor, a guitar tutoring system that restores practice visibility using a paper-thin RFID tag attached to the fretboard. TagTutor senses string vibration from backscattered phase signals and recovers played notes without relying on external audio. It then converts recovered performance into structured feedback by identifying pitch, string-position, and timing errors, and presents them through a two-level interface for immediate awareness and post-run review of recurring problem passages. In private listening settings where microphone baselines drop to 12%, TagTutor maintains 94% note recognition accuracy by sensing string vibration directly rather than relying on airborne sound. A one-month study with 20 learners further shows that TagTutor yields a 13.5-point larger gain in playing accuracy than baseline self-practice and promotes more targeted repetition of difficult passages, demonstrating the value of restoring practice visibility for self-practice.

contents.title: V-Hook: Morphology-Mediated Vibration-Driven Locomotion through 3D-Printed Hook Structures
contents.abstract: Vibration is a lightweight and widely available actuation source, yet existing vibration-driven locomotion systems often rely on specialized mechanisms, additional electronics, or extensive empirical tuning, making them difficult to reproduce, adapt, and integrate into everyday objects. To address this limitation, we present V-Hook, a morphology-mediated locomotion design approach that biases motion behavior through hook-shaped structures fabricated by FDM 3D printing. By leveraging asymmetric contact and stick-slip interactions between the hooks and the supporting surface, V-Hook transforms simple vibration input into distinguishable motion tendencies under specific contact and excitation conditions. We systematically investigate how hook forms, array configurations, lengths, and vibration conditions influence motion directional accuracy, stability, and load-bearing performance, and explore a design space of morphology-mediated locomotion from these results. Building on this foundation, we develop a guided design software and online platform that support morphological fabrication and sharing for lightweight interactive objects, and demonstrate the approach through a series of application prototypes. By reframing vibration-driven locomotion as a problem of hook morphology design, this work offers a new perspective for integrating motion capabilities into digitally fabricated interactive systems.

contents.title: InvisiSpeech: Making Silent Speech Invisible through a Miniature Intraoral Sensor
contents.abstract: Silent speech promises private interaction, but existing implementations often rely on visible sensors or conspicuous articulation, which limits their discretion in everyday use. We present InvisiSpeech, an intraoral interface that remains hidden from outside view and supports silent speech input with minimal lip movement and without drawing visual attention. Our custom flex-PCB device is housed in a biocompatible SLA-printed dental brace and attaches around the back molar. This mount couples a voice-pickup sensor to the tooth for input sensing, which our embedded microcontroller transfers via Bluetooth. Our evaluation with 15 participants shows that InvisiSpeech achieves up to 91.5% recognition accuracy on 50 sentence-level commands and maintains robustness in noisy environments. Participants also reported high wearability and perceived social acceptance, highlighting the practicality of our approach for everyday use. We demonstrate three applications of our system: hands-free human-AI interaction in public, discreet interaction in a quiet public place, and subtle communication in a privacy-sensitive context. Our results establish invisible silent speech as a practical interaction paradigm for real-world use outside controlled settings.

contents.title: RegulAR: Graph-Grounded Error Recognition and Assistance for Procedural Tasks in Augmented Reality
contents.abstract:
Errors are inevitable in procedural tasks, yet most AR guidance systems focus on step-by-step instruction delivery rather than helping users recognize and recover from mistakes. We present RegulAR, an AR task assistant for procedural error recognition and recovery.
RegulAR models task instructions as a hierarchical dependency graph and combines this structure with a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to interpret egocentric observations during execution. This enables RegulAR to track progress, identify deviations by error type, estimate their impact on later steps, and deliver appropriately salient interventions through an in-situ head-up display that visualizes task state and recovery guidance. By making procedural structure explicit, RegulAR supports not only next-step guidance, but also reasoning about what went wrong, why it matters, and how users can get back on track. In a within-subject study (N=12), participants reported better task-structure understanding and recovery support with RegulAR than the MLLM-only baseline.

contents.title: BlimpMate: A Quiet, Long-Endurance Flying Display for Hands-Free Intelligent Interaction
contents.abstract:
Digital information in everyday environments is still primarily accessed through fixed or handheld screens, which often divert attention away from ongoing physical activity. Flying displays offer an alternative by positioning information directly in three-dimensional space, near the user and near the task. However, most existing aerial interfaces rely on multirotor drones, whose noise, limited endurance, and exposed propellers make them less suitable for calm, sustained indoor interaction.

We present BlimpMate, a long-endurance flying display robot for hands-free intelligent interaction in everyday indoor environments. Built on a helium blimp platform that provides passive buoyant lift, BlimpMate supports quiet and energy-efficient operation while integrating a lightweight projection-based display, multimodal sensing, custom low-level flight control, and a networked interaction stack with AI-supported services. Its display architecture enables a large-area, visually expressive onboard display while remaining compatible with the severe payload constraints of a small indoor blimp. Rather than using the blimp as a passive carrier, we frame it as a mobile visual interface \hl{that supports controlled repositioning near users and task locations. Through technical characterization and proof-of-concept scenarios, we position blimp-based flying displays as a promising platform for calm, persistent, and spatially situated indoor interaction beyond conventional screens and drone-based platforms.

contents.title: PrejSense: Non-intrusive Gaze-Informed Prediction of Implicit Prejudice Against Machine for Proactive Interface Adaptation
contents.abstract: Implicit prejudice against machine can critically undermine the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration by limiting trust, cooperation, and system acceptance. Despite its significance, such prejudice is rarely addressed in real world usage and is often assessed retrospectively through self-report measures or implicit association test, lacking automated and adaptive interface essential for responsive system design. Drawn from dual process theory, we propose and test PrejSense, a proof-of-concept adaptive interface loop that uses non-intrusive gaze signals to predict users’ prejudice states and adapt interface support accordingly. First, we develop interpretable deep learning models to predict prejudice from gaze features. Second, we develop adaptive interface using LLM agents to dynamically respond to estimated prejudice states, with expert-informed refinement. Third, we build a full-stack system for automated prejudice prediction and adaptive interaction, enabling non-intrusive integration into collaborative AI systems. We conduct a user testing experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of PrejSense. Compared with baseline, PrejSense significantly enhanced emotional trust and showed marginal positive effects on cognitive trust and WOA. These results provide preliminary evidence for state-contingent prejudice-aware adaptation in a low-risk decision-support task. By combining gaze-informed prejudice prediction with adaptive interaction design, this work opens a design space for prejudice-aware adaptive interfaces while highlighting the need for larger-scale validation.

contents.title: AeroPixels: Repurposing Ubiquitous Displays as Imperceptible Schlieren Light Sources for Airflow Interaction
contents.abstract: Airflow is an invisible yet ubiquitous phenomenon in everyday environments, encoding rich information about human activities and environmental conditions such as exhalation, thermal convection, and ventilation. We present AeroPixels, a method that leverages ubiquitous display surfaces as an airflow sensing infrastructure. AeroPixels embeds the source grid pattern required for focusing schlieren imaging, an optical technique that visualizes airflow through light refraction, into displayed visual content and perceptually hides it via alternating complementary, high-frame-rate frames, allowing users to perceive only the intended imagery. A schlieren camera synchronized with the display refresh captures each complementary frame independently and reconstructs airflow information. We address key challenges in display-based sensing, including geometric misalignment between the embedded source grid pattern and the sensing camera, as well as content-dependent noise, enabling robust schlieren imaging under non-ideal conditions such as projection mapping environments. We build a prototype system and demonstrate stable airflow visualization on projected surfaces while preserving the intended visual content for human observers. Finally, we present three representative projection modes for human-computer interaction enabled by AeroPixels, including exhalation visualization, breath-based input, education, and entertainment.

contents.title: SplatXR: A Toolkit for Multi-Layered Extended Reality via On-Headset 3D Gaussian Splatting
contents.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting, 3D foundation models, and video-passthrough mixed reality offer unprecedented fidelity for capturing and blending physical and virtual worlds. However, established XR methods rely on polygon-based pipelines that treat physical and digital environments as separate domains, making seamless integration across recent novel representations difficult. Because splats lack explicit surface geometry, they impede standard graphics techniques necessary for cross-reality interactions, such as shadow or collision handling. Furthermore, while 3D foundation models can reconstruct physical objects on-the-fly into digital splats, current XR systems fall short of leveraging this capability for user experiences that transition seamlessly between physicality and virtuality. To address this, we organize XR as a multi-layered reality of interacting primitives, letting pixels and objects move across physical and digital boundaries. We contribute SplatXR, a Unity toolkit that operationalizes this structure as building blocks for interactive, immersive apps leveraging 3D Gaussian splatting: a standalone renderer, splat-to-mesh reconstruction, splat physics, splat blending, and offloaded splat object reconstruction via on-headset capture. SplatXR unites vision and graphics techniques to make splat-based XR development broadly available, and we validate it through demonstrative applications and a small developer study.

contents.title: Hear-to-Hear: Uncertainty-Aware, Head-Tracked Interaction for Personalized Spatial Audio
contents.abstract:
Selecting a personalized head-related transfer function (HRTF) is essential for accurate spatial audio, but remains challenging due to substantial user variation and noisy subjective feedback.
We present a real-time, uncertainty-aware perceptual interaction loop for HRTF personalization: after each paired comparison, the system updates a posterior belief over candidate HRTFs and immediately adapts the next query to maximize informativeness.
Our system couples Bayesian preference learning with real-time head-tracked binaural rendering, enabling head motion to actively inform comparisons.
In a controlled within-subject psychophysical study, uncertainty-aware interaction (with optional head tracking) provides directional posterior evidence for localization improvements---primarily suggestive reductions in azimuth error and front--back confusions concentrated in the front hemisphere---alongside participant-level heterogeneity and a partially mitigated elevation trade-off, rather than uniformly decisive effects across all metrics.

contents.title: Surpassing Human Wrist Constraints: Dexterity-Enhanced Techniques for Teleoperated Robotic Manipulation
contents.abstract: Free-hand teleoperation enables intuitive robot control by mapping human hand and arm poses to end-effector motion. However, its effectiveness in complex tasks is constrained by the mismatch between human wrist biomechanics and robotic arm capabilities. From 60 demonstration videos across four task categories, we identified three end-effector motion capabilities that surpass human constraints: unbounded axial rotation, omnidirectional alignment, and path-constrained orientation maintenance. Inspired by enhancement techniques in virtual reality (VR), we propose two interaction strategies---finger-based motion extension and non-isomorphic rotational gain---instantiated in four methods: FingerCircle, FingerRaise, WristSpin, and WristDNR. We evaluated these methods in VR using three representative teleoperation tasks, with a clutch-based control mode as the baseline. Results showed that finger-based methods improve efficiency and agency in continuous rotation tasks, whereas wrist-based methods enhance alignment and orientation control, at the expense of predictability. We further deployed them on a UR5 robotic arm in two application scenarios. Overall, these techniques better leverage robotic dexterity while reducing operator workload.

contents.title: SketchMind: Toward Executable Pen-Based Sketching for Constructing Sorting Algorithms
contents.abstract: Pen-and-paper tracing is commonly used to think through algorithms before writing code, allowing learners to step through concrete executions and explore possible solutions. However, this process does not readily support abstraction. As traces grow, they lose structure. Steps accumulate into long sequences and are often skipped or compressed, leading to incomplete or inconsistent reasoning. As a result, learners struggle to extract reusable algorithmic patterns or generalize beyond individual instances. We present SketchMind, a proof-of-concept sketch-based programming system in which users construct executable traces of sorting algorithms through pen-based interactions. By performing operations directly on visual representations (e.g., arrays and variables) using pen strokes, users can construct and refine sorting algorithms without writing code. SketchMind supports four key capabilities: (1) executable tracing, where actions are recorded and replayed as runnable steps; (2) reusable pens, which encapsulate trace segments into user-defined procedures; (3) multi-level trace views across values, indices, and symbolic parameters; and (4) cross-instance validation, which applies learned procedures to new inputs and generates minimal counterexamples.

contents.title: Language Scent: Exploring Cross-Language Information Navigation
contents.abstract: While multilingual users often switch between languages when seeking information, this process remains undersupported by current systems where information is typically siloed by language. Our formative study reveals that users select their search language based on its perceived value for their current information need, a concept we formalize as language scent. Language scent extends Pirolli and Card's information foraging theory – which explains how users navigate among already-encountered sources – to the multilingual case, where users' choice of query language determines which sources they can encounter in the first place. Building on this insight, we designed Niffler, a multilingual information seeking system that provides proximal cues for gauging the language scent of different languages. Finally, we conducted a lab study with 16 multilingual speakers to understand Niffler's utility, usage patterns and application contexts.

contents.title: Preemptive, Buffered or Guided? Empirical Studies on Human-AI Interaction Strategies for Software Test Case Development
contents.abstract: Applications of large language models (LLMs) in software engineering are soaring quickly. Despite ample evidence supporting LLMs’ capabilities of generating high-quality and creative suggestions, human-LLM interactions in software testing remain under-explored, and there lacks empirical evidence supporting efficacious human-LLM system designs. In software testing, the industry’s pursuit of “autonomous” systems neglects intensive human involvement in prior-design and post-review processes. This paper discusses two empirical user studies for a test case brainstorming task: (1) exploring user behaviors in human-LLM interactions compared to web search ( \(N_{1}=16\) ) and (2) investigating three modified interaction strategies—preemptive prompting, buffered response and guided input ( \(N_{2}=24\) ). We consolidate nine cross-disciplinary metrics to quantitatively evaluate the holistic performance of the human-LLM system, covering three perspectives: test quality, creativity, and attention span. Our findings reveal that users spend 126% more time interacting with LLMs compared to Google search. Moreover, preemptively prompting the LLM system significantly improves test quality and task creativity by over 30%, while simultaneously reducing user idle time by up to 49%. Based on the results, this paper discusses three interaction design principles—mixed initiative, acceptability, and appropriation—as guidance for future iterations of an efficacious LLM-assisted software testing system.

contents.title: Simulating Word Suggestion Usage in Mobile Typing to Guide Intelligent Text Entry Design
contents.abstract: Intelligent text entry (ITE) methods, such as word suggestions, are widely used in mobile typing, yet improving these systems remains challenging because the cognitive mechanisms underlying suggestion use are poorly understood and evaluating new systems often requires long-term user studies to account for behavioral adaptation. We present WSTypist, a reinforcement learning-based model that simulates how typists integrate word suggestions into typing. We extend recent hierarchical control models of typing by identifying and implementing important cognitive mechanisms that underlie high-level decision-making when integrating word suggestions into manual typing: considering orthographic processes, assessing efficiency gains, and accounting for personal preferences regarding AI support. Our evaluations show that WSTypist simulates diverse human-like suggestion-use strategies, reproduces behavioral differences, and generalizes across different systems. Through four design cases, we demonstrate how a computational rationality model can inform what-if analyses during the design process by simulating how users might adapt to changes in the UI or algorithmic support, thereby reducing the need for user studies early in the exploratory design phase.

contents.title: TactiPlay: Multi-Granularity Tactical Parsing and Video-Anchored Match Review for Amateur Badminton Players
contents.abstract: Amateur badminton players increasingly record matches, yet existing tools provide only aggregate statistics or generic summaries, leaving most unable to extract tactical insights without expert guidance. A formative study (N=8) reveals the need for multi-granularity, video-anchored tactical analysis centered on rallies. We derive a taxonomy of performance issues from national-level athletes’ annotations and present TactiPlay, an interactive system that instantiates an expert-taxonomy-guided, rally-level, video-anchored review workflow. The system’s analytical pipeline organizes match events into taxonomy-grounded feedback, while its interface links structured reports to rally summaries, video evidence, and court visualizations. A within-subjects study (N=16) shows that TactiPlay elicits more frequent, concrete, actionable, and appropriate reflections than a report-and-statistics baseline. These findings show how organizing reviewed match evidence into a taxonomy-guided, video-linked workflow can support amateur players’ tactical reflection.

contents.title: Explorable Proofs: Making Written Proofs Explorable by Grounding Them in Formal Representations
contents.abstract: LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed, tinkered with, or stepped through. In this paper, we explore how grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension in explorable proofs, an approach that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging between steps. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on an example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study (n = 16) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-understanding task, participants who used the explorability features wrote proof descriptions that an instructor preferred over those written with a proof-and-chatbot baseline, and gave more correct and more detailed answers to proof comprehension questions.

contents.title: Stund: Activity-Enriched Collaborative Workspaces Mediated by Artificial Intelligence
contents.abstract: Time is a second-class citizen in most collaborative software: activity traces are fragmented across tools or entirely ephemeral. We introduce Stund, an activity-enriched collaborative workspace where all activities—voice, video, interactions, and content edits—leave traces that become part of the medium of the ongoing collaboration. Unlike traditional chatbots or meeting assistants, artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded in the medium as well, allowing users to directly leverage traces through it. We demonstrate this through scenarios such as: spontaneously creating an instrument during the meeting to play back the recorded conversation around a particular spreadsheet edit; automatically detecting when someone is absent to summarize what was missed when they return; or detecting and resurfacing when sticky notes have been shaken in excitement when ideas are presented. The entire workspace is queryable, transformable, and reifiable through AI. Stund introduces a new approach to malleable collaborative software, where activity traces and AI are an integral part of the workspace medium.

contents.title: Inertia in Your Hand: Rendering Virtual Tool Dynamics via In-Hand Cutaneous Deformation
contents.abstract: We present the Inertia Handle, a handheld haptic device that renders virtual tool dynamics through in-hand cutaneous deformation. The device reproduces relative motion between the handle and the hand when users swing virtual tools with different lengths, weights, and mass distributions. We model hand-tool coupling as an axis-specific rotational spring-damper system and update its parameters from the measured grip force. Through three studies, we evaluate (1) hand-tool rotational impedance, (2) perception of virtual tool direction and length, and (3) haptic experience in VR tool-use scenarios. Results show that stiffness and damping increased across grip force levels and differed across axes. Users identified virtual tool direction across multiple directions and discriminated rod length from in-hand cutaneous cues. In VR scenarios, the device improved haptic experience over a commercial VR controller, and tool-specific rendering further improved the realism and visual-haptic congruence of tool use. These findings show that in-hand cutaneous deformation can render virtual tool dynamics in VR without external weights or large actuators.

contents.title: SnapAxis: Axis Based Interaction for Object Manipulation in Mixed Reality
contents.abstract: Accurate 3D object manipulation in mixed reality remains difficult when targets are distant or partially occluded. Existing techniques often improve local stages such as target acquisition or fine adjustment, but pay less attention to maintaining a stable and interpretable manipulation reference across acquisition, placement, and refinement. This forces users to repeatedly reinterpret control mappings, increasing cognitive load and reducing refinement stability. We present SnapAxis, an Axis based Interaction framework for MR object manipulation through smartphone. SnapAxis is organized around the Semantic Axis Handle, a shared object centered reference that links acquisition, placement, and refinement. The framework consists of three stages: ZoomCapture for target acquisition, Coarse Manipulation for Semantic Axis Handle establishment, and Fine Manipulation for continued refinement around the established reference. A within subject user study showed that SnapAxis significantly improved task efficiency and 3D alignment accuracy while reducing phone movement, head view search burden, and subjective workload.

contents.title: ChatMuse: Supporting In-Person Small-Group Conversation Experience with a Proactive Assistive AI Agent in Mixed Reality
contents.abstract: In-person small-group conversations play a crucial role in social interaction. However, achieving effective group conversations can be challenging and cognitively demanding. While Mixed Reality (MR) headsets show promise as a conversational support system by presenting relevant information through MR overlays, it remains unclear how such supporting information should be designed for in-person group conversations. We propose ChatMuse, an MR-based proactive assistive system for in-person small-group conversations. ChatMuse analyzes verbal and nonverbal cues from all conversation participants and proactively provides guidance on the user's verbal and nonverbal behaviors. The behavioral responses of the supported users are then used to improve ChatMuse's support capabilities in subsequent interactions. Our within-subject studies alongside focus groups with six participant groups (N = 18) revealed seven key benefits that ChatMuse provides in supporting users' engagement and contributions to in-person small-group conversations. Our research around ChatMuse represents a design exploration of a new interaction space that investigates the feasibility of supporting in-person small-group conversations through a proactive assistive AI agent in MR.

contents.title: TailorCoPilot: Enabling Agentic Pattern Making with Version-Controlled State Tracking
contents.abstract: Experience-driven manufacturing, such as garment pattern making, faces a severe generational skills gap because its core expertise relies on undocumented tacit knowledge forged through day-to-day practice. To address this challenge, we present TailorCoPilot, an agentic pattern-making system built upon a specially designed version-control backend TailorTrace. TailorTrace models sewing patterns as structured, discrete states and records their transformations during the pattern-making process as explicit operation sequences defined upon the geometry primitives in the sewing pattern (panels, edges, vertices and stitches). Integrated into a conventional pattern-making GUI, TailorTrace enables seamless documentation of senior experts' tacit pattern-making knowledge without breaking their daily workflow. The documented knowledge further offers interactive, pedagogical scaffolding for novices, while providing a robust foundation to power TailorCoPilot and train future generative AI models. In a user study with novices and advanced novices, TailorCoPilot improved task completion rates, reduced time and perceived workload, and yielded higher-quality artifacts compared to skill-appropriate baselines. Ultimately, TailorCoPilot demonstrates a viable pathway to capture practice-based expertise, operationalizing it to support both generative AI advancements and human apprenticeship.

contents.title: Print&Fold: Printing and Folding Shape-accurate 3D Models
contents.abstract: This paper introduces Print&Fold, a tool to allow FDM 3D printing of complex models with less time and material while preserving shape accuracy. Key to this work is a folding algorithm that planarizes foldable faces internal to the 3D model. While folding techniques typically discretize a target model's surface, thereby fabricating low fidelity counterparts, our method preserves the surface features in the physical print. Our design tool allows users to unfold 3D models to be FDM-printed flat before manually folding these into their target shapes. We showcase a variety of applications and evaluate the material and time savings across a range of 3D models.

contents.title: SnowEcho: End-to-End Blind Skiing Assistance System Using Spatial Audio for Simulated Dynamic Slope
contents.abstract: Blind skiing usually relies on a sighted guide, limiting opportunities for independent participation. Prior ski assistance systems mainly use route guidance and assume static obstacles or ideal sensing, making them less suitable for crowded, dynamic slopes. We present SnowEcho, a skiing assistance system for people with visual impairments (PVI) that uses spatial audio to convey obstacle direction and distance, allowing skiers to choose their own line. In a simulator study with visually impaired skiers, SnowEcho improved obstacle avoidance and increased clearance in dense dynamic environments compared with a route-guidance baseline, while also improving perceived independence and consistency. We further tested an end-to-end sensing pipeline with depth-based detection and segmentation. Performance remained close to simulator ground truth conditions under moderate noise, but severe noise reduced clearance, confidence, and feedback consistency. These findings indicate both the promise of spatial audio scene awareness and the importance of cue stability under realistic sensing noise.

contents.title: EIJaw: Non-Invasive Intraoral User Interface with Electrical Impedance Sensing
contents.abstract: Oral interfaces provide an alternative to conventional input methods for hands-free interaction in assistive and multitasking scenarios, yet existing solutions are limited by lacking capability of detecting internal muscle movements or safety risks from intraoral electronics. Inspired by electrical impedance (EI) tomography, we introduce EIJaw, a non-invasive prototype that characterizes intraoral movements through impedance variations in suprahyoid muscles. We demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments with six participants performing kana pronunciation, silent pronunciation, and tongue movement tasks, achieving feasible classification of diverse intraoral movements via deep learning. By eliminating the need for electronics inside the mouth while maintaining feasible recognition accuracy, EIJaw offers a proof of concept for future oral interface applications with electrical impedance measurement technology.

contents.title: TangiMap: Context-Aware Generative Function Mapping for Tangible Input Devices
contents.abstract: While tangible input devices with physical controls such as knobs and sliders enable efficient interaction, they often lack the flexibility to adapt to dynamic contexts, limiting their use to predefined applications with fixed functionalities. In this paper, we introduce TangiMap, a proof-of-concept system that bridges tangible input devices with dynamic software contexts by generating adaptive function mappings for hardware controls. To achieve this, TangiMap analyzes the user's declared hardware specifications, the available controls, and the target software context, and uses large language models (LLMs) to assign suitable functions to each control element. To support diverse contexts, TangiMap presents multiple strategies such as API queries and screen parsing. We demonstrate the system through four scenarios: interactive adjustment of natural language parameters in 3D modeling, live music performance, task-aware mapping of on-screen controls in image editing, and dynamic puppeteering in animation.

contents.title: ITO: Real-time Browser Tab Orchestration Through Intent Detection
contents.abstract: People routinely interleave activities while browsing the web, often simultaneously and with overlapping boundaries. Yet organizational primitives in modern browsers treat every tab uniformly, offering no structural awareness of which items serve which purpose. While task-based organization approaches exist, they typically require users to manually organize or invoke reorganization features, and quickly fall out of sync as user intents evolve. To address this, we present Ito, a mixed-initiative approach that infers user intent in real time and organizes browsing activities into dynamic collections called Flows. Ito continuously reads unfolding user context, determines moment-to-moment focus, and creates, restructures, hibernates, and awakens Flows in real time while preserving user control through a mixed-initiative loop of proposals and corrections. In a controlled lab study (N=12) and a two-week field study (N=11), results suggest that Ito's intent-driven Flows aligned more closely with participants' mental models, facilitated task switching and navigation more effectively, and reduced management burden without loss of perceived control.

contents.title: Offline Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Support in AI-Assisted Decision-Making
contents.abstract: AI decision-support tools typically offer a fixed type of assistance, like AI recommendations and explanations, regardless of the specific decision, individual, or broader context. This fixed design has been shown to hinder both human-AI decision accuracy and human skill improvement in the task. We posit that AI assistance needs to be dynamic, changing in response to contextual factors (e.g., AI uncertainty, task difficulty), individual differences, and specified objectives (e.g., decision accuracy, skill improvement). To enable such adaptive support, we propose reinforcement learning (RL) as a general approach for modeling human-AI decision-making to optimize human-AI interaction for diverse objectives. RL enables optimizing various objectives in AI-assisted decision-making by tailoring and adaptively providing decision support to humans — the right type of assistance, to the right person, at the right time. We instantiated our approach with two objectives: human-AI accuracy on the decision-making task and human skill improvement (i.e., learning about the task) and learned decision support policies from previous human-AI interaction data. We compared the optimized policies against several baselines in AI-assisted decision-making. Across two experiments (N = 316 and N = 964), our results consistently demonstrated that people interacting with policies optimized for accuracy achieve significantly higher accuracy — and even human-AI complementarity — compared to those interacting with any other type of AI support. Our results further indicated that human learning was more difficult to optimize than accuracy. While the policies learned the best available actions to optimize learning, participants who interacted with learning-optimized policies showed significant learning improvement only at times. Our research (1) demonstrates offline RL to be a promising approach to model the dynamics of human-AI decision-making, leading to policies that may optimize various objectives and provide novel insights about the AI-assisted decision-making space, and (2) emphasizes the importance of considering skill improvement and other human-centric objectives beyond accuracy in AI-assisted decision-making, opening up the novel research challenge of optimizing human-AI interaction for such objectives.

contents.title: Collascope: Supporting Serendipitous Asset Exploration for Collage-Based Storytelling
contents.abstract: Collage-based storytelling requires visual elements that support emerging narratives and inspire creative reinterpretation. Existing tools, however, rely largely on keyword- and image-based retrieval, offering limited support for serendipitous exploration beyond existing assets. We introduce Collascope, an interactive system that helps creators (1) concretize story intent with interactive element groups, (2) expand the exploration space based on concepts or cutouts towards conceptual and visual dimensions, and (3) develop grounded, traceable ideas in parallel with collage composition. Collascope's attribute-aware visual retrieval method, instantiated with collage-relevant visual dimensions, enables creators to retrieve cutouts through dimension-specific visual projections rather than holistic similarity. In a within-subject study (N=12) against a conventional search baseline, our participants used unexpected results and even gaps in the asset collection to redirect narratives, shift tone, and enrich compositions. Scene Parts helped organize exploration into manageable subtasks, while participants used association in distinct ways depending on whether exploration was guided by a clear goal, an evolving story, or visual intuition.

contents.title: XTick: Rendering Omnidirectional Hit-and-Hold Impact Feedback All Round a Controller by Integrating Impact and Pressing Force
contents.abstract: Impact feedback, characterized by a sharp force increase and short duration, is common in VR. In some scenarios, it includes an impact peak followed by sustained force with smaller magnitude, extending overall duration of such hit-and-hold impact feedback, e.g., swords pressing, or shields resisting projectiles or falling rocks, which is critical but less discussed. Rendering impact at position and direction corresponding to VR is also crucial. We propose a controller, XTick, rendering omnidirectional short-duration instant impact and long-duration hit-and-hold impact all round the controller by integrating impact and pressing force. XTick enables omnidirectional pressing force integrated with impact at various positions and directions for any duration. To achieve seamless integration, we investigated two factors: force magnitude alignment between impact and pressing force in Study 1, and transition between initial impact and sustained force in Study 2. A VR study verified that XTick's integrated feedback enhances VR experiences and demonstrates applications.

contents.title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
contents.abstract: AI programming tutors provide scalable support, yet lack the behavioral context human tutors rely on to adapt support to learners' needs. We present TutorTrace, a dataset and behavioral abstraction pipeline that makes learners' behavioral context visible and computable in real time from low-level IDE telemetry. Across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480), TutorTrace captures approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics. From this foundation, we derive a taxonomy of learner activity before the first AI query, between consecutive queries, and across the full session, enabling systems to respond not just to what learners say, but to what they have done leading up to the help-seeking moment. In a preliminary classroom evaluation, behavior-aware prompts were associated with a decrease in intervals between queries with no independent work from 50.0% to 20.7%. As an additional demonstration of downstream utility, we evaluate TutorTrace on two held-out prediction tasks: whether a learner will query within the next 60 seconds (AUROC=.726) and whether an upcoming query reflects guided or dependent help-seeking (AUROC=.717). Together, these findings show how behavioral context can enable adaptive AI tutoring at scale.

contents.title: TwistForm: Shaping Reconfigurable 3D Surfaces via Pre-programmed Torsional Deformation of Chains
contents.abstract: In this paper, we propose TwistForm, a novel shape-forming method that leverages torsion-actuated chains to reconstruct pre-programmed 3D surfaces. By parametrically designing the geometric interlocking of individual ring units, our approach encodes 3D surfaces into continuous, 1D kinematic chains. Upon the application of torsion, these chains undergo a structural phase transition, physically deploying into the pre-programmed 3D shapes. Because this 1D encoding inherently enables significant volumetric compression, TwistForm effectively addresses spatial constraints associated with the transportation and storage of physical objects. To realize this, we developed an end-to-end fabrication framework for designing and physicalizing these chains. Users can utilize this system to import arbitrary 3D models, design the corresponding interlinked chain structures, and export optimized print data for fabrication. We detail the underlying algorithms for unit design and spatial layout, and demonstrate practical use cases, including compact shipping, reusable molds, and shape-changing interfaces.

contents.title: A Text-Native Interface for Generative Video Authoring
contents.abstract: Everyone can write their stories in freeform text format -- it's something we all learn in school, yet authoring video requires one to learn specialized and complicated tools. In this paper, we introduce Doki, a text-native interface for generative video authoring. In Doki, writing text is the primary interaction: within a single document, users define assets, structure scenes, generate shots, refine edits, and add audio. We articulate the design principles of this text-native approach and demonstrate Doki's capabilities through examples. We ran a week-long diary study with 10 participants of varied expertise. Participants produced 46 videos, reporting faster idea‑to‑draft flow, improved coherence through parameterization, and clearer comprehension of narrative structure in the document view; they also surfaced limitations around model predictability, precise control, and temporal expressivity. With Doki, we explore a fundamental shift in generative video interfaces, and demonstrate a powerful and accessible new way to craft visual stories.

contents.title: PACEE: Parent-Centered AI Scaffolding for Emotion Education in Early Childhood Conversations
contents.abstract: Emotion education is critical for children aged 3 to 6. However, existing technologies depend substantially on direct child-AI interaction, overlooking the central role of parents in guiding early emotional development at home. To address this gap, we conducted co-design sessions with five kindergarten teachers and five parents to identify key parental challenges and opportunities for AI support in family emotion education. Based on these insights, we developed PACEE, an LLM-based assistant designed around an asymmetric triadic interaction framework: AI primarily supports parents while preserving parent-child interaction. PACEE provides parent-centered AI scaffolding that supports parents in real-time conversation through personalized guidance, post-hoc reflection through trackable feedback, and understanding children’s emotional states through modeling. We evaluated PACEE with 16 families. Results showed that PACEE increased parent-child conversational engagement and improved parents’ overall experience when guiding emotion-related conversations. Together, we contribute an asymmetric triadic interaction framework for AI-supported family education, offering design insights for AI systems that support parents while preserving parent-led parent–child interaction.

contents.title: CLOAK: A Privacy-Preserving Assistant for Online Social Media Users
contents.abstract: Many people share personal details on platforms like Reddit under the assumption that a pseudonymous account keeps their identity safe. They do not realize that a profession mentioned in one subreddit, a hobby in another, and a neighborhood in a third can be pieced together to narrow down exactly who they are. Large language models have made this kind of cross-post profiling easy to do at scale. Yet existing tools offer little help: PII scanners catch names and emails but miss contextual cues, and even LLM-based privacy systems analyze only the current post in isolation, missing the cross-post combinations that actually compromise anonymity. We present CLOAK, a system that examines a user’s full posting history alongside their draft comment and shows them the identification risk before they post. A pipeline of four LLM agents extracts a structured attribute profile from prior posts, identifies cross-post interactions that narrow the anonymity set, ranks risky phrases, and suggests minimal edits that preserve the user’s intent. CLOAK is designed as an awareness tool for informed self-disclosure: rather than blocking or redacting content, it helps users understand the trade-offs and decide for themselves. In a technical evaluation on 368 Reddit profiles, CLOAK detected cross-post tipping points in 77% of cases while the status quo baseline detected none. In a user study (N =20), CLOAK was unanimously selected as the most helpful tool (trust: 6.5/7 vs. 1.5/7 for PII scanning), and every participant reported changed posting behavior.

contents.title: Sticki: Personalized Content Moderation Using Image Overlays for Recontextualizing Aversive Videos
contents.abstract:
As digital content consumption increases, users are frequently exposed to aversive stimuli. Yet, conventional moderation methods often disrupt content context by obscuring objects and do not account for individual sensitivity. 
To address this, we present Sticki, a context-preserving moderation framework that supports reappraisal of aversive objects through animated image overlays. Sticki also enables users to select moderation targets and methods before exposure, supporting autonomy and psychological comfort.
In a user study with 32 participants using surveys and interviews, Sticki achieved a better balance between two goals (i.e., disgust reduction and context preservation) than conventional methods.
Sticki also provides users with a greater sense of autonomy and psychological comfort. We further discuss how individual sensitivity and viewing motivation shape users' prioritization between the two goals, with implications for personalized content moderation system design.

contents.title: PressMic: Multi-Level Press Input on Commodity Devices Using Built-in Microphones
contents.abstract: We present PressMic, a passive acoustic method that enables multi-level press input on commodity devices using built-in microphones. PressMic introduces a notched annulus around the microphone vent, forming a compact press-sensitive acoustic interface. Upon finger contact, the device enclosure and the annular boundary create a local acoustic configuration near the vent. A light press produces a detectable resonance from the front cavity, whereas a hard press blocks the vent and suppresses acoustic coupling. PressMic uses an event-driven signal pipeline to detect press events and classify press levels from short segments. We validate the mechanism with controlled cavity-variation experiments and then evaluate the system on a commodity smartphone across diverse scenarios. For light-versus-hard classification, PressMic achieves 95.9% accuracy, 0.94 Macro-F1, and 0.92 AUC. Across the complete two-stage pipeline, PressMic achieves 94.2% accuracy and a Macro-F1 of 0.932 for three-state recognition. These results demonstrate that passive acoustic modulation using built-in microphones—especially noise-canceling or array types—enables multi-level press input with only a low-profile, cleanable structure around the vent, without active sensing or extra sensors.

contents.title: Map2Video: Guiding Real-World-Grounded AI Video Generation
contents.abstract: AI video generation lowers barriers to video creation, but existing tools provide limited support for grounding content in real-world locations, restricting their use in applications such as film previsualization and scenario generation. In practice, users rely on verbose textual descriptions or reference images using on-site photos or street view imagery (SVI), which are cumbersome and unreliable across shots. Our formative study with five filmmakers revealed challenges in shot composition, character motion, and camera control when using SVI with an image-to-video tool. We present Map2Video, a system for guiding SVI-grounded AI video generation through map-based character trajectory annotation and direct manipulation of cameras and character masks defined in geodetic coordinates and projected onto panoramic screen coordinates. In an evaluation with twelve filmmakers, Map2Video provided stronger controllability for both scene replication and open-ended creative exploration, reduced cognitive effort, and improved spatial consistency across multiple shots compared to an image-to-video baseline.

contents.title: MuTable: Composable and Reusable Table Transformations for In-Situ Data Exploration
contents.abstract: Tables are central to data work to support precise lookup and full detail, but they can be limiting for overview and pattern-finding tasks. Visualizations are then created to gain richer perceptual support. In practice, moving between tables and charts often requires maintaining parallel representations, introducing context switching, and extra coordination work. Building on prior hybrid table-visualization systems, we present MuTable, a prototype that reifies transformations as persistent, composable, and reusable modifiers to support in-situ data exploration. Users reshape the table through layout, style, and computation actions, with the ability to inspect, revise, and reuse these transformations. An expert interview with eight data workers suggests that MuTable can support coordination between representations, rapid exploration, and greater user agency in constructing visualizations, highlighting the potential of MuTable as a low-commitment data exploration space.

contents.title: Textro: A Prototyping Toolkit for Solderless and Chipless Smart Textile Interfaces
contents.abstract: In this paper, we present Textro, a prototyping toolkit for designing, fabricating, and testing solderless and chipless smart textile interfaces. Unlike prior approaches that rely on rigid components or soldered connections, Textro enables users to build functional textile interfaces using only readily available materials and tools. The toolkit integrates three parts: (1) a web-based design environment for importing sewing patterns, defining sensing elements, and automatically generating optimized component and circuit designs based on empirical experiments; (2) a fabrication pipeline that generates fabrication files for embroidery and cutting machines, with embroidery optimized for one-stroke continuous stitching paths and components assembled through glue-based attachment methods via capacitive coupling; and (3) a reader device and software for wirelessly retrieving sensor data and visualizing real-time sensor signals. We demonstrate Textro through four application examples and conduct a user study with fashion experts, makers, and novices, highlighting its usability and potential for smart textile prototyping.

contents.title: Interactively Teaching Collaborative Physical Tasks in Simulation to Generative AI with Narrated Demonstrations
contents.abstract: Enabling users to teach computers how to perform physical tasks is a long-standing goal in HCI. Prior work has explored learning from demonstration, but demonstrations often underspecify intent. Advances in generative AI enable a combination of demonstration and verbal narration to disambiguate intent. However, it remains largely unexplored how to design interfaces that leverage such narrated demonstrations to teach collaborative physical tasks. To probe this design space, we present a prototype system, Apprento, that models physical tasks as programs via generative AI with three integrated interfaces: (1) a teaching interface for providing narrated demonstrations in mixed reality, (2) an inspection interface for visualizing generated programs as decision-flow diagrams and program executions, and (3) a correction interface for iteratively refining generated programs. Across these interfaces, narrated demonstrations serve as a communication modality between users and the system. In a study with 20 participants teaching soccer skills, we identify differing user expectations around authoring and teaching collaborative tasks, as well as key design tensions between task complexity and program interpretability, and between program expressivity and accuracy. We discuss implications for designing future systems that support symbolic modeling of collaborative physical tasks through narrated demonstrations.

contents.title: Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making
contents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly equipped with augmented reasoning capabilities to generate rationales that support human decision-making. Yet these text-dense rationales often impose substantial cognitive burdens. Building on a formative co-design study that identified user preferences for non-linear reasoning representations, we we developed Graphionale as a testbed for empirically studying argument-map-style rationale visualization. This system transforms linear LLM rationales into interactive, multi-level graph visualizations. It explicitly structures logical relationships (e.g., conclusions, premises, support, and objections), while further extracting entities and relations within each statement to construct condensed node-link representations. We conduct a large-scale online user study (𝑁 = 204) to examine when graphical rationales are more effective than textual ones, across varying task modality (verbal vs. visual reasoning), rationale format (textual vs. graphical), and question difficulty (easy vs. hard). Our results show that graphical rationales do not help uniformly: they improve trust calibration for verbal reasoning yet feel more cognitively demanding and less satisfying; for visual reasoning, they impair calibration yet feel more engaging and helpful. In each modality, the format that better supports calibrated decisions is not the one users prefer, highlighting that matching rationale format to task modality is key to effective AI explanation design. Our findings contribute empirical design knowledge about when and how graphical rationales support human decision making, and inform the next-generation reasoning-aware AI interfaces.

contents.title: From Scaffolding to Internalization: Enhancing CPR Training with In-Situ Visualization and Kinesthetic Feedback
contents.abstract: CPR training requires learners to not only understand explicit procedural targets, such as compression depth and rate, but also to internalize these targets as stable psychomotor skills. However, existing CPR training systems often rely on feedback presented outside the action space, which divides learners' attention between performing compressions and monitoring external guidance. This separation weakens the coupling between action and bodily sensation and may lead to an over-reliance on external feedback, compromising skill retention once support is removed. To address this challenge, we conducted a formative study with novice trainees and certified BLS instructors, from which we derived three design goals: embedding feedback within the task space, providing active kinesthetic guidance, and gradually fading assistance based on learning phases. Informed by these insights, we designed Kinesthetic-CPR, a stage-adaptive multimodal mixed reality CPR training system, and evaluated it in a controlled user study across two sub-studies (N = 60). This work offers design implications for CPR training systems that aim to better support skill retention.

contents.title: Cellery: Gradual, Composable Structure for Spreadsheets
contents.abstract: Structure in spreadsheets is typically restricted to ranges of cells and flat tables. However, replacing the open-ended two-dimensional grid with a more structured alternative risks limiting users' freedom and impeding exploratory workflows. How can we enable expressive structure in spreadsheets while preserving their flexibility? We propose a model that allows users to gradually add structure on top of the traditional grid. To identify common structural patterns, we conducted a content analysis of 30 real-world spreadsheets. Based on our findings, we developed Cellery, a novel spreadsheet system that makes these structures explicit. In Cellery, users gradually define the structure of their spreadsheets using named groupings of cells, composing together four structural primitives: Atoms, Lists, Tables, and Blocks. Once defined, users can directly manipulate structures, dynamically reference them in formulas, and incorporate them in reusable abstractions. We evaluate Cellery with an expressiveness study reproducing spreadsheets from our sample, demonstrating that it is capable of representing types of structure that traditional spreadsheets cannot. In a preliminary user study of five participants, we find that they successfully use Cellery to design spreadsheets with explicit structure, and we uncover opportunities for further work on the formula language.

contents.title: Spatula: Exploring On-Demand In-Situ Interfaces and Interaction for Attribute Control
contents.abstract: Controlling attributes is a critical step toward achieving the final creative outcome, yet current approaches fall short in supporting users in the iterative refinement of generative content. We propose Spatula, a proof-of-concept system that generates on-demand, in-situ attribute control interfaces and interactions for creating motion graphics. Building on a technical probe that automatically analyzes animation context and generates corresponding attributes and UI, we frame attribute control as an explorable landscape and explore the attribute control space along four key dimensions: Discoverability, Resolution, Scope, and Expandability. Findings from a user study (N=12) show that our system provides intuitive and convenient interactions while supporting diverse needs for fine-grained parameter control. Furthermore, our applications demonstrate that the plug-and-play design generalizes to other domains, such as web design and 3D modeling.

contents.title: "What Are You Really Trying to Do?": Co-Creating Life Goals from Everyday Computer Use
contents.abstract: Recent advances in user modeling make it feasible to conduct open-ended inference over a person's everyday computer use. Despite longstanding visions of systems that deeply understand our actions and the purposes they serve in our lives, existing systems only capture what a person is doing in the moment, not why they are doing it, limiting these systems to surface-level support. We introduce striving co-creation, a process for inferring broader life goals from unstructured observations of computer use. Grounded in Activity Theory and Emmons' personal strivings framework, our system progressively constructs a hierarchical representation of a person's activities. Strivings are, however, difficult to fully resolve from observation alone, as the same action can be driven by many different goals. Our system therefore supports an editing interface that gives people agency over how they are understood by the system, feeding their corrections back into subsequent rounds of striving induction. In a week-long field deployment (N = 14), we find that our co-creation process produces strivings that participants recognize as representative of their long-term goals and gives them greater agency than baseline methods.

contents.title: SilkSense: A Craft-Inspired Fabrication Method for Silk-based Functional Textile
contents.abstract: While silk is attractive for on-body sensing due to its biocompatibility and skin affinity, its smooth fiber surface and limited capillary absorption make it poorly suited to existing fabrication methods based on liquid infiltration and mechanical anchoring. Inspired by Gambiered Canton Gauze (Xiangyunsha), a traditional craft with a centuries-long history of silk surface modification, we present SilkSense, a fabric-level workflow for functionalizing commercially available silk. By analyzing the craft's core processing stages and identifying the underlying interfacial mechanisms, we organize the responsible material components into a two-stage workflow: Dioscorea cirrhosa polyphenol pretreatment followed by Fe-HA/FA and PEDOT: PSS composite coating. The resulting fabric supports mask-based patterning (up to 1.5 mm resolution) and freehand painting and exhibits wash durability (approximately 15.6% resistance drift after 20 high-intensity cycles)  under our test conditions. SilkSense fabric enables three on-body input modalities, including pressing, bending, and pinching, whose sensing characteristics can be translated into wearable interface designs across different body locations, validated through a drone control demonstration in which subtle single-hand finger movements drive three-channel real-time closed-loop interaction. Together, these results show how craft-derived interfacial principles can support patternable, maintainable, and multimodal silk-based interaction surfaces.

contents.title: Electrotactile Retargeting in Orientation Perception of Teleoperated Tools
contents.abstract: In robotic teleoperation, operators rely mainly on visual feedback; however, misalignment between hand posture and tool orientation, often caused by collision-induced deviations, cannot be fully resolved from a single viewpoint due to limited spatial information. To address this, an electrotactile retargeting method is proposed that uses electrotactile stimulation to render palm pressure distribution patterns, enabling perception of tool orientation under hand–tool misalignment. In Study 1, an electrotactile retargeting model based on a separable variable formulation is developed to quantify how cutaneous sensation modulates the mapping between controller orientation and perceived tool orientation. In Study 2, the method is validated in peg-in-hole and trajectory tracing tasks. Results show improved performance and telepresence compared to baselines. This work extends electrotactile feedback for orientation perception in teleoperation and advances multisensory spatial integration.

contents.title: RemiAssist: A Therapist-Supporting System for Photo-Based Reminiscence Therapy in Dementia Care
contents.abstract: Despite growing interest in applying AI to photo-based reminiscence therapy (PRT) for people with dementia (PwD), existing systems primarily focus on PwD-AI interaction and often overlook therapists' critical role in practical PRT delivery. We present RemiAssist, a system that supports therapist-in-the-loop PRT through AI-assisted planning and real-time facilitation. RemiAssist incorporates two core techniques: (1) a Memory Graph, which organizes key life events from a PwD's photo collection into a hierarchical graph to support theme-centered intervention planning; and (2) a Context-Aware Guiding Strategy, which provides real-time suggestions to help therapists guide reminiscence conversations and respond to sensitive situations. A field study with eight therapist–PwD dyads suggests RemiAssist was associated with a 44% improvement in planning efficiency, a 54% increase in conversation duration, and timely support for handling sensitive situations. We highlight opportunities for AI systems to empower therapists and enable more personalized reminiscence therapy in dementia care.

contents.title: Tap2Stop: Pedestrian-Activated Emergency Stop for Autonomous Vehicles
contents.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) remain imperfect in close-range interactions, where sensor blind spots and unpredictable pedestrian behavior lead to safety-critical failures. Existing emergency-stop mechanisms are typically limited to remote operators or passengers, leaving pedestrians unable to intervene. We propose Tap2Stop, an externally accessible mechanism that enables pedestrians to "actively'' stop vehicles by tapping on the surface. A formative study (23 pedestrians, 8 AV developers) reveals a gap between pedestrians’ desire for intervention and developers’ concerns about misuse. Guided by these insights, we develop a tapping-based system integrating two classifiers (tapping detection and intent classification) with a gating and accumulation mechanism to balance robustness and reaction time. Study 1 constructs a dataset across multiple conditions to train the classifiers and optimize parameters. Study 2 evaluates the system in a field study (N=18), showing promising performance (100% detection rate, 24% false positive rate), user acceptance, and providing insights for future bidirectional human-vehicle interaction.

contents.title: Stayin' Aligned Over Time: Towards Longitudinal Human-LLM Alignment via Contextual Reflection and Privacy-Preserving Behavioral Data
contents.abstract: Current human-AI alignment and evaluation methods for large language models (LLMs) often rely on preference signals collected immediately after an interaction. This practice implicitly treats preference as static, even though many LLM-mediated decisions unfold over time and may be re-evaluated differently after real-world consequences and observed outcomes. Therefore, we argue for a methodological shift from single-moment preference elicitation to longitudinal, context-situated alignment measurement. We present a methodological framework and system for longitudinal preference collection that combines (1) in-situ evaluation, (2) context-triggered follow-up reflection, and (3) privacy-preserving behavioral traces that help contextualize evaluation revisions. As an instantiation of this methodology, we introduce BITE, a browser-based system that detects consequential LLM interactions, prompts reflection across later decision points, and supports progressive, user-controlled consent for sharing behavioral data. Through a two-week proof-of-concept deployment with eight participants, our approach captured differences between participants’ immediate and delayed evaluations of LLM outputs across dimensions including accuracy, trust, and relevance. Our findings highlight the limitations of single-moment preference datasets and underscore the importance of longitudinal methods for alignment evaluation in everyday use.

contents.title: From Words to Widgets for Controllable LLM Generation
contents.abstract: Natural language remains the predominant way people interact with large language models (LLMs). However, users often struggle to precisely express and control subjective preferences (e.g., tone, style, and emphasis) through prompting. We propose Malleable Prompting, a new interactive prompting technique for controllable LLM generation. It reifies preference expressions in natural language prompts into GUI widgets (e.g., sliders, dropdowns, and toggles) that users can directly configure to steer generation, while visualizing each control's influence on the output to support attribution and comparison across iterations. To enable this interaction, we introduce an LLM decoding algorithm that modulates the token probability distribution during generation based on preference expressions and their widget values. Through a user study, we show that Malleable Prompting helps participants achieve target preferences more precisely and is perceived as more controllable and transparent than natural language prompting alone.

contents.title: Remapping Time in Augmented Reality
contents.abstract:
Video see-through augmented reality (VST AR) mediates the physical world through a camera capture--processing--display pipeline, making visual time computationally controllable. Yet this capability as a design consideration remains underexplored. 
We define and formalize time remapping as the intentional, real-time manipulation of how visual world time is presented to the user, and model it as a first-order dynamical system that balances delay accumulation and recovery. To evaluate its perceptual effectiveness, we conducted a within-subjects study (N=21) in which participants identified briefly visible playing cards under baseline and remapped conditions, varying temporal anchor (self vs. external) and control (user vs. system). Time remapping approximately doubled identification accuracy without significantly reducing comfort, with gains consistent across all remapped conditions. Building on these findings and qualitative interviews, we derive a six-dimensional design space and instantiate it through three application prototypes. This paper establishes time remapping as a practical design material, introducing programmable time as a new dimension for AR experience design.

contents.title: UXCascade: Scalable Usability Testing with Simulated User Agents
contents.abstract: Simulated user agents are increasingly deployed in usability testing to support fast, iterative UX workflows, as they generate rich data such as action logs and think-aloud reasoning, but the unstructured nature of this output often obscures actionable insights. We present UXCascade, an interactive tool for extracting, aggregating, and presenting agent-generated usability feedback at scale. Our core contribution is a multi-level analysis workflow that (1) highlights patterns across persona traits, goals, and outcomes, (2) links agent reasoning to specific issues, and (3) supports actionable design improvements. UXCascade operationalizes this approach by listing agent goals, traits, and issues in a structured overview. Practitioners can explore detailed reasoning traces and annotated views, propose interface edits, and assess their impact across personas. This enables a top-down, exploration-driven analysis from patterns to concrete, actionable UX interventions. A user study with eight UX professionals demonstrates that UXCascade integrates into existing workflows, enabling iterative feedback during early-stage interface development.

contents.title: KnitARobo: Industrial Machine Knitting of Electromechanical Textile Interfaces with Liquid Crystal Elastomer Fibers
contents.abstract: Electromechanical textiles combine the unique properties of controllable shape-changing materials with the affordances of conventional fabrics. However, most actuation mechanisms are fabricated using bespoke techniques incompatible with mass manufacturing. We present KnitARobo, a technique for automatically machine-knitting liquid-crystal elastomer textile actuators. Parameterized variations in the knitting pattern produce various morphologies. Additionally, we provide an open-source PCB design for wearable, untethered actuation control. By characterizing these actuators and demonstrating three morphing garments, we demonstrate the value of our three guiding principles for electromechanical textile design: clothing-centric design, compatibility with mass manufacturing, and integration of controllable actuation.

contents.title: MAESTRO: Adapting GUIs and Guiding Navigation with User Preferences in Conversational Agents with GUIs
contents.abstract: Modern task-oriented chatbots present GUI elements alongside natural-language dialogue, yet the agent's role has largely been limited to interpreting natural-language input as GUI actions and following a linear workflow. In preference-driven, multi-step tasks such as booking a flight or reserving a restaurant, earlier choices constrain later options and may force users to restart from scratch. User preferences serve as the key criteria for these decisions, yet existing agents do not systematically leverage them. We present MAESTRO, which extends the agent's role from execution to decision support. MAESTRO maintains a shared preference memory that extracts hard and soft preferences from natural-language utterances and provides two mechanisms. Preference-Grounded GUI Adaptation applies in-place operators (augment, sort, filter, and highlight) to the existing GUI according to preference strength, supporting comparison among options. Preference-Guided Workflow Navigation detects conflicts between preferences and available options, proposes backtracking, and records failed paths to avoid revisiting dead ends. Through a controlled experiment (N=33), we demonstrated that MAESTRO improved decision quality in movie ticketing: final bookings left fewer hard preferences unmet, and users made fewer selections that violated their stated preferences during the process than in the baseline condition, although task success rate and completion time did not differ significantly. In addition, we showed that using MAESTRO in voice mode can increase users' active engagement as well as their mental burden, revealing the nuanced tension in agentic interaction design for conversational agents with a GUI.
