contents.title: Spray and Etch: Personal Fabrication of High-Resolution Electroluminescent Displays
contents.abstract: We present Spray and Etch, a novel personal fabrication method for bespoke-shaped high-resolution displays through alternating spraying of electroluminescent materials and laser etching. Personal fabrication of custom shaped displays has opened the door to fully free-form interactive devices. However, developments have been limited to low-resolution segmented displays, monochromatic output and methods that are prohibitively complicated for non-specialists. Spray and Etch combines low-cost deposition methods (airbrushing) and the use of common makerspace infrastructure (laser etching) to address these limitations, enabling high-resolution displays through easy-to-use methods. We contribute eight performance characterisations of this process and demonstrate its potential with a functioning passive matrix display that can dynamically display images and video. We show that Spray and Etch has the potential to be expanded to both non-planar topographies and dynamic multicolour displays. Improvements in resolution and usability through Spray and Etch represent a step change in the personal fabrication of free-form displays.

contents.title: Ptolemy: A Semantic Map of Exploratory Data Analysis
contents.abstract: A central challenge in exploratory data analysis (EDA) is keeping track of what has already been examined in order to decide what to analyze next. In practice, analysts often run dozens of analyses while building an understanding of a dataset. However, most tools provide little support for maintaining an overview of this evolving process, instead exposing only a linear history of analysis steps. These tools show sequence, what came before, but not position, how a current analysis relates to the broader space of possible analyses. As a result, analysts must mentally reconstruct which parts of the space they have explored and where gaps remain, increasing the risk of redundant work or overlooked patterns. We present Ptolemy, a navigational interface that externalizes analysis history as a semantic map. Each analytic step is represented as a point positioned by embeddings derived from a structured description of its effective data view (e.g., columns, filters, transformations), allowing spatial distance to reflect analytic similarity. In a mixed-methods study comparing map, canvas, and tree representations, we find that maps improve global orientation and local comparison, while ordered layouts reduce decision cost. These findings surface a trade-off between orientation and actionability, and highlight design principles for supporting strategic exploration in EDA.

contents.title: While You're Still Busy: Context-Aware Approach Optimization for Proactive Mobile Robots
contents.abstract: Robot assistants are increasingly capable of assisting users in everyday environments, yet they don’t take users’ cognitive context into consideration. As a result, proactive behaviors may interrupt users during cognitively demanding tasks, before they can acknowledge or respond. We identify this pre-acknowledgment window as a critical phase and introduce our real-time optimization approach that adapts how robots approach and communicate during this window, using user engagement signals and task context. Our system jointly optimizes movement and speech by solving structured, closed-form quadratic subproblems that balance disturbance, clarity, and efficiency online. This enables continuous adjustment of approach movement, timing of intent expression, and level of detail without explicit user input. In a within-subjects ablation user study (N=12), we find that adapting speech to context improves intent clarity, that speed adaptation alone has limited impact without paired speech adaptation, and that coordinating both channels yields the strongest animacy. We also demonstrate the real-world application in three everyday scenarios.

contents.title: The Future of 5DOF Laser Cutting Is Personal
contents.abstract: There has been a recent advent of diode-based laser cutters and a significant uptake among makers. In this paper, we reason that this new technology will also lower the bar for making laser cutters capable of tilting their heads, creating the opportunity to bring 5DOF laser cutting to makers. We anticipate this evolution and present a prototype of a diode-based 5DOF laser cutter built on technology available to makers today. Using this prototype, we explore how to embed 5DOF cutting into makers’ existing software ecosystem to ease adoption. We tackle this by starting from a popular toolchain and then, step-by-step, extending every program, file format, and workflow to 5DOF: We present a 5DOF variant of SVG, we extend Adobe Illustrator with a plugin, and we present a converter for 3D models. We then use our prototype and toolchain to explore what future makers might fabricate using such machines, including hidden joints that provide models with a clean look, load-bearing joints that take 5.8x times higher loads, and cut-in-place mechanisms.

contents.title: DocuDebug: A Graph-Supported Interactive Editor for Verifying and Maintaining Internal Logical Consistency
contents.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) accelerate report generation, maintaining logical consistency during revisions increases the cognitive load, and delegating this task to LLMs often results in unpredictable global overwrites. To address this, we present DocuDebug, an interactive editor that reframes document verification as a software engineering task. The system models a document's logical structure and citations as an explicit dependency graph. Through a linter-like interface, users receive real-time warnings for logical conflicts and propagate localized edits with guided precision. In a within-subjects study with 12 professional writers, DocuDebug guided precise, necessary corrections, improving precision over threefold and reducing over-editing from over 40% to under 5%. Furthermore, objective logs revealed that users avoided blind acceptance, actively deliberating over each warning for nearly three minutes. This work demonstrates how structured visual diagnostics can shift AI-assisted writing from opaque global generation to systematic, user-controlled co-creation.

contents.title: Declarative Dragging
contents.abstract: Drag-and-drop interactions realize the vision of direct manipulation, allowing objects to be manipulated in intuitive and responsive ways. However, implementing such interactions typically requires managing complex spatial, temporal, and visual behaviors. We present a higher-level alternative, declarative dragging (D2). D2 is model-driven: An interface author makes an element draggable by specifying which future model states should be accessible by dragging it. An engine speculatively renders these states to view trees, extracts the position of the dragged element in each of these renderings, and uses these to synthesize a drag-and-drop interaction, all without detailed work required by the interface author. To provide greater expressive range and customizability, D2 is composable: simple model-driven drag-and-drop behaviors can be combined to create more complex ones, and modifiers can layer features like floating, snapping, and transitions. To test D2, we built a prototype engine called Dragology. We demonstrate that Dragology's model-driven primitives can concisely express a broad range of high-quality drag-and-drop interactions. Interviews with 13 interface developers suggest declarative dragging lowers the floor for building polished, varied drag-and-drop interactions – while surfacing barriers to learning and adoption.

contents.title: Compass: Continuously Aligning Social Media Feeds via In-Situ Reflections
contents.abstract: Social media recommendation feeds often optimize for users’ immediate impulses rather than preferences they would hold after deeper reflection. Some systems address this misalignment by incorporating users’ explicit preferences via a configuration page or in-feed controls instead of just behavioral signals. However, users typically have evolving preferences, and their stated preferences and behavior naturally diverge, necessitating continuous reflection and feed realignment. But existing strategies require the user to take initiative and are often effortful; as a result, in practice they are rarely invoked. We present Compass, a system that aligns a user's feed with their reflective preferences by helping users reflect on and articulate their preferences given their behavior. To enable continuous reflection during everyday browsing, Compass surfaces in-situ reflections via lightweight notifications, while feed alignment is achieved by periodically simulating behavioral signals and directly manipulating feed content. We embedded Compass within YouTube Shorts and compared it against a baseline without continuous support through a 10-day field study (N=15). We found that Compass promoted more reflective and purposeful feed consumption, iterative preference adjustment, and stronger feed alignment, without sacrificing the casual nature of feed browsing.

contents.title: CaseSense: Mapping the Legal Case Landscape with Multi-Dimensional Visual Exploration
contents.abstract: Legal case research requires combining facts, legal principles, and timelines into persuasive arguments. Yet existing retrieval tools return one-dimensional ranked lists, hiding this structure into a single relevance score. A formative study with five lawyers confirmed this flat output leads to missed cases, temporal gaps, and fragmented reasoning. We present CaseSense, a visual analytics system for multi-dimensional exploration via tri-axial mapping with dynamic weighting, anchor-based navigation, and purpose-constrained view projections. A within-subjects study with 16 legal professionals compared CaseSense against conventional workflows. CaseSense achieved complete key-case discovery in Fact Synthesis task, with the largest gains in organization and connection identification. Participants adopted task-matched interaction strategies without instructions. These findings suggest encoding domain reasoning dimensions as manipulable spatial axes supports expert sensemaking, while separating spatial organization from AI-generated content preserves verification behavior.

contents.title: Priors of U: Dynamic Preference Learning for Embodied Interaction
contents.abstract: People have their own habits; from how they organize their workspace, over which mug they reach for in the morning, to how they prepare for cooking. Such preferences are context-dependent, dynamic, and often difficult to articulate. As embodied AI agents, such as robots, enter personal spaces, effective interaction requires understanding these implicit and evolving preferences; otherwise, such systems risk being more hindering than helpful. We propose an architecture that learns user preferences from real-world behavioral observation without requiring explicit instruction or feedback. We introduce a factor-graph-based user model that captures preferences across spatial arrangement, tool selection, and workflow, and continuously adapts as tasks and contexts change. The model expands with new observations, enabling open-ended, in situ learning of user-specific preference patterns. Our evaluation shows accurate, calibrated predictions across domains and robust adaptation over time. We demonstrate personalized robot assistance scenarios illustrating seamless, and context-aware human–agent interaction.

contents.title: ArtAnno: Annotating Implicit Semantics in Artworks through LLM Agent-Driven Bidirectional Human-AI Augmentation
contents.abstract:
High-quality annotation of artworks is essential for computational art research, yet extracting implicit semantics remains challenging due to the reliance on culturally grounded meanings and deep contextual knowledge behind the images. 
Current AI-assisted annotation tools often lack assistance or rely on one-way workflows where experts have to perform extra manual calibrations to improve AI models, resulting in limited efficiency.
To address this, we propose Bidirectional Human-AI Augmentation(BiHAA), a closed-loop framework in which skills and domain knowledge base evolve through real-time interaction and bidirectional HAI augmentation.
Informed by a formative study with 20 artwork annotators from different backgrounds, we implement this framework in ArtAnno, an artwork annotation system driven by a multi-agent architecture. 
The system includes a Proactive Agentic Support Module, where AI augments humans through semantic mining and label suggestion, and an Interaction-Driven Evolution Module, where human expertise continuously enhances the AI through distilling annotation trajectories into reusable experience. 
Evaluation through a user study and two case studies demonstrates that our framework and system improve annotation efficiency, enable knowledge accumulation, and reduce the effort of information seeking and verification for
annotators with limited domain expertise.
We conclude by discussing broader implications and future directions.

contents.title: Neighborhood: Dynamic Spatial Alignment for Traversable Telepresence Across Remote Spaces
contents.abstract: We propose Neighborhood, a mixed reality (MR) telepresence system that allows users to experience an illusion of walking between local and  remote spaces as if they are physically connected. Prior studies transmit either the avatar or the space alone to the remote space. Works that transmit both limit either remote space's visibility or traversability to specific areas. Our work builds upon prior works by transmitting both the avatar and the space, while also supporting full visibility and traversability of local and remote spaces with user’s activities grounded with their real furniture and objects, distinct from VR traversal. Our system begins with users moving to the specific area they wish to connect. Using the chosen spaces, the optimization function aligns them to initiate  Walking In Mode, visualizing a traversable area with remote spaces augmented. If users wish to move to a different area, the system transits to Panning Mode. Here, the moving user's avatar appears stationary while the background shifts from the observing user's perspective. We quantitatively measure metrics including the size of the neighborhood and ablate each term to evaluate the optimization function across diverse spatial configurations. We also conducted an exploratory user study with 21 participants, showing that traversing within Neighborhood evokes a compelling sense of real spatial adjoin.

contents.title: Faster Than Muscle: Executing Action based on Voluntary Nervous Signals
contents.abstract: Human augmentation enables actions that surpass biological limits, but earlier intervention in the action loop can undermine user agency. We introduce human-in-the-loop action acceleration, a design approach that anchors action acceleration to voluntary initiation. Using forearm EMG onset, the system triggers actuation within the electromechanical delay (EMD), enabling earlier execution without relying on predictive inference. We implement this approach in Faster Than Muscle, a system with three instantiations: (1) on-body finger actuation achieving a 51 ms speedup, (2) EMG-triggered software input for a shooting task (82 ms speedup), and (3) bionic-hand actuation for catching a falling object (19 ms speedup). Across two studies (temporal binding experiment and qualitative interview study) and accompanying system evaluations, we show that EMG-triggered acceleration improves performance in time-critical tasks, while users retain a sense of agency. These results show that actions can be accelerated beyond biological limits while remaining grounded in voluntary initiation, and outline a design space spanning execution targets and feedback timing.

contents.title: TextBand: Writing by Visualizing and Editing the Sound of Text
contents.abstract: Traditional writing tools focus on how text looks, not how it sounds. We introduce TextBand, a writing tool that helps edit the sonority and musicality of text using a design inspired by music composition software: text is on a timeline to help visualize and edit rhythm; sentences can be heard through text-to-speech playback; and sonorities can be viewed and edited on a phonetic grid similar to a MIDI editor. Results from a user study showed that TextBand helps identify 35% more sonority patterns and successfully fix 57% more sonority issues while helping consciously use figures of speech such as assonance and alliteration. Our work challenges the design of existing writing software and paves the way for more sound-based support when writing.

contents.title: ChronoMantic: A Natural Language Interface for Interactive Time Series Pattern Query
contents.abstract: Finding time series patterns is an important problem in finance, healthcare, climatology, and manufacturing, where temporal data analysis informs critical decision-making processes. Existing approaches use examples, sketches, and natural language (NL) for time series pattern querying, but precisely formulating complex queries, inspecting query interpretations, and refining queries iteratively remain challenging. Nevertheless, NL is a promising modality for pattern specification, balancing expressiveness and preciseness while providing an intuitive means of articulating query intent. This paper introduces ChronoMantic, an NL-driven interactive interface for time series pattern querying. The tool provides glyph-based feedback on query interpretation and supports iterative querying through by-example refinement. We illustrate ChronoMantic’s workflow through two usage scenarios, assess its retrieval performance on a manually annotated benchmark, and evaluate its query effectiveness and usability via a two-stage user study.

contents.title: MolecularCanvas: LLM-assisted Small-Molecule Drug Discovery via Structure-Guided Constraints
contents.abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery relies on iterative molecular optimization, where chemists repeatedly modify candidate compounds to balance multiple competing properties such as efficacy, toxicity, and solubility. Recent advances in generative AI (GenAI), have shown promise in accelerating this process by automatically proposing new molecular structures or targeted modifications. However, existing GenAI-based molecular design tools remain poorly aligned with experts’ real-world workflows. Specifically, they offer limited support for specifying structure-level modification intents on molecules, provide insufficient transparency into model-generated modifications, and lack integrated support for downstream property evaluation with external computational tools. To address these challenges, we introduce MolecularCanvas, an interactive system that enables users to iteratively construct an optimization context by integrating high-level goals, structure-level annotations, property constraints, and reference-based preferences. This context guides the generation of candidate molecules across diverse molecular structures. MolecularCanvas further enhances transparency by providing evidence for AI-generated suggestions, and streamlines molecular evaluation by integrating commonly used property computational tools into a unified interface. Finally, a user study with 12 participants demonstrates the usefulness and effectiveness of MolecularCanvas in helping users optimize candidate molecules.

contents.title: Object-Agent Twins (OATs): Expressive Micro-Agent Avatars for Inanimate Everyday Objects
contents.abstract: We introduce Object-Agent Twins (OATs), a toolkit for creating Tamagotchi-like companions for inanimate everyday objects. OATs allow non-expert users to easily author small personality-bearing agents tied to real-world artifacts such as a tea kettle, pet bowls, and a trash can. These OATs act as expressive proxies for physical objects, using real-time sensed data to drive simple needs, moods, and behaviors. In contrast to conventional smart-object interfaces that expose raw status and data, OATs render object state through character, making everyday infrastructure more socially legible and emotionally engaging. Through deployments, we show how this approach enables users to transform ordinary things in their lives from passive infrastructure into lightweight companions that invite attention, interpretation, and care.

contents.title: KnowTap: A Knowledge-Driven Tool for Fine-Grained Tappability Assessment and Design Iteration of Mobile UIs
contents.abstract: Visually perceived tappability, defined as the degree to which a static UI component looks interactive, is critical to interface usability and distinct from physical target acquisition, yet existing task-specific models generally provide binary labels. However, designers need finer-grained tappability assessments to make informed modifications during iterative design. To address this, we propose KnowTap, a Figma-compatible interactive tool that predicts continuous perceived-tappability scores from mean human ratings collected on a 0–5 annotation scale, visualizes them in six display bands, and provides optional LLM-generated feedback to suggest context-aware improvements. Using a new dataset of 800 mobile UIs and 9,751 components whose GPT-4o pre-labels were corrected by three independent crowdworker groups, KnowTap combines structured design knowledge, text-derived features, and deep embeddings in a random forest regressor that achieves SRCC .745 and R² .564 under UI-grouped five-fold cross-validation, compared with .646 and .387 for an adapted, randomly initialized Taperception-style ResNet-18 baseline, while offering attribute-level explanations complementary to prior pixel-level saliency. In a within-subjects study with 12 designers, paired comparisons showed higher reported satisfaction and perceived task success and lower mental demand, temporal demand, and frustration in the six-band condition, and independent raters preferred its resulting designs in three of four test UIs. Our research contributes a knowledge-driven tool for continuous perceived-tappability prediction, along with a new dataset, to support Figma-compatible mobile-UI design iteration.

contents.title: Democratizing Extensive Reading by Tailoring Web Content
contents.abstract: Extensive reading helps foreign language learners build proficiency through large amounts of interesting, level-appropriate text. However, providing enough material matched to learners’ interests and evolving proficiency is resource-intensive and difficult to sustain. To address this challenge, we present Adapt-ER, a browser extension that leverages the web to support scalable self-selected reading by adapting pages in place to each learner’s vocabulary profile. Adapt-ER estimates lexical proficiency, tailors web content in real time, and supports lightweight profile refinement through click-based interactive learner feedback during reading. To make adaptation practical during live browsing, we compare LLM-based strategies and develop a hybrid pipeline that balances lexical difficulty control, semantic preservation, latency, and cost. In a within-subject study, Adapt-ER increased reading speed, reduced the need for dictionary and translation support during reading, and improved self-reported engagement. Our findings suggest that in-place adaptation of self-selected web text can make web reading better suited to sustained extensive reading.

contents.title: FontCopilot: A Designer-in-the-Loop System for Chinese Vector Font Design
contents.abstract:
Designing Chinese fonts is challenging due to the structural complexity of ideographic characters and the scale of character sets (e.g., over 80,000 characters in GB 18030). Existing font generation methods often produce non-editable raster images or offer limited stylistic control, which restricts their use in professional design workflows.
We present FontCopilot, an interactive designer-in-the-loop system for Chinese vector font design. Through an exploratory interview study with 10 professional designers, we identify Component Assembly as a major production bottleneck. FontCopilot targets this labor-intensive phase using a component-based affine transformation model that generates editable vector glyphs from few-shot inputs. The workflow lets designers refine generated results and use their corrections to update the model. These interactions provide direct control over component layout and style.
We evaluate CAR through model ablations and a comparison with a prior Chinese vector font generation method, study FontCopilot with 9 professional designers, and document a four-week production case. FontCopilot received "Excellent" ratings on five of six UEQ dimensions, and one designer used 300 seed characters to produce 10,461 editable glyphs for AI Song. Together, these evaluations show how editable component completion can carry local structural decisions from a small seed set to a complete Chinese typeface.

contents.title: FabDreamer: Exploring the Image-to-Physical Workflow Through AI-Assisted Layered Fabrication
contents.abstract: Generative AI lets anyone create rich visual content in seconds, yet translating that content into a physically fabricable artifact still demands manual decomposition, occlusion repair, and structural verification that most tools leave entirely to the user. We present FabDreamer, an image-to-physical system that carries an image to fabrication-ready SVGs through three stages with deliberately staged AI initiative: (1) AI leads decomposition into depth-ordered layers, (2) assists on demand during creative editing with real-time 3D preview, and (3) advises on structural integrity before export. We instantiate this workflow for layered laser-cut art and evaluate it through three rounds including a formative analysis, an early prototype user evaluation (N=13), and a cross-domain practitioner study with specialists from 6 fabrication domains (N=6). Our findings show that physical awareness during design opens creative opportunities beyond error prevention, that practitioners appropriate the system's generic geometric operations for their own domains, and that the fabrication agent covers geometry-readable constraints while domain knowledge remains with the maker.

contents.title: Zoro: Active Controls to Support Rule Following in Vibe Coding
contents.abstract:
Rules files (e.g., AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are the primary mechanism for human-agent alignment when developers vibe code. However, they remain passive: it is not immediately apparent when rules are being used or followed, or how to improve them. To transform
rules from passive text into active controls, we introduce Zoro, an interactive interface that integrates directly with a coding agent and anchors rules to every step of the coding process. After an agent generates an initial plan, Zoro enriches the plan with rules, enforces the rules during implementation by requiring the agent to prove that each rule was followed, and allows users to provide in-situ feedback when they are unsatisfied with a rule application to evolve the scope of the rules. A technical evaluation shows that coding agents follow rules more with Zoro than without. A user study demonstrates a change in people’s behavior and cognitive strategies when rules are at the forefront of vibe coding. We discuss how making rules active in agentic systems unlocks broader opportunities for human-agent alignment in coding settings and beyond.

contents.title: CogChat: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Conversational AI with Heterogeneous Graph Transformer for Cognitive Grounding in Design Generation
contents.abstract: LLM-based chat systems have become valuable tools for design practice, enabling rapid ideation and flexible task support. Yet these systems process designer utterances as generic sequences, maintaining context through recency rather than through any model of how the speaker organizes knowledge. In design conversation, this gap compounds as relational context decays between turns, identical words go unresolved across designers, and the conversation loops or restarts rather than deepens. We present CogChat, a real-time chat framework that grounds conversational AI in a personal heterogeneous knowledge graph constructed from each designer's input. The system extracts typed entities and relations into a heterogeneous graph, then applies a HGT (Heterogeneous Graph Transformer) to select structurally relevant nodes for response generation and to generate both intentional and exploratory probing questions. Technical evaluation shows that HGT-based entity selection outperforms both ungrounded LLM interaction and naïve KG augmentation, which introduces noise that degrades response quality. A within-subjects study with nine professional designers indicates that grounding conversation in a relationally structured, designer-specific semantic context improves context retention, personalized intent interpretation, and conversational depth while reducing cognitive load. These findings suggest that structuring a designer's expressed concepts and relations as a dynamic knowledge graph can preserve relational context that fades across turns, pointing toward a graph-grounded approach to long-term context management in LLM-based interaction.

contents.title: Mirror Skin: In Situ Visualization of Robot Touch Intent on Robot Skin
contents.abstract: Effective communication of robot touch intent is essential for safe and predictable physical human-robot interaction. While intent communication has been widely studied, existing approaches lack the spatial specificity and semantic depth necessary to efficiently convey robot touch intent. We present Mirror Skin, a cephalopod inspired concept that mirrors in-situ visual representations of a human’s body parts onto the corresponding robot’s touch region to communicate who shall initiate touch, where it will occur, and when it is imminent. We informed the design of Mirror Skin through a structured design exploration with experts and demonstrate the real-world feasibility of Mirror Skin with a proof-of-concept prototype. User studies in VR and with the physical prototype showed that Mirror Skin significantly improves accuracy and response times for interpreting touch intent and improves the user experience during physical human-robot interactions.

contents.title: OmniTex: Omnidirectional Haptic Rendering of Surface Texture on VR Handheld Controller using 3-DOF Motion Mechanism
contents.abstract: Extensive research has explored haptic rendering of surface textures in virtual reality (VR). However, it is still challenging to provide realistic texture-based haptic feedback that aligns with users' fingertip motion in VR. We present OmniTex, a handheld haptic device that enables continuous omnidirectional texture rendering in VR. OmniTex integrates a 2 DoF rotational mechanism to support fingertip-aligned motion and deliver directional shear feedback, together with a linear translation mechanism for dynamic texture switching. Technical evaluation revealed low latency averaging around 250ms with our system for texture switching and motion synchronization. Our user studies further demonstrated the effectiveness of our design in improving user-perceived visual–tactile congruence in VR with different finger movements and different types of virtual textures, and our system offered significantly better sense of realism in VR compared with controller-based vibration achieving performance comparable to that of real-surface proxy interaction.

contents.title: Enriching Writing Ecosystems at The Fifth Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants
contents.abstract: Writing assistants have become increasingly multidimensional and sophisticated, fueled by advances in AI and interaction design. As this landscape expands, it is timely to consider how different underlying technologies (e.g., text analytics, LLMs), interaction designs (e.g., next-word prediction, chatbots, material interaction), and design goals (e.g., productivity, friction) fit together into broader ecosystems of tools and workflows. Future writing tools should support writers' idiosyncratic, multi-tool, and social writing processes. In this hands-on, systems-centric workshop, we challenge the UIST community to explore and develop ecosystems of writing assistants through the lens of interoperability. Participants will engage in a highly interactive tool-swapping collaborative writing exercise where research and commercial systems are used side-by-side. Through playful provocation and intentional defamiliarization, participants will identify system interplay friction and collaboratively outline design guidelines for building adaptable writing assistants that enrich diverse workflows and integrate into lasting technological ecosystems.

contents.title: Haptics Beyond Vibration: Generative AI to Advance Multisensory Interfaces
contents.abstract: Immersive experiences are increasingly moving beyond conventional vibrotactile and force-based feedback toward multisensory forms of interaction. This workshop examines the intersection of generative AI and such nontraditional haptics, asking how AI might support the authoring, prototyping, personalization, and evaluation of multisensory feedback that is often difficult to describe, simulate, or standardize. The workshop will combine live demonstrations of recent multisensory interfaces, short talks on how these systems were developed, and group discussions on where generative AI may or may not change the process of creating haptic experiences. Our goal is to identify emerging research gaps, design vocabularies, and potential evaluation methods for future AI-mediated multisensory interfaces.

contents.title: Proxemics of Physical AI: Opportunities and Challenges of Augmenting Intimate, Personal, Social, and Public Spaces
contents.abstract: Physical AI, systems that perceive, reason, and act through actuated bodies, moves interaction off the screen and into the space around us. Wearable robots and on-skin interfaces now operate inside the wearer's intimate space, while foundation models of robotics and simulation platforms scale embodied agents into shared social and public settings. What has not scaled is our understanding of how such systems should occupy human spaces and interact with them in intimate, personal, social, and public zones. This workshop explores what proxemics means for Physical AI by discussing perspectives on design, agency, adaptation, and ethics.

contents.title: The AI-Augmented Maker: Challenges and Opportunities in Designing Intelligence for Community-driven DIY Cultures
contents.abstract: At its core, the maker movement is driven by a highly adaptable community that repurposes new creative technologies through the open exchange of skills and knowledge. Recent advances in generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) have enabled makers to synthesize, on demand, the knowledge traditionally curated by the maker community. As AI tools become increasingly integrated into creative ecosystems, this workshop aims to chart new directions for maker-centric tools by unpacking the concept of the  "AI-augmented maker''. Bringing together interdisciplinary experts across fabrication, AI, and community-centered design, this workshop will explore how integrating on-demand AI to different facets of making can preserve—or disrupt—the conditions that give the maker movement its meaning.

contents.title: Revibing HCI: Agentic Reimplementation as Community Practice
contents.abstract: Agentic AI coding tools can now reimplement, or “revibe,” the systems described in research papers. Revibing could give the HCI community what it has long lacked: prior systems that can be run, act as strong baselines, and be extended. However, before revibing becomes common practice, our community must shape norms around how revibes are conducted, how they are verified, and what widespread revibing means for how HCI research is practiced, shared, and valued. Our workshop brings together the UIST community to discuss and form these early norms. Participants will revibe a classic UIST system in a hands-on session, brainstorm evaluation approaches for revibed artifacts, and discuss what revibing means for research methods, open science, and the future of HCI system contributions. The workshop aims to foster a community around revibing by consolidating guidance and outputs into a shared community document.

contents.title: The World as a Canvas: Materializing Imagination through Prompting the Physical World
contents.abstract: This workshop brings together researchers and practitioners in HCI, eXtended Reality (XR), and AI to explore how generative AI can lower barriers to creating XR experiences. Generative AI can now turn rough ideas into images, videos, and apps within minutes, yet creating XR experiences remains demanding. XR creations must be grounded in physical space, previewed before they exist, steered through multimodal user inputs, co-created across heterogeneous devices, inspected for AI errors that unfold in interaction, and shared beyond a single headset. Through keynotes, posters and demos, and hands-on prototyping activities, we will turn these challenges into design considerations and a shared research agenda. We will publish the outcomes on the workshop website to seed a growing community advancing generative AI-powered XR for everyday creativity: worldascanvas.github.io

contents.title: Cyber-Physical Systems for Accessibility and Ability Augmentation: Bridging Diverse Communities
contents.abstract: The powerful convergence of wearables, robotics, extended reality, and smart environments is expanding the design space for cyber-physical systems (CPS) that support and augment human abilities in daily life. By sensing real-world contexts, modeling user needs, and providing situated assistance, these systems can improve accessibility for people with disabilities while enhancing broader human abilities such as perception, memory, learning, and mobility. However, realizing this potential requires addressing key challenges in context sensing, user modeling, adaptive interaction, privacy, and evaluation to ensure that CPS are reliable and effective in real-world contexts. This workshop will bring together researchers and practitioners across HCI, AI, wearables, robotics, XR, smart environments, accessibility, and ability augmentation to examine shared strategies and challenges for designing accessibility- and ability-centered CPS. Through panel discussions, interactive demos, and mixed-group design activities, participants will identify recurring design principles, technical challenges, and future directions for CPS that support and augment human abilities in real-world settings. For details, please visit: https://cps4all.github.io.

contents.title: Bobapedia: A Workshop on Archiving Living Flavor Experiences
contents.abstract:
Flavor is an embodied, multimodal, and culturally situated design material. 
However, computational flavor systems often represent food through ingredients, chemical compounds, recipe corpora, or machine-generated recommendations, leaving limited space for people to document and iterate their subjective experiences. 
We propose Bobapedia, a full-day participatory workshop exploring how computational interfaces scaffold collaborative flavor creation of a popular drink---boba tea. 
We will use an LLM-supported Flavor Wiki system to record participants' sensory impressions, personal and cultural associations, flavor interpretations, and finally guide them to iteratively create customized drinks.

contents.title: Workshop on Augmenting Human Dexterity: From Multisensory Feedback and Motor Capabilities to Skill Acquisition
contents.abstract: Human dexterity enables versatile and precise manipulation in everyday life. Recent advances in wearable and mobile computing have opened new ways to augment this dexterity. These efforts go beyond traditional assistive tools—whose primary function has been to restore or enhance strength—and instead aim to support more precise and complex performance across diverse domains, such as playing musical instruments or performing precision tasks at a workbench. A range of technologies has been explored, including multimodal sensory cues, adaptive learning schemes, robots, and exoskeletons. Yet individual projects remain limited in scope, often confined to a specific technology or application domain. Because dexterity is inherently multifaceted, no single perspective is likely to capture it fully—yet UIST has not seen a dedicated effort to bring these perspectives together. We therefore propose this workshop, framing the topic as a broad goal: augmenting human dexterity. We aim to bring together researchers including those from mechanical engineering, neuroscience, learning science, domain-specific expertise, to discuss what dexterity entails and how technology might support it in a more holistic way. Through interdisciplinary talks, interactive demonstrations, and collaborative discussions, we hope to map out a broad research agenda in this direction.

contents.title: The Personalized Computer for the 21st Century
contents.abstract: A long-standing vision in computing has been to create truly personalized computing systems. For example, in 1987, Apple introduced the ``Knowledge Navigator,'' which envisioned a computer that could seek out relevant information based on the user's context. Microsoft's Clippy similarly aimed to anticipate what users needed help with and provide assistance. These early systems share an underlying ethos that while personal computers are owned by a user and hold their data, we ought to pursue personalized computers that proactively learn about the user and initiate actions on their behalf. The primary interest of our workshop is this personalized computing paradigm: computing systems powered by intelligence that both knows the user and acts on their needs.

contents.title: Drawing on Materials and Processes: A Hands-on Workshop on Building Creative Tools with Grain Spaces
contents.abstract: In this half-day workshop, we will use the grain space framework to build novel creative tools for pen plotters. After learning the definition of a grain space, attendees will discuss various grains for pen plotting, define a parametric space for a Truchet tiles grain, and implement interactions with it. We will discuss how HCI researchers can use the grain space approach to guide and refine their systems for working with creative and novel computational materials.

contents.title: Toward Experience Augmentation in Everyday Augmented Reality
contents.abstract: cus in HCI. Most prior work treats AR as a spatialized screen for information augmentation: the user explicitly needs knowledge or data, and the system offers it at the right spot (e.g., show the nutrition of this food). However, users’ needs for everyday AR can go beyond information retrieval, extending to emotion, culture, and experience. For example, a user stuck on a creative task might ask their AR system to “make me more creative,” or, when feeling down, simply ask it to “make me laugh.” For these requests, there is no single piece of information being the correct answer. Instead, AR might need to offer a wider range of experiential artifacts: cultural, perceptual, emotional, or social. They are open to interpretation, allowing participants to make sense of them and hence reach their goals, which I name it as experience augmentation in Everyday AR. In my dissertation, I explore experience augmentation from four aspects through four systems and related user studies: ShadAR (visual perception), MemeAR (cultural artifacts), Embodied Spatial Simulation (embodied experience), and facial-expression change (social signals).

contents.title: Computational Tools for Modular Design and Debugging in Machine Knitting
contents.abstract: From shirts to car seats to space suits, machine knitting is used to create a variety of textiles that people interact with on a daily basis. Industrial knitting machines are reliable and capable of producing complex garments. Existing knitting machine CAD software, however, is typically proprietary, cumbersome, and requires extensive training to understand, making it difficult to fully use the machine's capabilities. Small adjustments to garment designs can be herculean tasks even for experienced knitwear designers. As a result, despite these machines being used daily in factories across the world, their use is typically limited to commonly-worn garments, such as socks and sweaters. Improving the process of designing complex knit programs can both expedite and facilitate more complex design work. Towards this end, my thesis is focused on improving the design process. I will contribute two CAD tools that support modularity in knit programming, specifically allowing users to combine programs. I also present a debugging tool to assist during the creation and merging of knit programs.

contents.title: Accessible Human-AI Collaboration
contents.abstract: Humans and AI increasingly collaborate to complete everyday tasks, learn new skills, and co-create artifacts. For effective collaboration, users must understand AI work in order to verify and intervene, while AI systems must understand human work in order to provide relevant guidance. Yet, current AI collaborators often rely on visual or text-heavy communication channels that presume particular perceptual abilities, making AI work difficult to perceive and interpret for users with disabilities (e.g., blind users). AI collaborators also assume normative interaction patterns, making their guidance less applicable to users who work through different tools, strategies, or assistive technologies. My dissertation addresses this accessibility gap by designing Human–AI collaboration across diverse perception and behavior. I explore two complementary thrusts: (1) legible oversight of AI work and (2) actionable AI guidance for human work. My research support people not only to access AI systems, but to effectively collaborate with them.

contents.title: From What Is in Textbooks to What Is in Experts: Human-AI Systems for Externalizing Surgical Expertise
contents.abstract: Surgical expertise spans more than what textbooks can include. Trainees must acquire explicit knowledge, such as operative decision-making; psychomotor skills accumulated through thousands of hours of practice; and attentional skills, such as knowing what to attend to, which even experts often struggle to articulate. Current training resources address the explicit level well but offer little support for these tacit levels, while access to expert time in the operating room continues to shrink. My dissertation develops human--AI systems that externalize surgical expertise across these three increasingly tacit levels. Surgment and SurgGraph use computer vision to turn surgical recordings into visual exercises with feedback. eXplainMR teaches ultrasonography in mixed reality, explaining why each movement is recommended to help trainees build three-dimensional mental models. SurgGaze enables accurate gaze capture in the operating room through implicit calibration, revealing how experts allocate attention, including strategies such as focus and anticipation. I plan to integrate these levels into residency training through post-operative debriefing that reviews decision-making, action efficiency, and attention allocation in one loop.

contents.title: Robotic Functionality through Mechanical Intelligence
contents.abstract:
Interaction is shifting off the screen and onto the body, leveraging the adaptivity of wearable devices. However, most wearables today remain static and limited to a single fixed state. To provide physical output, conventional approaches rely on robotic systems with motors and batteries that make the devices heavy, expensive, and inaccessible to many users. My dissertation argues that for many crucial wearable devices, providing physical output does not require full robotics. Instead, we can deliver robotic functionality through mechanical intelligence.
My approach is especially impactful for wearables that support rehabilitation and mobility assistance. With the targeted functions built into the fully passive structures, wearables can provide functional assistance adapted to contexts and user needs, without any actuation or power. Moreover, these devices are tailored to each user, integrate function-switching seamlessly into daily life, and remain low-cost and lightweight. This paper provides an overview of my approach: (1) how a bistable finger brace can support both dexterous tasks and rehabilitation (UIST ’25); (2) how an unpowered knee exoskeleton can automatically adapt while walking on different surfaces (CHI ’26); and (3) how to fabricate wearables with many functions for any body part (CHI ’25).

contents.title: Scene-Aware Augmented Reality for People with Low Vision in Complex, Dynamic Environments
contents.abstract: People with low vision (PLV) retain functional vision but have difficulty perceiving real-world environments, which are visually complex and change continuously, requiring PLV to rapidly perceive multiple objects. While augmented reality (AR) has been developed as a low-vision aid, prior systems either amplify low-level visual features, adding clutter, or augment objects for a single task in relatively simple settings. Neither can effectively support PLV in complex scenes, since augmenting a single type of object is insufficient, yet augmenting every important object would exceed a user's perceptual and cognitive limits. A system must therefore decide which objects to augment and how to augment them without causing overload, and adapt both as the scene and the user's task change. My doctoral research studies scene-aware AR to address this gap: augmenting multiple objects and adjusting the augmentation to the scene and the user's context, such as the user's task and position, and each object's function and risk. I examine what and how to augment in cluttered scenes through a controlled study, how PLV use and adapt such augmentation through a real-world deployment, and how to extend it to dynamic scenes where the user and objects move. Ultimately, I aim to contribute design knowledge for scene-aware augmentation to guide future AR systems that help PLV perceive and act in the complex, dynamic environments of daily life.

contents.title: Visual Communication for Low-Vision Information Access: From Personalized Highlights to AI Agents
contents.abstract: Charts, slides, and web pages remain difficult to access for the estimated 295 million people globally with low vision (LV). Much accessibility research translates visual content into speech, sound, or touch, but LV people often prefer to use their residual vision. My dissertation follows ability-based design to create tools motivated by residual vision use. My ongoing work extends this to ability-based AI systems that adapt AI interaction to LV users' abilities. The central method is visual communication between tools and LV users. My completed work explores tool-to-user communication: VeasyGuide highlights instructor actions for LV learners in videos, while on-cursor interactions restore chart context hidden by magnification. Both systems improved access in studies with LV participants. My ongoing work examines user-to-tool communication through an AI assistant that receives the user's magnified view and point of interest during chart exploration. My planned work asks how AI can answer visually, combine both directions, and balance assistance with user agency. I plan to extend this communication beyond charts to the web, documents, and eventually the physical world. Ultimately, my dissertation advances personalized AI that uses bidirectional visual communication to support the independence and agency of LV people.

contents.title: Toward a Haptic Codec: Composing Perceptual Mechanisms Into a Programmable Haptic Medium
contents.abstract: Sound and images are programmable through common primitives such as audio samples and pixels, which largely decouple content specification from device-specific rendering and allow the same representation to be manipulated across systems. Haptics rendering, however, has not converged on a comparable representation, and many haptic effects remain tied to bespoke devices. My work provides initial evidence that perceptual mechanisms can shape the mapping between physical stimulation and perceived sensation within individual stimulus dimensions: JetUnit showed how temporal dynamics shape perceived force quality; TherMosaic showed how spatial summation and thermal adaptation alter perceived temperature change; ongoing work explores how tactile apparent motion can construct continuous motion from discrete stretch inputs. These findings motivate a broader hypothesis that haptic rendering could be organized around shared skin-level primitives such as vibration, force, stretch, and temperature. A key next question is whether perceptual rules established within individual dimensions remain predictable when these primitives are combined. I propose the Haptic Texel as a next step to test this question by integrating the four forms of actuation within a unit and examining their perceptual composition. If reliable composition can be established, shared primitives and perceptual rendering rules could provide a basis for re-rendering cutaneous sensations across devices, moving haptics toward a programmable medium.

contents.title: Building Automation for Insight
contents.abstract: Artists and scientists leverage computation to create, iterate on, and share digital artifacts, but physical automation remains prohibitively difficult without engineering expertise. This stifles the adaptation of machines for use in new contexts and subsequent adoption by new practitioners. To support emerging machine practices, I argue that we need tools for material experimentation alongside infrastructure for sharing the resulting processes. Following insights from digital fabrication, end-user programming, and online communities, my dissertation develops a set of tools for creative automation: a mode of working with machines and code in which domain-specific goals are iteratively discovered. With this approach, machine behaviour is expressed in code, documented alongside its physical output, shared in online communities, and modifiable by others. I ground creative automation in empirical studies of makers and computational artists and draw these parallel practices together in four systems, which I evaluate using demonstrative workflows from art and science. My research suggests that creative automation can catalyze domain-specific discovery by supporting the development of practitioners who blend machine knowledge with disciplinary expertise.

contents.title: User-Aware Wearable Assistance: Sensing When and How to Intervene
Designing Mixed-Initiative Collaboration Between Humans and Increasingly Autonomous AI Systems
Together from Afar: Toward More Natural Spatial Telepresence
contents.abstract: Telepresence technologies help people stay connected, by keeping friends in touch, sustaining love across distance, and enabling global collaboration. Yet today’s systems still fall short of the ideal: making people feel naturally co-present, as if sharing the same space. Despite advances in Mixed Reality (MR), current systems face limitations. RGB-D reconstruction and 360° video trade off between realism and interactivity, while most systems prioritize virtual over physical interaction. This dissertation moves toward more natural telepresence by enhancing three key aspects: realism, interactivity, and collaborative awareness. For realism, I investigate hyper-realistic scene representations (e.g., 360° video, NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) and develop techniques for efficient delivery. I also explore spatial alignment across heterogeneous environments, from surface-based to full 3D merging. For interactivity, I enable users to navigate remote spaces and share 2D and 3D physical objects across distance. While the focus is primarily technical, the work draws on groupware and proxemics literature to guide design and reflect on collaborative awareness. Ultimately, this dissertation envisions a future where telepresence not only enables effective collaboration, but also preserves a sense of physical warmth across distance.

contents.title: Toward Context-Adaptive Extended Reality: Dissolving the Trade-offs between Experience and Protection
contents.abstract: Extended reality (XR) devices are leaving the lab and entering everyday, socially rich settings, yet they still make largely static decisions about what to display, what to sense, and what to share. Under such one-size-fits-all designs, immersion appears to trade off against spatial awareness, expressivity against realism, and security against usability. My dissertation argues that many of these trade-offs are artifacts of static design. It develops the empirical foundations and interactive systems for context-adaptive XR: interfaces that adapt what they display, express, sense, and share to users' abilities, physical surroundings, and social context, so that experience and protection no longer come at each other's expense. Completed work spans three threads: (1) understanding the limits of users' motor control, their virtual–physical discrimination, and wearer–bystander privacy expectations; (2) building interfaces that adapt virtual environments to physical rooms, avatar expressions to emotions, and private conversation to social settings; and (3) safeguarding interaction through motion-based two-factor authentication, context-adaptive privacy pathways, and defenses against reality-blurring attacks. Adaptation dissolved several of these trade-offs; my studies also locate tensions that remain structural and demand negotiation and accountability. I outline a design framework that maps this space, ongoing system work, and questions for the symposium.

contents.title: Representational Alignment in Interactive Guidance Systems
contents.abstract: Many interactive guidance systems follow a human-in-the-loop control structure: estimate the current task state, compare it with a target or objective, and map the resulting difference into cues for the user. Across my work, I have found that this state-to-cue mapping shapes whether guidance is understandable and actionable. I frame this recurring design problem as representational alignment: how systems can organize computational task state around the actions users can take, reference frames that reflect how users reason about movement, and domain representations they use to plan and evaluate their work. I explore these three forms of alignment through four interactive systems. Personal Time-Lapse (UIST 2024) demonstrates action alignment by decomposing a high-dimensional capture state into lower-dimensional guidance organized around camera movement and subject configuration. ARticulate (CHI 2025) investigates reference-frame alignment by learning a user-aligned coordinate system from demonstrations and finds that spatial guidance improves when the learned frame matches how users reason about and control movement. CineCraft (CHI 2026) and Micro-Edits (UIST 2026) explore domain alignment in creativity support. CineCraft uses an authorable, storyboard-based shot plan to carry creative intent from planning into capture guidance and footage review. Micro-Edits guides fine-cut editing by discretizing the continuous space of frame-level adjustments using established editing idioms, helping editors shape rhythm and direct viewer attention. My ongoing work will explore multifunctional representations that make domain-specific requirements more accessible to non-experts, adapt guidance to collaborative settings around shared goals, and provide criteria for evaluating generative AI guidance.

contents.title: Toward Human–AI Co-Creation of Analogical 3D Learning Experiences
contents.abstract:
Teachers routinely explain abstract concepts through analogies, yet those
analogies stay verbal because building an interactive 3D learning
environment demands expertise most educators lack. My research asks how
human--AI co-creation can help educators and eventually learners translate
a tacit analogy into an interactive experience while preserving pedagogical
intent. Two completed systems ground this work: \emph{AGen} generates
personalized analogies for learning, and \emph{MCP-Unity} lets
language-model agents build Unity scenes autonomously. I first put that
generative tool directly in young learners' hands: 17 students learned from
multiple embodied analogies, then authored their own. Modifiable analogies
aided their reasoning, but open-ended iterative prompting proved a poor
vehicle for young authors' intent. My ongoing system, \emph{AGen3D},
responds by shifting the author to educators: a teacher-in-the-loop
multi-agent pipeline externalizes, visualizes, and realizes the analogy
across inspectable checkpoints. A formative pilot with three instructors
produced usable starting-point scenes---elements survive, relational
structure degrades---and surfaced two working hypotheses: generation acts
as an \emph{externalizing mirror}, exposing underspecification invisible
until the artifact is experienced; and \emph{authorship migrates
downstream}, from specifying mappings to iterating on built scenes. My research plan tests both hypotheses with more
educators, and extends co-creation toward student authorship, classroom
deployment, and evaluation methods for generated 3D learning experiences.

contents.title: Augmenting Physical World Interactions across Material Scale from Artifacts to Environments
contents.abstract: Physical interaction with the world is an essential part of human experience and development which refines our tactile and spatial perception skills. Yet developing interactive systems that service and supplement the breadth of physical perception remains challenging. First, sensing the subtleties of touch typically requires complex, embedded electronics. Second, the ability to augment kinesthetic interactions with the built environment is hampered by limited working volumes of traditional fabrication tools. My doctoral work addresses these challenges by developing novel systems that leverage material affordances at different scales—from individual objects to environments—to enrich the spectrum of touch, spatial, and kinesthetic senses. I accomplish in two key ways: 1) using commodity hardware to detect and decode interactions by leveraging material and form of fabricated, passive artifacts and 2) developing new systems to alter and augment environments by working directly on and across real-world surfaces. Grounded in themes of sustainability and accessibility, my work demonstrates how integrating digital fabrication, robotics, and mobile computing can reduce the reliance on batteries and adapt our physical surroundings to suit the needs of people with disabilities. My future research will explore additional material affordances like deformation and extend to larger city-wide scales to enrich interactions with the physical world.

contents.title: Interactions for Human-AI Knowledge Extension
contents.abstract: AI systems are widely used to produce knowledge, and they perform well on tasks that rework existing knowledge, like retrieving or summarizing it. They are harder to use for knowledge-extension tasks: developing new knowledge that builds on what already exists. Because these tasks are open-ended, their outputs cannot be verified beyond their utility to the user. Moreover, there is little precedent (and parametric knowledge) for what this new knowledge should look like. This makes knowledge extension a rich testbed for studying human-AI interaction. My research develops novel systems for people to extend knowledge with the assistance of AI. I demonstrate this approach across the arc of knowledge extension: from understanding existing knowledge, to situating new knowledge within it, to creating knowledge beyond it. My key insight is that existing knowledge should be represented in a way that is structured, by explicitly encoding its relations to the new knowledge being developed, and also dynamic, meaning interactions can make these relationships malleable and explorable. My dissertation contributes to a vision of human-AI collaboration for the productive (and hopefully enjoyable) development of new knowledge.

contents.title: Toward Computational Design of Dynamic Culinary Experiences
contents.abstract: Eating unfolds over time: anticipation forms before the first bite, flavor and texture emerge through chewing, and post-tasting impressions can inform future meals. Computational food fabrication can precisely specify the physical properties of food, yet provides limited support for authoring how its perceptual experience unfolds through eating. My dissertation investigates how computational design can make these unfolding experiences authorable, creating dynamic culinary experiences whose anticipation, sensory progression, and reflection are designed as a connected whole. So that these experiences work in real dining settings, I embed the dynamics in food itself through fabrication, rather than in devices that diners wear or use while eating. My fabrication systems encode intended perceptual trajectories into physical properties of food: hidden structures control when information becomes available, spatial taste placement and internal geometry shape how flavor and texture unfold during eating, and post-tasting preferences update subsequent fabrication. Through further work on food-side responses before the first bite, post-eating experience, and an integrated authoring pipeline, I work toward dynamic culinary experiences in which anticipation, eating, and reflection can be specified, fabricated, and evaluated as connected temporal experiences.

contents.title: Designing Embodied Interaction: Shaping Bodily Action, Experience, and Capability
contents.abstract: Despite advances in interactive technologies, many systems remain fundamentally disembodied, underusing the human body as a central medium of interaction. Prior work has explored gesture-based input and haptic feedback, but these directions are often studied separately. Moreover, research suggests that bodily capabilities can shape how people perceive and act within their environments, motivating interaction that engages not only with bodily action and experience, but also with what the body can do. My research investigates embodied interaction through three progressively connected perspectives: bodily action, examining how people act through their bodies; bodily experience, exploring how interactive systems physically shape what people feel; and bodily capability, studying how changing what the body can do affects perception and behavior. Building on my work in gesture and haptic interaction, I explore capability modulation as an emerging direction for investigating the relationship between bodily capability, perception, and action, with a cross-cutting goal of supporting inclusive interaction across diverse bodily capabilities.

contents.title: From Plastic to Porcelain and Beyond: Making Everyday Objects Interactive from the Material Up
contents.abstract:
Everyday objects---cookware, tableware, lamps, and tools---could be
interfaces, but today we make things interactive by adding electronics
onto them, with the object serving only as a housing. My doctoral
research makes everyday objects interactive from the material up: the
same material that gives an object its strength, heat tolerance, and
shape also senses touch and delivers power through its electrical
properties. Making interactivity native to an object's material is
hard: commercial touch hardware collapses a material's electrical response into a single
aggregate signal; the processes that make objects durable, like firing
ceramic, destroy embedded conductors; and the complex, soft shapes we
most want to touch break fixed electrode layouts. I take these barriers
on through three projects. With \emph{Impedius}, I read the individual
elements of impedance so that 3D-printed geometry itself encodes many
sensor values on a single circuit. With \emph{PorCuPrint}, I develop a
maker-friendly copper clay and an injection-based fabrication method
that carries copper structures through the kiln, so one fired object is at once
vessel, heater, sensor, and circuit. In my third, ongoing project, I
join soft conductive and non-conductive strips so that the same weave
that forms a complex, deformable 3D object also forms its touch-sensing
layout. Together, these projects work toward a reusable method and
design guidelines for objects that are interactive through the very
material they are made of.

contents.title: Human-AI-Robot Collaboration for Designing and Manufacturing Physical Objects with Generative AI and Robotic Assembly
contents.abstract: 3D generative AI enables people to rapidly create diverse digital objects through natural-language or image prompts. However, translating these outputs into physical objects remains challenging due to the constraints of the physical world. Recent work has focused on improving generative models to produce fabricable outputs, often relying on 3D printing as the primary fabrication method. This dissertation explores the integration of 3D generative AI with modular robotic assembly to create physical objects, investigating where their capabilities align, where they diverge, and where further alignment is needed. Across three projects, my research examines: (1) translating generated geometry into assemblies while accounting for fabrication constraints, time, and material use; (2) supporting functionality and structural performance; and (3) enabling larger-scale assemblies at lower cost. While these projects advance the use of generative AI and modular robotic assembly for making physical objects, further challenges remain in supporting material expression, aesthetic control, creative exploration, and iterative design within the process.

contents.title: Murmurations: A Wearable Piezoelectric Silent Speech Interface
contents.abstract:
Silent Speech Interfaces (SSIs) enable interaction through articulatory movements without vocalization, providing noise-robust and private communication for individuals with speech impairments.

We present Murmurations, a wearable SSI that captures articulatory vibrations using silicone-coupled piezoelectric film sensors on the chin. Using facial 3D-scanning, the device can be customized to conform to the user's face, thus minimizing information loss. The system integrates an ESP32-S3, a 24-bit ΣΔ ADC for simultaneous three-channel acquisition, and a programmable-gain analog front-end, enabling capture of subtle articulatory movements using off-the-shelf components in a battery-powered form factor. We validate the platform by mapping piezoelectric signals to text using a CTC-based phoneme prediction model, demonstrating their viability for speech recognition.

contents.title: AffAdapt: AFFect-driven ADAPTive  AI Personas for Seamless Conversations
contents.abstract: AI-generated personas are being increasingly used for support, training and simulations. While generative AI models possess abilities to generate affect-aware responses, their embodiment into visual personas is an active area of investigation. Naturalistic exchanges require understanding of the conversational partners' turn completions, whether the agent should respond or keep listening and rely on non-verbal cues aligned with one's emotional states. Seamless human-AI conversation in a multimodal setting requires all modalities being generated to act in coordination. We present \sysname, a seamless interaction design framework for AI-personas, which coordinates streaming speech recognition, proactive turn-management, persona-grounded response generation, a persistent emotional state, and synchronized embodied output into a single interaction loop. We demonstrate the architecture in the context of practicing sensitive, high-stakes conversations, and report an initial case study showing fluid turn management and adaptive, persona-consistent behavior, alongside open challenges in interruption handling, open-ended dialogue, and multimodal affective alignment. \sysname's interaction loop is a generalizable pattern for coordinating timing, identity, and affect in real-time AI personas - applicable to training, coaching, education, and simulation contexts wherever believable, responsive interaction matters.
