contents.title: DioramaCraft: A Human-AI Workflow for Transforming Personal Photographs into Layered Paper Theater Dioramas
contents.abstract: Transforming personal memories into layered dioramas typically requires complex spatial and structural decision-making, from conceptualizing a scene to preparing physical layers for fabrication. We present DioramaCraft, a system that helps users externalize photographed memories into printable paper theater templates through a four-stage human-AI collaboration pipeline. By synthesizing semantic elements across photo collections, users review detected elements, direct scene generation, and refine depth layers to produce a print-ready construction guide. DioramaCraft demonstrates how interactive human-AI workflows can aid creative memory-making by reducing technical friction while supporting user agency across digital design and hands-on assembly.

contents.title: Anteroom: Bounded-Choice Message Triage for Executive and Motor Access
contents.abstract: Incoming messages create more than notification cost: they require deciding, remembering, initiating, and closing a loop. For the first author, who has ADHD and a motor disability, these executive-function demands compound with interfaces built around repeated, precise pointing. We present Anteroom, a desktop client implementing bounded-choice message triage across Gmail, IMAP, Slack, and Telegram. When the user engages an arrival, Anteroom decomposes handling into a short, skippable sequence of closed choices. Deferral can create a message-linked to-do that completes when the message is opened or answered, while editable drafts support reply initiation. Each choice is available through a large cursor-adjacent target, one key, or a constrained voice command. We contribute bounded-choice triage as an interaction technique and a situated design rationale from ongoing first-person use.

contents.title: Playground: A Two-Part Visual Document Management and Script Editing Tool for Playwrights
contents.abstract: The writing support tools that playwrights use are often poorly attuned to the challenges and constraints of writing scripts for live performance. We present Playground, a two-part writing support and version control prototype for playwriting that displays documents spatially on a 2D canvas alongside a text editor tailored for writing stageplays. Playground's two components, the canvas and the text editor, afford playwrights the ability to flexibly create and visually arrange versions of their documents. Playground supports playwriting nonlinearity and stageplay script elasticity by allowing playwrights to easily restructure their writing, to navigate script histories, and to organize, connect, and differentiate documents.

contents.title: Air as a Soft Material: Introducing the Ionized-Wind Actuator (IoWA) for VR Haptics in Human–Computer Interaction
contents.abstract: Replicating the richness of real-world perception has long been a goal of virtual reality technologies. While vision and sound have advanced rapidly, touch remains constrained by haptic devices that are heavy, rigid, power-hungry, and tethered to external infrastructure. These limitations restrict mobility and scalability, often undermining immersion rather than enhancing it. Here, we introduce the Ionized-Wind Actuators (IoWA) as a new class of actuators for VR haptic devices. IoWA generates controllable airflow without moving parts, enabling lightweight, quiet, and low-friction tactile feedback. Their simple structure supports scalable, conformable fabrication, enabling dense actuator arrays for localized and programmable tactile cues. This work represents the first translation of ionized-wind actuation into a device level interface for human–computer interaction. We present the actuation mechanism, fabrication approach, and four proof-of-concept prototypes that instantiate IoWA in different configurations, illustrating its potential as a foundational actuation technology and outlining a path toward future VR haptic interfaces.

contents.title: PrivacyPeek: Showing Users What Their AI Chats Send Out, and When It Crosses a Line
contents.abstract: People send work, personal, health, and money questions to the same AI chat tools, and rarely see what left the browser. We present PrivacyPeek, a Chrome side panel that reviews chat history after the send and marks turns that crossed a context line, like a health question typed into a work chat. It never blocks. An on-device rule classifier labels each turn into six contexts, and three checks from Helen Nissenbaum's Contextual Integrity (CI) run per turn: context drift, recipient mismatch, and identity build-up. We also contribute a think-aloud coding scheme that tracks which CI slot a user reads first, re-reads, or skips. It is the first browser tool we know of to surface per-turn CI checks after the send, with on-device flags that keep the user in control.

contents.title: Reframing Undesirable Material Ageing: A Case Study of Pilling
contents.abstract: Material ageing can contribute to premature disposal when functional products become visually or socially unacceptable. Prior HCI and design research shows that responses to ageing vary across materials, products, cultures, ownership, use, and care. Yet less is known about how people negotiate acceptable and unacceptable ageing around everyday surface change. This study takes garment pilling as a common case of negatively perceived material ageing. We interviewed 12 participants about how they noticed, interpreted, and responded to pilling. Our analysis identifies three design opportunities: understanding ageing through material knowledge, exploring when ageing can be read as a trace, and negotiating ageing across social settings. We use these spaces to outline an early material vision for garment pilling. This work offers early insights into when pilling becomes unacceptable and what design could support different ways of noticing and responding to ageing.

contents.title: Climate Echoes: A Sound-Led Multisensory System for Non-Visual Climate Change Engagement
contents.abstract: To address the challenge of making slow and distributed climate change perceptible beyond visual representations, we propose Climate Echoes, a sound-led, non-visual multisensory interaction system. The system uses tangible NFC cards representing time, place, and climate-related events to transform climate phenomena into composable and comparable layered soundscapes. This process is achieved through card detection, soundscape-layer mapping, and the synchronization of tactile and microclimate feedback, enabling participants to engage in embodied listening by placing, replacing, and combining cards. The system further integrates an AI-assisted sound narrative pipeline that transforms personal memories into customized climate soundscapes, connecting global environmental change with individual experience.

contents.title: rowserLens: Interactive Diagnosis of Web-Agent Trajectories with a Layered State-Action Graph
contents.abstract:
A completed web agent run leaves only a trajectory: a long linear log in
which cross-step structure such as revisits, loops, dead ends, and stalls is
scattered across distant entries. We present BrowserLens, a read-only diagnosis
workspace that reorganizes a single logged trajectory around browser-state
identity rather than time. Normalized URLs, viewports, and state-anchored
actions form a three-layer graph in which revisits collapse into single
nodes and repetition becomes visible structure. Four visual cues mark
suspicious structure; each cue is an attention signal, not a failure
label, and links to the recorded evidence (screenshots, DOM/ARIA snapshots,
action logs, LLM context, and replay) against which a reviewer confirms or
rejects a failure hypothesis. We ground the design in benchmark-reported web agent failures and in HCI work on event-sequence and browsing-history
visualization.

contents.title: Evaluating Clickable Padding and Button Size for Smartwatch Touch Accuracy
contents.abstract: We present a controlled study of first-tap touch accuracy on a smartwatch (Apple Watch Series~9, 44\,mm): 30 participants, 23 realistic UI layouts, 11{,}610 trials. Overall accuracy was 82.2\% but ranged from 46.3\% to 100\% across layouts. Adding 4\,pt of invisible clickable padding raised mean accuracy from 63.0\% to 79.8\% ($p<0.001$), improving every single participant, with the largest gains for the smallest targets. Accuracy rose monotonically with target size, taps on near-edge targets drifted systematically toward the nearest screen boundary, and corner targets significantly underperformed edge-aligned ones (62.6\% vs.\ 79.4\%, $p<0.001$). Our results quantify clickable padding as a near-free accuracy lever and motivate edge-aware smartwatch target placement.

contents.title: ExpertLens: Bridging Physical Observations With Scientific Models through Computer Vision and AR
contents.abstract: While scientific novices often see surface-level attributes (e.g., objects in motion), experts see the underlying mechanisms (e.g., energy conservation) that govern them. Visualizations can help novices see like experts, but existing systems typically render these mechanisms over precomputed simulations or require complex sensors. ExpertLens visualizes these implicit mechanisms for novices in real time using only a mobile device.  Through a controlled physics lab study (N=52) and a biochemistry classroom field study (N=95 students), we discuss how ExpertLens helps students better understand their data and the underlying phenomena.

contents.title: MemoryLens: Pre-Resurfacing Governance for AI-Mediated Shared Memories
contents.abstract: AI memory systems increasingly resurface memories proactively, yet shared memories are not neutral: the same event can carry opposite meanings for different people, while the modality through which it resurfaces can change its emotional intensity. We present MemoryLens, introducing pre-resurfacing governance through a Divergent Meaning View preserving multiple readings, a Resurfacing Preview rehearsing relational consequences, and a Temporal Consent Dial governing whether, to whom, and how intensely a memory resurfaces. A walkthrough with eight participants suggests MemoryLens raises perceived control and emotional safety over a conventional reminder interface.

contents.title: CiteLen: In-Situ Multi-Lens Citation Analysis for Scholarly Reading
contents.abstract: Citations connect a paper’s claims to the evidence behind them, yet verifying them (whether a reference is real, supports the claim it accompanies, or is missing altogether) remains a manual task that readers and reviewers rarely have time to perform. We present CiteLen, a tool that brings citation analysis into the reading interface itself, beside the PDF being read. CiteLen unifies seven checks that existing tools handle only in isolation: whether a reference is authentic, whether it supports its claim, and whether relevant work is missing, along with document-level views of the reference list’s thematic structure, its balance across authors and years, its formatting consistency, and its fairness to prior work. All seven apply to the same document from a single upload. By situating these checks where reading already happens, CiteLen supports citation verification as part of reading rather than as a separate task performed afterward.

contents.title: Chameleon: Negotiating Machine Visibility with Programmable Privacy Surfaces
contents.abstract: Visual sensing is becoming common in everyday environments, but people have limited control over how ordinary objects are seen by machine vision. To address this gap, we present Chameleon, a prototype exploring programmable privacy surfaces that use dynamic, reconfigurable object-side displays to modulate how visual recognizers perceive covered objects. Using a 14-inch portable display as a surface proxy, Chameleon allows users to apply visual textures such as checkerboards, static noise, dynamic noise, moving stripes, and flickering blocks. We evaluated the prototype across seven everyday settings with two general-purpose object detectors, YOLOv8n and Torchvision SSDLite, using ROI-aware metrics to distinguish protected surfaces from unperturbed comparison objects. Preliminary results show that Chameleon, particularly the checkerboard pattern, effectively suppresses tv and laptop detections, supporting programmable privacy surfaces as an effective but context-dependent safeguard against the tested visual recognition systems. Chameleon contributes an HCI probe for shifting visual privacy from post-capture redaction toward visible, adjustable, and object-side negotiation of machine visibility.

contents.title: PreviewAR: Sketching Spaces for Scale-Aware Product Discovery in AR
contents.abstract: Current AR product-preview tools often lack two capabilities: previewing products without existing 3D assets and supporting space-first product discovery, where users can find items that fit a given space without testing products one by one. Recent 3D asset-generation systems address the first limitation by allowing users to create previews for products with missing 3D assets, but they often fail to preserve real-world scale. To address these limitations, we introduce PreviewAR, an AR application that supports space-first product discovery where users can sketch spatial preferences in their environment, generate scale-aware 3D assets of compatible products, and preview them in their environment.

contents.title: BIOral CapCell: An Intraoral Solution for Drug Release and Monitoring via Colorimetric Sensing
contents.abstract: There has been an increasing interest in developing intraoral sensors, as the oral cavity's discreet nature makes it ideal for continuous health monitoring. This paper introduces BIOral CapCell, an intraoral solution for drug release and monitoring.  It utilizes an edible colorimetric hydrogel and a digital color sensor integrated into a dental brace. Our technical evaluations demonstrate that our solution can monitor the controlled release of Vitamin B2 between 1h5m and 3h45m. We further validate BIOral through a preliminary in-mouth study.

contents.title: Somatic Dark Patterns: Synthetic Heartbeats Shape Trust in AI Agents
contents.abstract: AI agents talk, advise, and persuade, but they have no body. Human social judgment leans heavily on bodily signals, a racing heart or a calm breath, that we read off each other without thinking. We ask what happens when an AI agent is given a synthetic bodily signal. In two lab studies (N = 39), people interacted with AI agents while a faint heartbeat-like vibration played under the table. In an interrogation task, an elevated heartbeat tied to one AI suspect made people about seven times more likely to accuse it. In a smaller interview task, a slow, calm heartbeat tied to one AI candidate produced a directional preference for it. The heartbeat did not raise people's own anxiety; they read it as the agent's feeling and constructed plausible justifications for their choice. A synthetic heartbeat is a quiet, peripheral channel that shifts trust and suspicion toward AI, one that could support people or manipulate them; we call the risk somatic deception.

contents.title: SensorGen: Prompt-Driven Exploratory Design and Synthesis for Floating Capacitor Sensor Geometries
contents.abstract: Electrode geometry is foundational to capacitive sensing, where a sensor's shape directly dictates its electrical response. However, mapping how complex spatial patterns affect output signals is an arduous process, traditionally requiring manual CAD modeling and simulation loops. To lower the barrier to this exploratory design process, we present SensorGen: a proof-of-concept generative-AI-assisted workflow that embeds an analytical mutual-capacitance model within a Large Language Model (LLM) interface. SensorGen allows users to specify and iterate electrode shapes for a floating capacitor geometry via natural language with instantaneous visualization of predicted capacitance profiles. By wrapping an analytical model in a generative interface, our workflow strives to enrich exploratory design possibilities in two ways: (1) it introduces unexpected spatial patterns that a user might overlook when designing sensor geometry, thereby broadening creative exploration; (2) it facilitates an interactive, rapid prototyping loop that reduces the time-intensive manual CAD and simulation cycles characteristic of sensor design. Through a preliminary exploration of diverse symmetric and asymmetric patterns, we demonstrate that our workflow supports rapid, language-driven capacitive sensor design exploration.

contents.title: Vision-Language Models with In-Context Learning for In-Camera Portrait Composition Guidance
contents.abstract: Capturing aesthetically pleasing portraits requires specialized compositional knowledge that ordinary users often lack, making it difficult for them to achieve optimal camera framing. While vision-language models (VLMs) excel at general image understanding, they frequently produce overly positive feedback and lack the granular structural awareness needed to generate actionable compositional guidance. To address this, we present a visual in-context learning (ICL) framework that equips VLMs with augmented aesthetic evaluation capabilities. By retrieving structurally similar, professionally reframed image-composition analyses as visual prompts, our framework grounds VLM's reasoning in established aesthetic standards, e.g., the rule of thirds and leading lines, and enables mapping compositional flaws to specific camera instructions.

contents.title: Showcasing AdaptiveCue: Team-Customized Cue Tags for Live Collaborative Planning
contents.abstract: Collaborative group planning through live conversation imposes heavy grounding and working-memory demands as participants track alternatives, preferences, and practical constraints. We present AdaptiveCue, a web-based video-conferencing tool that pairs continuously updated, object-anchored cue tags with a tree-structured shared workspace. As discussion unfolds, the system analyzes live transcripts to structure the plan proactively and highlight the current conversational focus. Team-customized tags make inferred support, opposition, tension, and decision-relevant facts visible on the places under discussion, helping groups revisit trade-offs. Rich place details and a route probe further support evaluation of travel options. We showcase the system design and interaction model.

contents.title: Co-Grading Open-ended Assignments with Dynamic Rubrics
contents.abstract: We introduce GradePartner, a tablet-based interactive system that supports large-scale grading. Unlike prior rubric-based approaches for open-ended assignment grading, our system aims to position LLMs as teachable partners. The system operates across three integrated stages: rubric development through natural annotation, alignment of evaluative standards via dual-agent conflict detection, and synthesis of instructional feedback grounded in exemplars. In a user study involving graders, we demonstrated how our interactive system can enhance self-grading consistency and feedback quality by integrating diverse student work with graders' judgment.

contents.title: NeuraTriage: Quality-Gated No-Decision Interaction for Pre-Hospital EEG Triage Support
contents.abstract: Pre-hospital stroke triage needs rapid decision support, yet EEG recorded in a moving ambulance suffers motion artifacts and imperfect electrode contact, and spurious alerts erode clinician trust. We present NeuraTriage, a real-time EEG triage-support proparamedic fits a wearable headset on a suspected stroke patient and reads a glass-box risk panel; the utotype whose contribution is an interaction and sensing-layer design for cautious biosignal decision support, not a new classifier. A nderlying per-window probability is never surfaced unsmoothed. Smoothing, hysteresis and a cooldown suppress the flicker that drives alarm fatigue, and any window failing a signal-quality index (SQI) enters an explicit No-Decision state rather than a forced guess. Retrospectively, an SQI-only probe encoding no pathology separates our cross-source cohorts at AUC 0.998 — an acquisition shortcut, not a diagnostic signal; once the rig is controlled, the full feature set reaches macro-F1 0.774 / AUC 0.869. We argue such shortcuts should be routinely measured and disclosed. It is a research prototype, not a diagnostic medical device.

contents.title: InteractPost: Bridging the Last Mile of Interactive Programs through Agent-Mediated Publishing
contents.abstract: Interactive programs are commonly shared through screenshots and recordings that travel easily but eliminate direct manipulation, or through external links that preserve execution while separating the work from social discovery and response. We present Fil, an agent-mediated publishing system that turns heterogeneous interactive projects into focused, executable, mobile-first posts. A creator can import a p5.js sketch, Observable notebook, OpenProcessing work, or local codebase. Fil’s code agent identifies one core interactive experience, rewrites dependencies for browser-only execution, adapts layout and input to a 405 by 720 touch viewport, and packages the result as HTML, JavaScript, and assets. Creators preview and refine the result before publishing it to an interactive feed; Fil then reports audience interaction traces such as drags, clicks, replays, and time to first interaction. Fil explores program conversion as a publishing interaction: preserving an executable idea while deliberately adapting its runtime, presentation, interaction, and social context.

contents.title: LaserMorph:Water-Triggered Laser Fabrication of Soft Objects from Compressed Sponge
contents.abstract: Desktop laser fabrication is fast, inexpensive, and widely accessible, yet remains largely limited to planar cutting and engraving. Existing deployable fabrication methods support richer 3D transformations but often require specialized materials, complex actuation, or one-time shape change. We present LaserMorph a water-triggered laser fabrication workflow that transforms commercially available compressed cellulose sponge into reusable soft 2.5D and 3D objects. Laser engraving programs local sponge expansion along the compression direction, enabling flat sheets to self-form target geometries upon immersion in room-temperature water. The deployed objects can be dried to preserve their shape and recompressed into thin sheets for repeated deployment. We characterize the relationships between laser parameters, engraving depth, and recovered geometry, observing 85%–95% dry-thickness retention after 15 deployment cycles. Applications demonstrate how LaserMorph extends desktop laser fabrication into a simple, low-cost, and reusable workflow for soft shape-changing prototyping.

contents.title: CallEEG: Towards Cognitive Engagement-Aware Video-Mediated Communication for Copresence
contents.abstract: While video-mediated communications are now a central medium for work, learning and social interaction, they provide limited social and contextual cues compared to physical interactions, weakening copresence, the sense of being together with another person. We present CallEEG, an end-to-end system that integrates ear-EEG sensing and real-time cognitive engagement inference into video-mediated communication. CallEEG contains (1) 8-channel EEG sensing earbuds with a custom PCB board, (2) a real-time data processing pipeline that derives the user's engagement level, and (3) a video communication interface with adaptive audio-visual salience for engagement-aware communication facilitation. We validated CallEEG's engagement level processing pipeline with EEG data collected from 11 users. In addition, we conducted a 14-participant user study to evaluate the copresence enhancement of CallEEG under various interaction levels. The results indicate that integrating cognitive engagement in video-mediated communications enhances self- and mutual awareness and ease of awareness.

contents.title: Feelium: A Touchable Blimp Body for Aerial Telepresence
contents.abstract: Floating things invite touch. We present Feelium, a blimp-based telepresence platform that enables visual embodiment and touch interaction through its inflatable skin. Through a VR headset, a remote person inhabits the blimp, looking out of it first-person, appearing on its skin as a face or avatar, and steering it through the room. Partners in the room pat it, press a palm against it, draw on it, or lean into it; the skin senses each contact and renders it into the wearer's view in VR spaces. Touch thus provides a physical interaction channel for remote presence, turning the skin into a shared surface between remote and co-located partners.

contents.title: ToneCanvas: Visually Painting Character Tone and Terms for Narrative Consistency
contents.abstract: Revising long-form fiction requires writers to maintain each character's voice across dialogue that is often dispersed throughout a manuscript. Detecting gradual changes in how a character speaks therefore depends heavily on rereading, memory, and external notes. We present ToneCanvas, an interactive writing interface that uses persistent watercolor gradients to support character-centered tone comparison and revision within and across passages.  A formative study with five professionals involved in fiction revision and translation identified four recurring workflow breakdowns, which informed the design of character-focused dialogue views, adjustable tone dimensions, and integrated character references. This work contributes an empirical account of character-tone revision, corresponding design opportunities, and an interactive prototype that instantiates them.

contents.title: DLAP: A Protocol for Measuring Readability of Diegetic Text in Video Games
contents.abstract: Video games are among the most text-rich environments many young people encounter daily, yet research on games and literacy has largely examined academic outcomes independent of the in-game (diegetic) text players read. This work-in-progress presents DLAP, the Diegetic Language Assessment Protocol: a reproducible, four-step computational method for building and evaluating corpora of diegetic text from commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) games. We validate DLAP on three commercial titles—Animal Crossing: New Horizons, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and Baldur’s Gate 3—using Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) and the Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity (MTLD). All three titles read below a fourth-grade level, while lexical diversity is decoupled from syntactic difficulty: each title occupies a distinct quadrant of the difficulty × diversity space, consistent with its genre and audience rating. DLAP offers a scalable foundation for studying games as literacy environments.

contents.title: GateCast: Synchronized Mobile Edutainment Design for Teacher-Orchestrated Outdoor Cultural Tours
contents.abstract: Multi-device systems for co-present groups typically push content via proximity or timers, preventing physically present teachers from judging when a cohort is ready for shared media. We introduce Coordinator-Gated Broadcast (CGB), an interaction pattern where a leader privately previews multimedia before triggering synchronized delivery to all group devices with a single deliberate action. We formalize CGB via a five-state delivery model and a structured design space, then instantiate it in GateCast, a mobile edutainment platform for outdoor cultural tours delivering synchronized AI-reconstructed historical media. Grounded in formative field research (n = 32) and evaluated across user trials (n = 16) and cross-regional validation (n = 78 across Hong Kong, Jiangsu, Chengdu, and Toronto), GateCast significantly improved teachers’ perceived delivery control (4.4/5 vs. 2.1/5 for current practice) while aligning group attention.We discuss design implications for mobile classroom orchestration and co-present cultural edutainment.

contents.title: Art2Song: Enhancing Visual Art Appreciation with Contextual Music Generation
contents.abstract: Art2Song is a conceptual framework that expresses artworks as sound by separating Non-Visual Context, which is difficult to perceive from the image alone, from Visual Evidence. Visual Evidence, such as objects, colors, and spatial composition, is transformed into Lyrics, while the Contextual Mood derived from the historical and art-historical context in the museum's artwork description is reflected in the background soundtrack. Rather than describing artworks textually, Art2Song aims to explore the possibility of a new mode of art appreciation in which viewers experience hidden stories and emotional context through music. As future interaction directions, we plan an Emotional Layer Blending Slider interface and a structured, traceable song-generation scenario, presenting the possibility that users can explore the relationship between Visual Evidence and Contextual Mood.

contents.title: CORAL: Continually Learning Generative Interfaces from Collective User Interactions
contents.abstract: Large language models can now synthesize an interface on demand from a stated intent (a generative user interface). However, existing approaches treat every generative UI as a cold start, generating each one in isolation. We introduce CORAL, a system that instead treats a generated interface as a shared artifact that persists across users and retains their interaction signal. From that cold-start generation, users' implicit and explicit signals accumulate across those pursuing the same intent and harden the interface into a converging, reusable form, while idiosyncratic signals stay locally malleable. In an exploratory study (N=9) on a non-canonical task (authoring web audio with haptics), reshape effort fell and distance to the target sound shrank across three successive cohorts, and five of six participants from the earlier rounds preferred the hardened interface to the one they had shaped themselves.

contents.title: What Users Do Not Say: Inferring Latent Needs from Everyday Videos with VLM Agents
contents.abstract: People rarely say what they need, and often do not know it themselves. We ask whether AI can find those needs simply by watching. Our framework, inspired by collaborative ethnography, has four VLM agents observe the same everyday video from different perspectives, critique one another’s interpretations, and distill them into latent needs. In a preliminary study, twelve participants reviewed latent needs inferred from their daily videos. What impressed them most was that latent needs emerged without their explaining anything, and reading the system’s interpretations even led some to self-reflection. To others, however, the same interpretations felt like overreach, inferring more than their videos could support. Based on this duality, we discuss directions for VLM systems that infer latent needs from everyday behavior.

contents.title: RotorFlow: Overlaying Simulated Airflow onto a Physical Propeller Using Augmented Reality
contents.abstract: We present RotorFlow, a screen-centered tangible interface that couples manipulation of a physical variable-pitch propeller with situated augmented-reality airflow visualization. Two physical controls adjust blade pitch and rotor speed. A display mounted on the system combines a live camera view of the rotor with a CFD-derived flow-field overlay selected according to the current blade geometry and pitch. The same display also provides a CFD simulation view and a quantitative view showing measured RPM and estimated lift, drag, and lift-to-drag ratio. All views remain synchronized to the same physical inputs, allowing one action to be inspected as a situated flow pattern, an abstract simulation, and a numerical state. Users operate the propeller, change pitch and speed, and switch among the three linked views. RotorFlow demonstrates a walk-up interaction pattern in which a physical mechanism functions as the input device and a co-located embedded screen reveals a simulation of an otherwise invisible phenomenon.

contents.title: Towards Choice Blindness in Extended Reality
contents.abstract: Choice blindness refers to the failure of people to notice when the outcome of a choice they just made is covertly switched, along with their tendency to construct a justification for a choice they did not actually make. The effect was first shown with pairs of photographs of female faces swapped by sleight of hand, and later replicated on screens and in immersive Virtual Reality (VR). We propose extending choice blindness into everyday spatial Extended Reality (XR), where the manipulation targets the arrangement of full-size physical objects around a standing participant rather than images on a table. Using SwitchAR, a perceptual manipulation technique that imperceptibly substitutes a photorealistic 3D reconstruction for the live camera feed, we can covertly rotate or reconfigure an entire room to redirect a participant toward an object they did not choose. We outline a planned study in which participants choose among physical objects (e.g., wall clocks arranged in a circle) and discuss the safety, ethical, and design implications of covert spatial choice manipulation in everyday XR.

contents.title: CompactPack: From 3D Objects to Fabricable Packaging Inserts
contents.abstract: We present CompactPack, a browser-based design tool that generates fabricable paper inserts for packing multiple objects compactly and holding them in place inside a box. We take a set of 3D objects through an end-to-end pipeline: converting each object to a 2D silhouette, arranging the silhouettes into a tightly packed, multi-layer layout using simulated annealing with a quadtree-based distribution score, selecting and fitting the smallest box that holds the layout, and exporting a cut-ready insert that holds each object in place inside the box. We reflect on uses beyond shipping, where the tool helps people arrange existing objects.

contents.title: StoryLake: Exploring LLM-Generated Narratives for Older Adults' Life Reflection through Counterfactual Lenses
contents.abstract: Older adults often reflect on pivotal life decisions through counterfactual questions about paths not taken. Existing reminiscence technologies help users recall and share past events, but rarely support structured exploration of unrealized life possibilities. We present StoryLake, an LLM-guided ritual interface for later-life reflection. StoryLake uses a conversational agent to structure remembered life moments into key elements such as people, places, turning points, suspended goals, and roads not taken. These elements are transformed into reflective stones and visualized through a stone-skipping interaction, where ripples unfold counterfactual paths across life stages and domains. The system then generates narrative echo and reflection prompts to support meaning-making without presenting alternative lives as predictions. This research contributes StoryLake as an LLM-guided ritual interface for emotionally safe counterfactual life reflection, supported by counterfactual lenses and a stone-skipping visual grammar.

contents.title: ElectroNome: Limb-Agnostic Synchronous Gestures via Electric-Field Sensing
contents.abstract:
To address the need for customizable, adaptive, and efficient interaction methods for smart glasses, we propose ElectroGnome, a limb-agnostic, low-power, single-site passive electric field sensing approach, combined with intuitive synchronous gestures, where users move to match the frequency a visual cue.

Through two studies, we verify that (a) participants can match visual cues, (b) our signal processing methods can accurately determine movement frequency, and (c) participants enjoy using the system relative to existing interaction techniques, demonstrating ElectroGnome's potential contributions to greater flexibility of smart glasses input.

contents.title: TRACE: Relation-Aware Locative Memory Sharing for Intergenerational Place-Based Reminiscence
contents.abstract: Everyday places can hold traces of family memories that prompt intergenerational conversation, yet families often lack resources for connecting partial, uncertain, and unevenly distributed accounts. Drawing on distributed remembering and transactive memory, we explore how others' place-linked memories can serve as conversational resources for situated family reminiscence. We present TRACE, a relation-aware locative system that uses RAG-based relation analysis to connect memory fragments across people, places, and time. TRACE models five relation types among place-memory fragments and turns them into hints, progressive memory reveals, question scaffolds, and uncertainty-based revisit prompts. In a bounded deployment with five families, cross-family relation triggered prompts showed higher uptake and longer conversations than family-internal location triggers. These prompts helped younger participants ask follow-up questions while giving older participants occasions to correct, elaborate, and selectively make everyday place memories public.

contents.title: HeyFlora: A Tangible Role-Play Kit to Foster Children’s Empathy and Connection with Plants
contents.abstract: Children’s contact with plants has drastically decreased in the digital era, causing them to overlook plants. Most existing solutions still rely on screens. Our work takes a different approach: drawing children into direct, hands-on engagement with plants through role play. We present HeyFlora, a tangible interaction kit that reveals a plant’s hidden vital signs through audible and visual feedback. Children play “plant doctors,” observing, “diagnosing,” and “treating” real plants. Early user testing shows that this tangible approach meaningfully boosts children’s empathy toward plants and their curiosity to explore.

contents.title: Editing in the Dark: Edit-Propagation Opacity in a Staged Human-in-the-Loop Synthetic Interview Tool
contents.abstract: Synthetic user interview tools let researchers explore directions when direct user access is constrained, but prior work centers on output fidelity. We built a staged synthetic interview tool with three human-in-the-loop checkpoints, where the researcher reviews and edits AI-generated personas, questions, and analysis plans before each next stage. Five UX practitioners in one industry organization used it and reflected on how they would share its outputs. Reviewing intermediate outputs built trust, yet four of five avoided editing them, uncertain what an edit at one stage would alter in later ones — an opacity internal to the workflow rather than between people. We name this condition edit-propagation opacity and frame it as a design problem for staged human-in-the-loop interfaces.

contents.title: Sun Menu: An Outward Ray-Based Radial Menu for Accurate VR Selection
contents.abstract: In dense VR radial menus such as Pie Menus, each item's angular width shrinks as item count grows, making selection errors likely during rapid ray-based selection. We propose Sun Menu, which arranges 24 items into eight coarse regions, each connected to three terminal options on the outer edge. Sun Menu accepts the initial ray direction as a coarse directional selection and defers fine-grained candidate selection to the outer terminals, so that users need not aim directly at narrow angular sectors while selection remains a single outward ray movement. In a user study with a 24-item Pie Menu as a baseline, Sun Menu showed significantly lower error rates under all of the Accurate, Neutral, and Fast instruction conditions, and no significant increase in selection time was observed. These results suggest that Sun Menu reduces selection errors in dense VR radial menus without a significant increase in selection time.

contents.title: Text to Assembly: Functionality-Aware Component Assignment in Robotic Assembly using Vision-Language Models
contents.abstract: We present Text-to-Assembly, a system that converts natural language prompts and AI-generated 3D meshes into robot-executable multi-component assemblies. While text-to-3D models can generate visual geometry, their outputs do not specify which regions should become structural elements, functional surfaces, or robot-manipulable components. Our system addresses this gap by treating component assignment as an actionable visual perception problem. A generated mesh is discretized into structural units, then a vision-language model identifies functional parts requiring panel components and maps those parts to reachable labeled faces on the discretized geometry. The resulting component assignments are converted into pick-and-place operations executed by a UR20 robot. In a user evaluation with 32 participants across five object categories, VLM-generated assignments were selected as functionally appropriate 90.6\% of the time, outperforming rule-based and random baselines. These results suggest that constrained vision-language reasoning can help bridge high-level generative design and physical robotic assembly.

contents.title: Semipy: A Python Runtime to Program with Informal Spec
contents.abstract: We build semipy, a Python runtime that lets a programmer leave parts of a function as natural-language specifications instead of writing code ahead of time. The first time a specification is called with real input, semipy generates an ordinary Python function that fits the input and the surrounding formal code. Every later call checks that function against new input, keeps every version semipy has generated, and checks any external effect before letting it run unsupervised. We describe semipy via a use case scenario and summarize the design decisions. Code is available at https://github.com/ryanyen2/semipy-package

contents.title: Print-and-Integrate: Reversible Integration for Compostable Prototyping
contents.abstract: Early-stage interactive prototyping tends to force early commitment: as soon as sensing and computation are added, the workflow hardens into industrial thermoplastics, adhesives, and soldered wiring, none of which is easy to undo, repair, or recover. We present Print-and-Place, a direct-ink-writing (DIW) workflow that keeps electronics integration reversible and uses a biodegradable, cellulose-based substrate. Artifacts are printed from a compostable cardboard-based paste, with components added through two routes: in-print embedding, where elements are placed during a pause in printing, and post-print mounting, where screws and reversible fixtures attach electronics without adhesives. We demonstrate the workflow with feasibility-level sensing (a pencil-shaded-paper capacitive accelerometer and screw-based capacitive touch), example prototypes, and a small usability study of the two integration routes. Our contribution is a route to reversible, afterlife-separable interactive prototyping.

contents.title: CoGaze: Webcam-Based Gaze Sharing for Asymmetric Remote Collaboration in Practical Deployment Contexts
contents.abstract:
Shared gaze helps re-establish joint attention in asymmetric remote
collaboration, yet existing MR systems source the expert’s gaze
from a dedicated infrared eye tracker. We present CoGaze, which
shares webcam-estimated expert gaze into a local worker’s MR
view while an infrared reference records simultaneously, turning
estimation noise into a measured variable. A four-participant pilot
places that noise at 5.9° on average, with 95% of samples within 12.1°.
Whether workers tolerate it remains untested: an instrumentation
defect left the displayed cue dominated by the infrared stream, so
the reduction in grounding cost we observed under gaze indicates
the value of gaze presence, not tolerance of webcam noise. We
contribute the system, the measured in-situ error bounds, a speechbased grounding measure sensitive where task accuracy was at
ceiling, and a successor design calibrated to those bounds.

contents.title: When More Information Hurts: Visible Dependency Details and Causal Reasoning in Event Log Interfaces
contents.abstract: Event log interfaces must decide how much dependency information to expose for root cause reasoning. In a within-subject experiment (N = 34), we compared progressive disclosure against inline display of dependency information and found no significant overall differences between conditions. However, within the progressive disclosure condition, participants who chose not to retrieve additional dependency details achieved 100% accuracy across both scenarios, compared to 71.4% among those who did (p = .034, d = 0.781), despite clickers spending more time on the screen yet achieving lower accuracy. Notably, clickers showed marked accuracy decline in the more structurally complex scenario (40%), while non-clickers remained stable. These findings challenge the assumption that greater information visibility supports better causal reasoning, with direct implications for event log interface design in AI-assisted diagnostic contexts.

contents.title: Machine Knittable Yarns for Interactive Pressure Sensing Textiles
contents.abstract:
Physical AI systems that manipulate objects and interact with people need high-density tactile sensing distributed over large, deformable surfaces, much like human skin. Machine knitting is a promising route to such substrates: it is additive and scalable, and it produces stretchable, mechanically programmable structures. Achieving skin-comparable tactile resolution in knitted textiles, however, requires insulated conductive yarns that prevent electrical shorting between adjacent tactile pixels. The insulation must remain conformal and intact under the tight loop curvature and high flexural strain imposed by the knitting process, a requirement that existing yarns do not meet.

In this work, we present a yarn dip-coating process to create insulated conductive yarn optimized for machine knitting. Process parameters for coating silver-plated nylon yarns with thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) are guided by an adjusted dip-coating fluid dynamics model and linked to yarn-level electrical and mechanical characteristics compatible with machine knitting.

Knitted capacitive pressure sensors with multi-layered structures are created to demonstrate e-textile applications. Furthermore, these yarns show minimal deviation in electrical and mechanical properties after machine knitting and washing. Our process demonstrates a viable manufacturing technique to produce functional yarns for integrated knitted textile sensors.

contents.title: Immersive Setup of Autonomous Forklifts in Factories
contents.abstract: Autonomous forklifts (AFLs) are being introduced to address labor shortages and safety concerns in factory logistics, but existing setup methods rely on sparse LiDAR point clouds with insufficient spatial context. We propose a novel interactive system in VR for immersively setting up AFLs within a 3D reconstruction of the target factory. Our workflow leverages users' sense of presence and situational awareness, enabling them to quickly and easily annotate information essential for AFL operation through projective plane interaction. Users can then simulate the resulting 3D node-link task map at real scale and in real time. We conducted a case study in a factory and received positive initial feedback from stakeholders.

contents.title: SignWarriors: Gamifying Sign Language Practice with Hearing Parents
contents.abstract:
Hearing parents of deaf children often face challenges learning sign language due to severe time constraints, despite its critical role in their children's development. While digital games offer flexible learning opportunities, design guidelines for games that effectively enhance sign production skills specifically for hearing parents remain underexplored.
To address this, we developed SignWarriors, a Japanese Sign Language (JSL) learning game co-designed with hearing parents. Inspired by real-time strategy games, SignWarriors requires players to rapidly and accurately produce signs under time pressure against a computer-controlled opponent.
A preliminary workshop with hearing parents revealed key insights into the design trade-offs between pedagogical rigor and gameplay engagement, as well as critical considerations for mobile versus tablet deployment platforms.

contents.title: FeedQUAC: Quick Unobtrusive AI-Generated Commentary
contents.abstract: Design thrives on feedback. However, gathering constant feedback throughout the design process can be labor-intensive and disruptive. We explore how AI can bridge this gap by providing effortless, ambient feedback. We introduce FeedQUAC, a lightweight design companion that delivers real-time, read-aloud, AI-generated commentary from diverse personas based on live screenshots of the designer’s workspace. FeedQUAC is always available, context-aware, ambient, playful, and iteration-aware. In a design probe with eight experienced Fusion 360 users, FeedQUAC generated 106 feedback items across timed and manual triggers. Participants found AI feedback low-stakes, convenient, and enjoyable; they used personas to shift between critique, encouragement, aesthetic attention, and strategic framing. Findings also show two interaction patterns: timed feedback helped some designers remain in flow, while manual triggering supported rapid check-ins after small changes. FeedQUAC also prompted reflection by making designers “look again” at choices they had taken for granted. We discuss ambient AI feedback as a design value for future creativity support systems, while highlighting the tension between being noticeable enough to help and subtle enough to avoid disrupting flow.

contents.title: Batting Alignment and Visualization Using Batter-ball Distance
contents.abstract: The goal of this study is to provide a tool for reviewing batting motion, with a focus on timing in the preparation and swing phases. Using three-dimensional posture data captured by the Hawk-Eye system and videos as input, we present two alignment modes. Time Mode aligns batting postures according to elapsed time centered on pitch release, enabling review of motion during the preparation phase. Ball Mode aligns batting postures based on the distance to the pitched ball, helping to check timing during the swing phase. In a user study involving staff members from a professional baseball team, our application received positive feedback on its usability. Multiple participants also commented on important aspects of batting motion that can be observed using the proposed method.

contents.title: Targeted Interaction Agents for Web Accessibility Evaluation
contents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential for expanding the coverage of web accessibility evaluation. However, our experiments reveal that recent LLM-driven systems yield both high false positives and high false negatives on the Accessibility Conformance Testing (ACT) rules developed by the W3C. Our error analysis identifies three recurring causes: missing perception or interaction evidence, missing criterion support, and semantic judgments without sufficient grounding. We propose interactive tools and atomic rubrics for LLM agents to reliably assess accessibility. The interactive tools inspect or operate a page deterministically to collect evidence, such as focus appearances and error messages. Each rubric covers a testable aspect of a WCAG Success Criterion. They guide agents on how to use tools and interpret evidence. Our preliminary results on a subset of ACT test cases show substantially higher recall (99.1% vs. 68.7%) and precision (91.2% vs. 68.1%) than the strongest evaluated LLM-driven baseline.

contents.title: The Third Voice: Designing Intervention Placement in Conversational AI Interfaces
contents.abstract: Conversational AI increasingly delivers interventions that refuse unsafe requests and encourage responsible behavior. While prior work has primarily focused on what these interventions should say, little attention has been paid to where they should appear within conversational interfaces. We introduce intervention placement as a new interface design dimension by varying only the spatial location of identical intervention messages within a chat interface. Through a counterbalanced within-subject study (N = 33) combining quantitative measures and qualitative interviews, we found that placement alone systematically changed how participants interpreted the same intervention. In particular, center placement was frequently perceived as a third voice—an independent warning distinct from both the user and the conversational AI—making interventions more salient while preserving rapport with the AI. Our findings demonstrate that interface layout, independent of message content, fundamentally shapes users’ interpretation of AI interventions and provides new design guidance for ethical conversational AI interfaces.

contents.title: Trinketry: Materializing Design Elements as Trace Anchors in AI-Assisted Visual Exploration
contents.abstract: Generative AI tools allow visual designers to rapidly produce many visual ideas and alternative design directions. Yet valuable ideas often appear as fragments within otherwise flawed outputs, making them difficult to recover, trace, or reuse. We present Trinketry, an AI-assisted visual exploration system that lets designers extract promising fragments as trinkets: user-preserved design elements that function as reusable materials, provenance anchors, and retrieval queries. By materializing these fragments on the canvas, Trinketry supports element-centered navigation of generative exploration traces and shifts reuse from whole-image branching toward more deliberate reuse, recombination, and recovery.

contents.title: CTATutor: From Instructor-Guided Computational Thinking Blueprints to Adaptive Algorithm Tutoring
contents.abstract: Algorithmic problem solving remains difficult for many computer science students because it requires them to coordinate intermediate reasoning practices, such as decomposition, abstraction, pattern recognition, and algorithmic thinking rather than merely produce final code. LLM-based tutors can provide flexible support, but open-ended interactions may drift toward answer delivery and weaken instructor control over the learning process. We present CTATutor, an implemented research prototype that connects instructor-guided CT learning blueprints with adaptive student-facing interaction modules. CTATutor generates recommended module sequences, subgoals, expected student actions, and checkpoints for instructor review and approval. During student learning, runtime agents generate adaptive hints, feedback, and other interaction-level scaffolds within that approved structure. This design explores blueprint-level human-in-the-loop control for adaptive algorithm tutoring.

contents.title: Balancing User Preference and Positional Stability through Optic Flow Speed in Walk-in-Place Locomotion
contents.abstract: Walk-in-Place (WIP) enables virtual navigation but suffers from Unintended Positional Drift (UPD), raising safety concerns. Despite prior studies on factors affecting UPD, it remains unclear how the presence and motion of visual information influence UPD and how UPD changes across a wide range of optic flow speeds. To address these gaps, we conducted two user studies. Results showed that visual information significantly affected UPD, while moving visual information was associated with greater positional drift. UPD remained relatively stable at low optic flow speeds (0.00–0.25 m/s) but increased noticeably from 0.50 m/s onward. Participants generally preferred moderate optic flow speeds, with 0.75 m/s selected most frequently (42.9%). These findings suggest that maintaining optic flow at moderate speeds (0.50–1.00 m/s) may provide a practical operating condition for WIP locomotion that considers both positional stability and user preference.

contents.title: PSeeds: A Configurable Object-Centered Sensing Toolkit with Inspectable Routine Hypotheses
contents.abstract: Everyday routines often leave traces on objects, yet physical sensing configuration and routine inference are often treated separately. We present \textit{PSeeds}, an object-centered sensing toolkit that couples configurable multimodal hardware with an inspectable semantic pipeline. Sensor composition and placement determine the available evidence, while the registered object conditions temporal rules that map edge events and environmental tags to routine hypotheses. The pipeline retains the evidence behind each hypothesis; a large language model verbalizes this evidence after inference. In controlled sessions with ten participants across four predefined configurations, drinking and simulated bathing each achieved event-level F1\,=\,0.97, while prolonged sitting and nighttime phone use were detected in 10/10 scripted sessions. These results establish controlled feasibility and reveal ambiguity between object interaction and routine intent.

contents.title: Surf-Roll: Modulating Perceived Slipperiness and Stickiness through Finger–Surface Relative Motion
contents.abstract: Prior surface-rendering approaches often rely on switching materials or adding separate tactile stimuli, leaving fingerpad–surface relative motion underexplored as a control dimension for surface perception. We present Surf-Roll, a haptic system that renders slippery and sticky sensations by modulating the rotational gain of a wheel contacting the fingerpad, without switching physical materials. Across two studies, we quantified the perceptual gain ranges for slippery and sticky sensations and showed that material-specific gain mappings improved haptic experience in VR, indicating that fingerpad–surface relative motion can serve as a controllable parameter for modulating perceived slipperiness and stickiness.

contents.title: Co-Dial: Designing a Tangible Learning System for Promoting Cooperative Learning in Primary Mathematics
contents.abstract: Cooperative learning is an important approach to supporting early-primary children’s learning and social competence, yet balanced, interdependent participation is difficult to sustain in early primary classrooms. We present Co-Dial, which combines two tangible dials and a shared tabletop projection for cooperative mathematics learning. Co-Dial embeds both inputs into task progression, turning positive interdependence into an interaction structure.  A preliminary evaluation suggests that Co-Dial supports joint attention, negotiation, and more balanced participation, and better team performance. This work shows how tangible input, shared mathematical representations, and synchronized confirmation can structure cooperative mathematics learning.

contents.title: Beyond `Put-That-There': How Users Coordinate Speech and Gestures in Unconstrained VR Manipulation
contents.abstract: Speech and gestural input are increasingly combined for manipulating 3D objects in Virtual Reality. While the classic “Put-That-There” format being widely used, there is a lack of understanding on how users freely coordinate these modalities when no interaction vocabulary is prescribed. In a Wizard-of-Oz VR study (N=12), participants completed three scene-construction tasks using unconstrained speech and gestural input. We found that speech–gesture integration followed a structured coordination pattern rather than a uniform fusion rule. Users allocated modalities according to the operations being performed, used each modality to disambiguate the other, and coordinated speech and gesture across persistent interaction states. These findings suggest that multimodal 3D interfaces should move beyond command-level fusion and support operation-aware, bidirectional, and stateful coordination between speech and gesture.

contents.title: GlyphSpectrum:  A Direct Manipulation Interface for Cultural Bias in Cross-Lingual Typography
contents.abstract: Generative AI models reproduce dominant visual conventions, causing “domestication bias” in typography where subtle stroke changes shift a glyph's cultural attribution. Existing mitigation methods equalize outputs uniformly or use discrete, destructive text prompts. We present GlyphSpectrum, an interactive system for navigating cultural bias as a continuous spectrum via direct manipulation of a diffusion model's latent space (built on MX-Font). A macro slider (t = 0–1) interpolates between foreignized and domesticated forms in real time, while a node-based micro-control layer enables cumulative, non-destructive local edits. We also introduce the Domestication Threshold (DT), a perceptual metric for evaluating cross-lingual typography.

contents.title: Designing Chips in the Browser: Democratizing ASIC Prototyping with Gate Arrays
contents.abstract: Application-specific integrated circuit design remains inaccessible to non-experts because it requires specialized design environments and extensive domain expertise. Although gate arrays enable rapid and low-cost ASIC prototyping through prefabrication and abstraction, existing design tools still rely on expert-oriented workflows and limit their accessibility. This paper presents a web-based ASIC design tool for gate-array-based prototyping. The proposed system allows users to design circuits, perform SPICE simulation, and visualize chip layouts entirely within a web browser while hiding process-dependent confidential manufacturing information from end users. As a feasibility demonstration, we designed and fabricated a gate-array-based ASIC implementing a 31-stage ring oscillator composed of 132 MOS transistors. The complete process from design data generation to chip fabrication was completed within six hours. These results demonstrate the potential of browser-based environments to democratize rapid ASIC prototyping.

contents.title: FocusAdapt: Context-aware Adaptive Focus Assistance in Diminished Reality
contents.abstract: Diminished Reality (DR) can reduce visual clutter by removing irrelevant objects. However, removing all task-irrelevant objects may eliminate useful contextual information and reduce situational awareness. We present FocusAdapt, a context-aware DR system that predicts object-level distraction by integrating visual saliency and similarity, semantic relevance, and gaze behavior. Based on findings from a formative study, FocusAdapt selectively diminishes highly distracting objects while preserving useful context, enabling adaptive focus assistance during procedural tasks.

contents.title: Jacaranda: Grafting User-Editable Web Experiences Across Sites
contents.abstract: Today's web users often pursue goals that span multiple pages, tabs, and platforms, yet web interfaces remain organized around provider-defined pages and application boundaries. A user comparing products may move between shopping pages, review videos, search results, notes, and comparison tools, but the features that support this workflow are locked inside separate sites. We introduce Jacaranda, a working runtime browser environment that reimagines the web as a feature-oriented, user-editable workspace. In Jacaranda, online shoppers can add widgets that enrich a webpage with relevant content, such as product comparisons and YouTube video results. Jacaranda represents web pages as feature trees and enables cross-site capabilities through the Feature Context Protocol (FCP), which defines feature data constraints while supporting diverse UI/UX substrates. We describe its architecture as GRAFT (Generative Runtime Assembly of Feature Trees), a system model for how features are composed, modified, and connected across sites at runtime by a GenUI Runtime Builder.

contents.title: When Stories Stop Early: Supporting Depth in Intergenerational Storytelling
contents.abstract: Intergenerational storytelling (IGS) helps families preserve memories and allows younger generations to understand elders' lived experiences. However, many stories stop after brief factual exchanges, before emotions, personal meanings, and family context can unfold. This paper presents a question-driven bead art co-creation system that connects storytelling with shared craft. Informed by a co-design workshop with six real older-younger family dyads, the system uses AI-assisted question classification and progressive visual reveal to turn story details into emerging bead patterns. Rather than scoring questions or forcing emotional disclosure, it supports deeper IGS while keeping narrative control with family members.

contents.title: Play.Sim: A Reconfigurable Platform for Participatory Urban Design
contents.abstract: Participatory design of public spaces increasingly relies on 3D interfaces, yet existing tools still impose different barriers to community participation. Professional modelling software requires substantial expertise, sandbox games make large-scale spatial design laborious, and purpose-built civic games rarely outlive the projects for which they are developed. Play.Sim is a participatory platform for community design projects such as playgrounds, pocket parks, and streetscapes. It provides a grid-based direct-manipulation interface for composing design proposals and recording design histories to support Urban-Git, a version-control layer for collaborative community design currently under development. This paper describes the platform architecture, situates its design affordance through the Cognitive Dimensions of Notations Framework (CDs), and outlines a user study, currently underway, centered on the redesign of a public playground in Ottawa, Canada.

contents.title: Warping the Workspace: Expanding Visual Access with Adjustable Reach Mapping for Humanoid Teleoperation
contents.abstract: First-person humanoid teleoperation ties access to side and rear targets to operator rotation. We present coupled visual--motor remapping, pairing a panoramic azimuth warp with its inverse upper-limb yaw transform. A working prototype implements Global Zoom (GZ) and Focus+Context (F+C). In a within-subject study (N=8; 72 trials), GZ had the largest completion count (23/24; Fixed: 20/24; F+C: 21/24), whereas F+C was preferred by 6/8 participants. Thus, completion and preference favored different mappings in this sample.

contents.title: Supporting Design Exploration through In-Situ Guidance for 3D Modeling
contents.abstract: We present an LLM-based interactive system that supports design exploration during 3D modeling. The system interprets voice input together with the user's gaze and current model state, providing guidance and visual suggestions as users work through modeling problems and iterate on their designs. Preliminary findings suggest that the system helped users discover relevant commands, develop modeling strategies, and reflect on design ideas, while pointing to recognition accuracy, feedback specificity, and alignment with evolving design intent as key conditions. These results suggest the potential of state grounded visual feedback for supporting reflection in 3D modeling workflows.

contents.title: Ideaverse: Structuring and Steering Design Brainstorming with a Multi-Agent LLM System
contents.abstract: Brainstorming is essential to design ideation, yet designers often brainstorm alone, where they must simultaneously generate diverse ideas, evaluate alternatives, and decide when to shift between exploration and refinement. Existing AI tools can rapidly produce ideas, but often provide limited cognitive perturbation and weak support for moving between divergence and convergence. We present Ideaverse, a multi-agent LLM system for solo design brainstorming. Through stance-based agent discussions, flexible user participation, and interactive idea visualization, Ideaverse helps designers externalize, steer, and refine an evolving idea space.

contents.title: Dynamically Shape-Shifting Keyboard System
contents.abstract:
Keyboards provide tactile feedback and are well suited for text entry and shortcut use.
However, their fixed physical layouts cannot adapt to different applications and contexts.
We present a dynamically shape-shifting keyboard system that enables automatic physical reconfiguration of key layouts.
The system combines lightweight passive key units with a mobile electromagnet-equipped robot to achieve large-scale, fine-grained actuation with only a small number of electromagnets.
A soft magnetic plate suppresses magnetic interference between neighboring keys while shielding inactive electromagnets.
We demonstrate applications including application- and context-adaptive layouts and information display using key units.

contents.title: KnitID: Machine-Knitted RFID Antennas for Battery-Free Authentication, Localization and Interaction
contents.abstract: Battery-free RFID systems offer a scalable and maintenance-free approach to interaction. We present KnitID, a machine-knitted textile RFID antenna design that enables on-body authentication, localization, and interaction. Unlike prior antenna designs, KnitID achieves a compact antenna form factor (60mm × 8mm) by integrating magnet wire into the unique loop-over-loop structure of machine knitting. This structure reduces the size of conventional loop antennas by around 90\%, while also providing 30\% longer sensing ranges than standard dipole designs with similar size on the human body. The compact form factor creates new opportunities to embed multiple RFID tags across the human body, enriching backscatter signals and supporting a broader range of battery-free on-body interactions. To demonstrate this capability, we build an interactive sleeve to support wearer authentication, spatial localization, and interaction detection. Through technical evaluations, we show the feasibility of KnitID to provide diverse and battery-free interactions on knitted user interfaces.

contents.title: Creating LEGO Technic Parts on Demand through Bimanual Interaction in VR
contents.abstract: LEGO Technic is a powerful tool for prototyping moving objects. However, physical assembly requires users to maintain a large inventory of parts and repeatedly search this inventory for specific parts. In this study, we identified an essential set of LEGO Technic parts through a literature analysis. Based on the geometric and functional characteristics of these parts, we designed an intuitive bimanual interaction technique to instantly create them in VR. Finally, we applied this technique to build various moving objects, demonstrating its applicability to LEGO Technic prototyping.

contents.title: HexBot: Authoring Reconfigurable Multi-Robot Interfaces through Snap-On Capabilities
contents.abstract: We present HexBot, a work-in-progress system for authoring reconfigurable multi-robot interfaces. Identical mobile bases acquire sensing and output capabilities through self-describing, magnetically snap-on modules. Snapping or moving a module changes the composition, while capability discovery, simulation, spatial visualization, and inspectable Blockly Event--Condition--Action (ECA) rules keep physical roles and behavior available for revision. A ROS-inspired architecture separates this author-facing workflow from AprilTag localization, host coordination, ESP-NOW transport, and robot-local execution. We operated two mobile bases, each costing below US$10 in components, excluding the overhead camera, host, and modules. A light-sensing and light-output configuration illustrates how authors can reassign temporary roles by moving modules and revising an explicit ECA relation. We contribute the snap-to-author workflow, an architecture for capability reassignment, and a low-cost implementation being prepared for open-source release.

contents.title: RewindAI: Inspectable and Revisable Autobiographical Clones for Reflective Social Decisions
contents.abstract: Personalized AI systems increasingly support reflection and everyday choice, but many still infer users from short profiles or recent chat history. We present RewindAI, a prototype that builds an inspectable and revisable autobiographical clone for reflective social decisions. A natural interview becomes an editable decision biography, a relationship and decision graph, and tentative decision tendencies with provenance labels. Participants complete a shared campus simulation and receive structured self reflection, generic LLM reflection, or RewindAI clone reflection before a matched second run. This poster reports the system design and a preliminary export from 24 study participants. In the RewindAI condition, clone choices matched 124 of 176 matched card choices. We treat this agreement as bounded task calibration rather than real world prediction. Our analysis asks how agreement, mismatch, and artifact revision support privacy sensitive reflection.

contents.title: Craft-Aligned Pattern Design for Mosaic Yarncraft
contents.abstract:
MoYa enables yarncrafters to easily create patterns for the popular one-yarn-per-row "mosaic" colorwork technique using a combination of guided freehand drawing and
 image-based algorithms. The stitch-placement constraints of this technique are validated on the fly, providing immediate feedback for resolution of non-compliant designs. Charts can be used for all crafts or annotated with craft- and user-specific fabrication details.

contents.title: Wake2Adapt: Reframing Wake Words as In-Situ Labeled Speech for Personalized Voice Assistants
contents.abstract: We present Wake2Adapt, a system that personalizes voice assistants using wake-word utterances users already produce. Using recognition of Korean proper nouns uttered by non-native speakers as a representative task, we compare four wake-word types. Korean wake words improved recognition, whereas existing English wake words did not. Ablations show that the gains stem from phoneme coverage rather than length, and that a single utterance suffices.

contents.title: From Defense to Disclosure: Designing Interactive Systems with Multimodal Adaptive Guidance for LLM-Based Mental Health Counseling
contents.abstract: Immature psychological defense mechanisms are unconscious self-protective processes that emerge under emotional conflict and stress, often shaping clients' text-based expression through avoidance, rationalization, or suppression. To understand how AI systems can support clients in noticing such latent patterns, we conducted a formative study with six clinical counselors and four clients, deriving design requirements for structured defense recognition and adaptive reflective guidance. We present DefenseMitigator, an interactive system that helps clients notice latent defensive patterns through defense recognition and adaptive multimodal guidance. Rather than challenging or removing defenses, DefenseMitigator positions AI as a transparent reflective partner that supports clients' psychological self-awareness while preserving their autonomy over emotional disclosure.
