contents.title: Point-of-Release Detection with a Data Glove for VR Throwing
contents.abstract: Natural throwing in virtual reality (VR) is hindered by the difficulty of accurately detecting the Point of Release (PoR). We propose an automatic PoR detection method based on a data glove. First, we integrate a custom conduction-sensing circuit into the glove to detect the physical release, building a highly accurate ground-truth dataset paired with finger-tracking data during dart throwing. Then, using this dataset as supervision, we train models that predict the PoR from finger-tracking data alone, so that no physical object is required at inference. In our technical evaluation, the best model achieves 39.4 ms mean absolute error and detects the PoR in over 80% of throws at sub-frame inference latency, showing that online, real-time PoR prediction from finger tracking alone is viable.

contents.title: Implicit User Calibration Based on Binocular Corneal Imaging
contents.abstract: Accurate gaze estimation typically requires explicit user calibration, which interrupts seamless interactions. While existing implicit calibration methods alleviate this burden, they depend on prior knowledge, such as the gaze object or external geometric information. Therefore, we propose a novel implicit user calibration method based on the similarity of binocular images reconstructed from corneal reflections. Our method estimates the user-specific offset angles between the optical and visual axes without requiring prior information. We confirmed that the proposed method achieves gaze estimation accuracy comparable to a conventional implicit calibration method while relying on less prior information.

contents.title: Impression Sliders: On-Demand Sliders from Impression Descriptions for Parametric Design
contents.abstract: In parametric visual design, users often explore a parameter space, guided by a desired impression to convey to viewers—for example, seeking to make a photo look more "cinematic." However, manipulating the parameters in a direction that strengthens the intended impression is particularly difficult when the user does not understand the parameter space well. We present Impression Sliders, a system that turns a natural-language description of a desired impression into a slider for strengthening that impression. With a vision-language model (VLM) as the evaluator, the system uses preferential Bayesian optimization to estimate, in roughly 45 seconds, a design that strongly conveys the described impression. The resulting slider then lets users move the current design toward this estimate. We implemented the system in three domains, and a study with 19 raters indicated that the estimated designs conveyed the described impressions to viewers. An exploratory user study suggested that Impression Sliders help users adjust designs toward target impressions, particularly when the parameter space is difficult to interpret.

contents.title: StepLens: Supporting Inspection and Evaluation in Agentic Tabular Data Work to Narrow Down the Gulf of Evaluation
contents.abstract:
Agentic systems can democratize data discovery and preparation by allowing users to express data needs in natural language and delegate workflows that would otherwise require substantial coordination across people, tools, and datasets. However, especially in high-stakes settings, answers are useful only when users can assess how they were produced.

We present StepLens, an interface layer built on Pneuma-Seeker, an agentic system for question answering over tabular data. StepLens organizes the system's intermediate work into structured, inspectable stages, combining high-level summaries, artifact-level details, and lightweight interactions that help users trace and test how an answer was produced.

Through a formative study with 15 participants, we derive design insights into how users inspect and assess intermediate outputs. We then report a controlled experiment with 36 participants examining how the interface shapes confidence in the current answer, readiness to act on it, and overall trust in the system. Readiness to act was clearly differentiated between correct and incorrect answers under StepLens. Qualitative findings show structured visibility supported traceability and targeted inspection, but made inconsistencies more salient and sometimes complicated verification efforts.

contents.title: Can People Distinguish Human and AI Agency in Humanoid Teleoperation? A Preliminary Study of Agency Perception
contents.abstract: Can people distinguish between human and AI agency in humanoid teleoperation? To explore this question, we developed Ghost-in-the-Loop, a teleoperation framework that supports both human-operated and AI-generated control of a robot's voice, facial expressions, and gestures while maintaining a consistent embodiment. We conducted a preliminary online study (N=50) in which participants viewed short interaction clips generated by either a Human Operator or an AI Control and judged the perceived source of control. Results suggest that participants often struggled to distinguish between the two conditions in brief interactions. Qualitative responses indicate that judgments were primarily influenced by perceived naturalness, temporal coordination, and consistency across speech, facial expression, and gesture. These findings provide initial insights into agency perception in embodied human--AI communication and motivate future investigations of blended human--AI telepresence systems.

contents.title: YarnConnects: Towards Yarn-Level Rapid Prototyping For Smart Textiles
contents.abstract: While pipelines for fabricating functional electronic yarns with integrated computing components exist, they often present a high barrier to entry due to the need for a skilled fabricator, steep learning curves, or specialized equipment. To democratize electronic yarn in functional textiles platforms for designers and makers, we introduce YarnConnects, a modular, reconfigurable, plug-and-play prototyping toolkit composed of pre-assembled electronic yarns. Our pipeline mounts surface-mount device (SMD) components onto standard flexible printed circuit boards (FPCBs). These FPCBs are heat-pressed with an adhesive to a thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) substrate and connected via printed stretchable silver-ink traces before being rolled into a flexible yarn. This method allows for the integration of complex SMD components while maintaining the stretchability and robustness of the final yarn. The resulting toolkit utilizes a standardized six-pin connection interface centered on a microcontroller yarn and leverages the I2C protocol for chaining peripherals. By bypassing skill-intensive manufacturing, this system enables the rapid prototyping, testing, and iteration of e-textiles that integrate electronic yarn.

contents.title: Design Friction for Writing with AI Chatbots: Probing the Tradeoff Between Engagement and Burden
contents.abstract: AI chatbots can help people write faster, but they can also encourage overreliance by making it easy to turn minimal input into usable text. We study turn-level design friction: intentional constraints added to each chatbot exchange that slow, limit, or redirect how users request, access, or use model responses. We designed three friction probes for chat-based writing: input-scaled output, gated reveal, and sentence-limited output. In a within-subject study with 24 participants, these probes increased workload and task duration compared with a conventional AI chatbot baseline, while also increasing perceived ownership and recall of participants’ own writing. However, their effects were uneven. Interaction logs and interviews suggest that friction was most useful when added effort redirected users toward task-relevant decisions, such as decomposing the writing task, specifying intent, or assembling ideas themselves. It was less useful when users treated the constraint as a rule to satisfy, tried to restore a normal chatbot workflow, or shifted effort toward managing the interface.

contents.title: TractorBeam: Personalized AI Sensemaking Support via Collaborative Machine Annotation
contents.abstract:
Language model-based systems which allow asking questions of documents have become popular tools for sensemaking. 
Despite their implied capability, these systems still suffer from issues of factuality and provenance, while encouraging confirmatory, rather than exploratory, research. We present TractorBeam, a browser extension-based mixed-initiative system that uses collaborative annotation as an interface metaphor for sensemaking, re-framing language model (LM) outputs as suggested highlights in a process that we call collaborative machine annotation. This metaphor allows us to present LM results in-context on PDF documents, directly addressing concerns of provenance and factuality, while allowing users to iteratively construct mental schemas and queries for language models directly in the context of a document.  In a preliminary user study, all of our participants felt that TractorBeam enabled them to evaluate and iteratively improve the model's reflection of their intended highlighting, and several found suggestions that made them reconsider their original schema. TractorBeam suggests that systems that facilitate exploratory research on individual documents may lead to verifiable sensemaking for users and complement tools that work across broader corpora.

contents.title: SwirlSense: Quantifying Wine Swirling Skill and Exploring Motion-Derived Feedback Indicators
contents.abstract: Wine swirling is a common pre-consumption action, yet it is difficult to describe and practice because much of the technique is tacit. SwirlSense quantifies wine-glass swirling from motion trajectories and explores how expert-novice differences can become feedback-oriented indicators. In a motion-capture study with five wine experts and 14 novices, we extracted 18 kinematic features across two pour volumes; a linear SVM distinguished experts from novices with 89.5% accuracy in the 25mL condition and 68.4% in the 50mL condition. SHAP analysis identified orbit size and stability as interpretable markers, motivating a similarity score and smartphone feedback prototype.

contents.title: GEMINI: A Multi-Modal Augmented Reality Interface for Astronaut Guidance During Lunar Surface Operations
contents.abstract: As NASA's Artemis program moves toward sustained lunar surface operations, crew will need extravehicular activity (EVA) solutions that reduce reliance on ground support and operate reliably under suit mobility constraints and harsh lunar conditions. We present GEMINI, a multi-modal augmented reality (AR) heads-up display (HUD) that guides astronauts through a multi-stage lunar EVA sequence, controlled via a fine-tuned artificial intelligence assistant (AIA) with eye-gaze and a leg-mounted button as a redundant input path. We evaluated GEMINI at the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC) Rock Yard under simulated lunar conditions with two subject-matter experts (SMEs): a NASA engineer and an astronaut. Our findings provide preliminary evidence of the feasibility of multi-modal AR guidance for lunar EVA tasks, a step toward the crew autonomy that sustained lunar surface exploration will demand.

contents.title: STRAIGHT: Toward Consistent Archery Form via Video Pose Analysis and Language-Model-Based Coaching Feedback
contents.abstract: Accurate archery performance relies on consistent timing, alignment, and post-release follow-through across repeated shots, yet archery athletes often train without continuous feedback because a coach cannot observe every attempt. To address this gap, we introduce STRAIGHT, a system that turns simple practice clips into suggestions that resemble feedback from an experienced coach. STRAIGHT first detects the shot phase and estimates the archer’s pose. Each shot is evaluated in the context of the archer’s prior attempts, quantifying how consistently timing, alignment, and stability are reproduced across repetitions. An LLM-based feedback generation system then analyzes the results and delivers customized coaching-style feedback to the archer. Demonstrations with real practice footage show that STRAIGHT detects inconsistencies, instability, and subtle alignment changes, and provides feedback that helps athletes develop more stable and repeatable technique. The codebase will be released upon acceptance for the community to use.

contents.title: CueMate: Designing an Embodied AI Co-Performer for In-Person Public Speaking
contents.abstract: Public speaking is an inherently fragile live performance, requiring speakers to simultaneously navigate content delivery, personal presentation, and audience engagement. HCI has supported speakers before, during, and after presentations through rehearsal systems, real-time prompts, virtual co-presenters, and post-hoc feedback. However, existing in-talk support often relies on visual interfaces or screen-bound agents, which may redirect attention or expose the speaker's reliance on assistance. We introduce CueMate, an asymmetric embodied AI presentation partner that provides real-time support while remaining secondary to the human speaker. Before the talk, the system processes the speaker's script to generate \textit{rescue} lines for moments of hesitation and response behaviors for humor, emphasis, and audience engagement. During the presentation, the speaker selectively triggers context-aware speech, facial expressions, and physical motions. Findings from a preliminary field deployment indicate that CueMate helps redistribute cognitive pressure, facilitates graceful recovery from delivery breakdowns, and cultivates a more dynamic audience experience. Collectively, our work highlights embodied AI as a low-profile co-performer that transforms private assistance into a shared stage interaction without disrupting speaker authority or presentation flow.

contents.title: BuddyPlay: Designing a Two-Player Cooperative Game to Promote Social Development Between Autistic and Neurotypical Children
contents.abstract: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often face challenges in social play, especially when interacting with their neurotypical peers in mixed-group settings. Earlier studies largely focused on single-group game designs, with limited attention given to the requirements of cross-group interactions. We propose BuddyPlay, a cross-group social collaborative game system that integrates a virtual agent, gesture interactions, storytelling, and multilevel gameplay to help children with ASD collaborate with their neurotypical peers to foster social skill development. Preliminary results indicate an improved willingness to participate and increased proactive social behaviors among children with ASD, providing insights for designing social games for neurodiverse groups.

contents.title: Who Pays for Vagueness? A Visual Token-Metered Interaction Technique for Promoting Precise AI Commands with TokenTangram
contents.abstract: A command is vague when it leaves unsaid details the task needs. An AI resolves it anyway by committing to one reading, and when that reading is not what the user meant, the next attempt bills the full prompt and reasoning again. The cheapest command is therefore the one that succeeds on the first attempt, yet the price of retrying is never shown to the person who can prevent it. We present TokenTangram, a shape-assembly microworld that makes this per-attempt token bill visible. An AI places each tangram piece exactly where the user's words point, and it locks in only when the words pin it. Otherwise the user chooses who pays next: rephrase, or delegate to the AI, which resolves the leftover ambiguity in a further billed call. A meter shows the measured API tokens of every attempt, split between the user's commands and the AI's finishes. The meter prices one repair policy rather than estimating what a production assistant would spend; we offer it as a probe into how people and AI split that work. We contribute a token-metered command interaction, a literal-read and correction-replay technique, and a tangram microworld, leaving evaluation of learning and transfer to future work.

contents.title: ProposalGen: Showing Experts What Their Sources Can't Support
contents.abstract: Current AI document generation tools shift a hidden burden onto users: finding unsupported text inside finished drafts. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds output in a user's own corpus, yet hallucinates when sources fall short. ProposalGen instead checks coverage before generation: authors declare required topics, and a matrix shows which topics the corpus supports. This check can misjudge by falsely flagging a covered topic as missing, or passing an unsupported one. A preliminary study with eight experts (N=8) investigated how authors respond to gap flags and how false-missing and false-satisfied coverage signals affect trust. We found that false-missing flags tended to erode trust only when authors blamed the system, while false-satisfied flags were generally judged the more damaging error. Trust recovered when errors could be traced and repaired. We contribute ProposalGen and findings on how coverage errors shape expert trust.

contents.title: Lookover: Scaffolding Student Participation in Social Annotation
contents.abstract: Social annotation platforms such as Perusall and Hypothesis are widely used to support student engagement with course readings, often through required commenting. Yet visible participation does not necessarily produce sustained or substantive peer exchange. Analyzing six weeks of Perusall activity from a graduate course (2,873 comments), we found that participation was often fragmented: 53.5\% of comments received no reply, 38.3\% were posted within the final 12 hours before the deadline, and over one-third of a double-coded sample went no further than repeating or agreeing with the reading or a peer. Interviews pointed to two linked difficulties: locating a discussion worth entering and contributing something that meaningfully advances it. We present Lookover, an AI-assisted annotation system that scaffolds both stages without writing for students. Discussion Overview helps students identify active themes and relevant threads, while Spark Thinking poses questions that encourage them to move beyond reaction and restatement toward questioning, extending, and substantively responding to peers. A preliminary study with five participants revealed both the promise and limitations of these scaffolds. We plan to evaluate Lookover in a future course deployment.

contents.title: Tactile Voice Timbre: Haptic Speaker Signatures for Captioned Multi-Speaker Video
contents.abstract: Captions help Deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) viewers access dialogue, but following who is speaking in multi-speaker video remains difficult. We present Tactile Voice Timbre (TVT), a wrist-worn system that turns speaker timbre into tactile signatures. TVT isolates speech using voice activity detection and speaker diarization, then maps timbre descriptors such as F0, roughness, and sharpness to two heterogeneous linear resonant actuators (LRAs) on the wrist via phantom-sensation panning and roughness modulation. In a within-subjects study with 12 DHH participants, TVT was compared with a directly audio-driven voice-coil baseline for speaker-change detection. When audiovisual context was unavailable, TVT better preserved detection precision without increasing reported fatigue or distraction. These results suggest that timbre-informed haptics can complement captions by providing tactile cues for speaker tracking.

contents.title: RecalibrateGPT: AI Fatigue Resilient Conversational Interfaces
contents.abstract: Large language models are powerful, but their interfaces often devolve into a type → read → retype loop, creating conversational AI fatigue, cognitive load, and eventual task abandonment. To mitigate this, we present RecalibrateGPT, a system introducing five cross-turn operators (Anchor, Replay, Delta, Scope, and Steer) that each target a distinct fatigue type, recalibrating LLM responses through a structured panel by acting on the full conversation history with a single click. Users invoke these operators through the AssistiveButton in one of three operator palette layouts: Vertical, Arc, or Tablet. We conducted two pilot studies with the same 12 advanced LLM users. An initial formative qualitative study identifies a taxonomy of four fatigue types (retyping, scanning, decision paralysis, and context drift) and derives two design objectives for RecalibrateGPT. A follow-up quantitative evaluation finds it reduces perceived cognitive workload by half (NASA-TLX = 2.7) at high perceived usability (SUS = 86.5), suggesting AI fatigue is not just a model-quality issue but an interaction-flow cost that interfaces can remove.

contents.title: ReVision: Supporting Designers’ Interpretation and Exploration of Visuals in Concepts and Forms
contents.abstract: Visual designers get inspiration from references to expand their design space. They decompose what makes a reference evocative into conceptual and visual elements, ranging from explicit attributes such as objects and colors, to less readily articulated concepts and visual motifs. They then create different visual forms to explore how the selected elements could be combined differently. Novices often struggle with these moves, instead focusing on surface features or producing limited visual variation, thus becoming fixated on the reference. Existing tools support editable visual attributes and high-level themes, but provide limited control over how conceptual interpretations relate to expressive visual motifs or how their combinations can be systematically re-expressed. We present ReVision, an AI-based tool that decomposes visual and textual references into editable conceptual interpretations and visual motifs, enables their recombination across conceptual and visual spaces, and renders each direction as divergent visual-form variations, supporting more divergent exploration during the creation process.

contents.title: MopMate: Towards Task-Coupled AR Assistant for Routine Maintenance Tasks
contents.abstract: Routine maintenance tasks (RMTs), such as floor cleaning, are easy to postpone, difficult to sustain, and effortful to resume after interruption. We conducted a formative study with 61 survey responses and six interviews, deriving design objectives for efficiency, engagement, and situated learning. Based on these findings, we developed MopMate, a task-coupled augmented reality assistant for floor cleaning. MopMate tracks floor states, detects and localizes stains, provides gamified multimodal feedback, and offers context-aware cleaning guidance. We also outline a controlled user study to evaluate its effectiveness in future work.

contents.title: Bimanual Interaction Technique for Controlling Humanoid Robot Walking and Working
contents.abstract: Humanoid robots are difficult for novice users to control intuitively due to their high degrees of freedom. We propose a novel interaction technique that enables users to control the locomotion and manipulation of a humanoid robot by holding and moving a virtual 3D plane with both hands. We implemented our technique using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot model in a VR physics simulation and compared it against gamepad and exoskeleton baselines on tasks from an open-source humanoid robot benchmark in a user study with 24 participants. Our technique was 59% faster and improved benchmark results by 17% in a locomotion task, while it was 41% faster and improved benchmark results by 20% in a manipulation task. It also outperformed the baselines on most subjective workload measures.

contents.title: ParenTalk: LLM-Based Communication Training for Parents in Children's Academic Support
contents.abstract: Parent-child communication plays a fundamental role in children's academic and developmental outcomes, yet in the Chinese educational context, parents' heavy involvement combined with limited communication competency often produces frustration and conflict rather than support. Informed by interviews with 10 parents, we designed ParenTalk, a three-stage system powered by LLMs and grounded in Satir's communication model. ParenTalk is designed to help parents reflect on and practice communication with their children through interactive, personalized exercises. Preliminary evaluation with 40 parents suggest that ParenTalk offers a practical and immersive learning experience, effectively improving parents' communication skills and family relationships.

contents.title: Towards Benchmarking Screen Reader Use in Computer Use Agents
contents.abstract: Computer use agents perceive graphical interfaces through screenshots or accessibility trees and act through clicks and keystrokes. Blind and low vision users often rely instead on screen readers, which present the same interfaces as sequential views navigated through focus and keyboard commands. Agents that operate through this same screen reader interface could collaborate with blind and low vision users, audit interface accessibility, and provide screen reader guidance for complex interfaces. Yet tools and benchmarks for such screen reader agents remain limited. We present an OpenClaw toolkit that lets agents directly control screen readers and receive structured spoken output. We use the toolkit to build a benchmark of 30 web and desktop tasks and compare agents across observation and action spaces. We find that with the right tools, screen reader agents can match the task success of standard computer use agents on simple tasks while using fewer input tokens, but may still bypass expected interaction paths and struggle to verify task completion.

contents.title: Hangulo: Demonstrating Workflow-Embedded AI Support for Korean Lettering Implementation
contents.abstract: The design process is commonly understood as an iterative cycle of ideation, implementation, and evaluation. During implementation, designers refine and develop their ideas into meaningful outcomes through ongoing micro-level reflection. Unlike tools that automate this process in a single step, we present Hangulo, a Korean lettering tool featuring workflow-embedded agents, demonstrating how AI can augment designers' in-progress edits within existing implementation workflows. Leveraging Hangul's compositional structure, Hangulo propagates style edits across structurally related letters and translates rough sketches into vector-level suggestions, replacing tedious vector control steps while preserving opportunities for micro-level reflection throughout implementation.

contents.title: CalliSenseAR: In-Situ AR Guidance for Corrective and Immersive Chinese Calligraphy Training
contents.abstract: Chinese calligraphy depends on fine-grained brush control, yet novices cannot easily extract expert techniques from final characters or instructional videos. We present CalliSenseAR, an augmented reality system requiring no external sensors, which overlays expert hand motion, inferred brush pose, rotation, pressure, and upcoming stroke trends onto real brush-and-paper practice using only the HMD’s built-in cameras. Adaptive soft-alignment follows the learner’s writing rhythm to preserve flow. A within-subject study with nine novices showed larger mean brush-technique gains with CalliSenseAR than with video self-learning, while flow scores were similar to teacher guidance.

contents.title: EvidenceLens: A Declarative Evidence-State Interface for Human-AI Visual Inspection
contents.abstract: AI-assisted inspection interfaces commonly expose a prediction and confidence score, but rarely show whether the system has enough task-critical evidence to decide. EvidenceLens is a declarative evidence-state interface for bounded visual inspection. A task schema maps uncertain telemetry into satisfied, weak, missing, contradictory, or unavailable states and routes users toward commit, recovery, repair, or escalation. In a 24-participant study, EvidenceLens reduced inappropriate reliance from 64% to 23% (mixed-effects odds ratio 0.17, 95% CI [0.11, 0.28]) while preserving correct AI acceptance (−2 percentage points, 95% CI [−5, 2]). Matched controls replicated the effect. Five-state interpretation reached macro-F1 = 0.84; frozen thresholds retained macro-F1 = 0.84 under camera, lighting, and OCR shifts; and mutation testing detected every critical seeded fault in the asynchronous commitment guards.

contents.title: AirFloat: 3D-Printable Air Bearings for Tangible Interaction
contents.abstract: Air bearings enable contactless motion and ultra-low friction through a thin pressurized air film, yet their reliance on precision manufacturing has limited their adoption in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI). We present AirFloat, a practical digital fabrication guide for creating custom air bearings using commodity FDM 3D printers. Conventional air bearings typically employ discrete orifice-based air bearings; however, under load they often suffer from pneumatic hammer and pressure oscillations, resulting in unstable levitation and vibration. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel gyroid-based porous air-bearing that distributes airflow more uniformly and suppresses pressure oscillations. Through systematic experiments across varying loads and operating pressures, we characterize the optimal design space of gyroid air bearings and show that they achieve significantly more stable levitation than conventional orifice-based designs. Finally, we demonstrate a range of tangible interaction applications enabled by AirFloat, including hovering 3D-printed objects for frictionless motion, thruster-driven air caster, self-propelled air caster, contactless conveyor system, and friction-modulated haptic interface.

contents.title: Street2Sea: Street-Level AI Visualization of Predicted Flood Depth to Support Flood Risk Understanding
contents.abstract: Helping residents quickly understand the severity and personal relevance of an impending flood can facilitate timely evacuation. Generative AI has the potential to support this by producing photorealistic images that depict forecasted flooding in everyday scenes. However, prior approaches offer limited control over flood depth, reducing their utility for supporting informed evacuation decision-making. We present Street2Sea, a pipeline that generates street-level images of individual properties, with water synthesized to a target depth from operational forecasts. As a next step, we plan to evaluate how these visualizations affect residents' evacuation decisions compared to conventional flood risk communication methods.

contents.title: FilaTwin: A Rotating Digital Preview For Multi-Material 3D Printing
contents.abstract: 3D printing involves repeated cycles of printing, inspecting results, and redesigning, which wastes material and time when physical outputs diverge from user expectations. While digital previews are integral to design workflows, current slicing tools only visualize tool-paths, and cannot simulate how filaments actually appear when printed. We present FilaTwin, a system that generates realistic 3D previews capturing the true visual properties of printed objects before fabrication. FilaTwin analyzes photos of users' previous prints to extract material properties including surface finish, translucency, color gradients, and metallic characteristics, then synthesizes these properties into procedural shaders for accurate real-time rendering. We implemented FilaTwin as a Blender plugin which can integrate seamlessly into existing design workflows. In an evaluation with 12 participants, FilaTwin achieved significantly higher similarity ratings to real prints than the baseline, demonstrating accurate representations of final printed appearance.

contents.title: Pocket Hatch: A Tool For Mortise Cuts with a Laser Engraver
contents.abstract: Despite their utility in woodworking and hybrid fabrication, blind mortise or "pocket" cuts — recessed areas carved into wood surfaces — typically require considerable manual skill or specialized CNC equipment to create. This paper presents a technique for cutting surface pockets with any laser engraver using vector paths generated at consistent spacing. The method produces fine slices of material that can be manually cleared with finger pressure. This approach reduces on-machine time compared to raster engraving, especially for larger patterns, and reduces setup time as compared to CNC routers. While the bottom of cuts produced this way are rough rather than smooth, the technique enables rapid prototyping of complex pockets using commonly available graphic design software, or a lightweight companion tool we developed for generating these cut patterns directly.

contents.title: PianoSense: Multimodal Visual-Haptic Feedback for Student-Instructor Interaction in Remote Instrument Lessons
contents.abstract: Remote piano lessons offer affordability and convenience, yet lack synchronized visual references for hand form and tactile feedback. We present PianoSense, a tool that integrates an interactive 3D visualization of the instructor's hands with a vibrotactile glove conveying key press events. A preliminary design probe with three student–instructor pairs revealed that PianoSense's multimodal cues functioned as a shared instructional language when video alone was insufficient. We also discuss how remote instrument-learning technologies can support reflective, learner-centered practices, and how researchers can best design interaction-aware scaffolding that adapts to evolving instructor and student needs.

contents.title: Tasteply: Externalizing Stable and Situational Preference as Manipulable Spatial Objects
contents.abstract: Most recommender systems treat user preferences as a single signal to infer and optimize, yet human preferences are a mix of stable preferences and situational preferences that turn on and off depending on context. Through Tasteply, we externalize this preference structure as manipulable spatial objects. Tasteply represents each situational preference as an attractor and the stable preference as an underlying global field. Users can adjust their feed by moving around the space and adjusting the strength of the global field, turning the preference structure that remains latent within the model into something they can see and act on directly to steer the recommendation algorithm. Through an exploratory study (N=5), we found this spatial control effective, and identified its limits and future direction as a means of manipulating preference-based recommendations.

contents.title: Brush-to-Node: Semantic Overpainting for Structural Reinterpretation of AI-Generated Product Concepts
contents.abstract: Generative AI enables designers to rapidly produce product concept images, but these images often lack explicit structural relationships and are difficult to refine parametrically. We present Brush-to-Node, a post-generation editing system that converts semantic overpainting into editable structural nodes representing product parts and their relationships. Each marked region becomes a node with attributes such as material, layer, depth, thickness, offset, and embedding relationships. Designers can adjust these attributes parametrically, while the system automatically compiles them into coordinated appearance, Canny, depth, and segmentation maps. These node-derived control maps guide structurally constrained generation and produce more coherent, controllable, and physically interpretable product representations. We demonstrate the system through running-shoe, eyewear, and water-bottle examples.

contents.title: Procedural Collapse: A Structural Account of Disengagement in LLM-Assisted Writing
contents.abstract: When students use large language models for writing, the dominant explanation for disengagement is dispositional: they are over-reliant, and the remedy is to scaffold self-regulation. We argue that a structural explanation is needed, offering an alternative basis for design interventions to support appropriate AI-assisted writing. Current LLM writing interfaces induce \textit{procedural collapse}: the replacement of an iterative, self-paced writing process with a single output that shifts the writer's task from generation to comprehensive evaluation. Because that evaluation is costly, shallow engagement becomes the default, and the cognitive work writing was supposed to produce goes unperformed. The framework points toward design directions that reduce the burden on writers to self-regulate, including decomposed interaction, goal elicitation as a default first step, and single-level output. They complement metacognitive scaffolding by restructuring the interaction itself.

BrewBit: Enabling Beverage-Aware Interaction Through Real-Time Beverage Sensing
contents.abstract: Preparing beverages involves continuous changes in both drink composition and the user's preparation activities, yet existing interactive systems have limited awareness of these evolving states. We present BrewBit, a real-time beverage sensing platform that enables beverage-aware interaction, a paradigm in which interactive systems continuously sense and interpret evolving beverage properties alongside the user's preparation activities. BrewBit combines Electrical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) with deep learning to recognize dynamic beverage states and preparation activities in real time. In this demonstration, participants prepare beverages such as tea and lemonade while BrewBit continuously tracks ingredient transformations, preparation progress, and user interactions. The system provides real-time feedback and guidance based on both the current state of the beverage and the user's preparation activities. By enabling beverages to communicate their evolving states, BrewBit illustrates how drinks can become interactive materials, where drinks participate directly in the interaction, creating new opportunities for beverage-aware interfaces, interactive support for baristas and bartenders, and broader human-beverage interaction.

contents.title: TeleTangibles: Haptic Tangible Interfaces for Embodied Learning in STEM
contents.abstract: The digital transformation of education has reduced opportunities for embodied and tactile learning, particularly in STEM domains. This work demonstrates TeleTangibles, a suite of modular mechatronic learning devices designed to bring embodied and haptic interactions into digital learning environments. Tangible interactions are particularly important for learners who rely on touch as a primary mode of accessing information, including blind and low-vision (BLV) learners. In this demonstration, we showcase TeleTangibles in three STEM learning contexts: vectors, trigonometry, and molarity while detailing the interdisciplinary, iterative design process employed across simulation content designers, learning scientists, engineers, and BLV learners. Together, these examples illustrate the potential of TeleTangibles to enhance accessibility and engagement in digital STEM learning through embodied and haptic interaction.

contents.title: Augmenting Smartwatch with a Rollable Tentacle
contents.abstract: We present a novel tentacle actuator that integrates into a smartwatch form factor. Unlike prior work on tentacle robotics, this tentacle can be rolled into a rounded casing beneath the smartwatch screen, measuring 50 mm in diameter. Motors can extrude the tentacle on demand to a maximum length of 90 mm and control its direction via driven cables. We explore everyday interactions enabled by this new actuator. We demonstrate applications including adding expressiveness to remote communication and navigation cues, providing a tangible controller, and actuating lightweight objects. We envision this prototype as one of the first steps towards embedding robotics in our everyday wearables.

contents.title: Demonstrating HexBlocks: An Open-Source Framework for Prototyping Reconfigurable Interactive Physical Interfaces with Semantic Continuity
contents.abstract: Physical prototyping is a coupled exploration of hardware and behavior: an initial idea may specify neither the modules nor their mappings. HexBlocks is an open-source software–hardware framework that reframes LLM-assisted physical computing from code generation to hardware–behavior co-exploration. Given an under-specified intent, its Companion Authoring Environment uses a module catalog to recommend hardware roles. As modules are connected, a topology-aware live schema grounds behavior proposals in the current assembly. Accepted proposals become inspectable and editable Blockly rules, while a UID-keyed Event–Condition–Action runtime preserves their physical referents when the same modules are rearranged. At the demonstration, visitors iteratively develop an artifact’s physical composition and interactive behavior together. Changes in physical composition reshape the authoring context, while observed behavior motivates further reconfiguration. This coupled exploration is instantiated across creative, body-worn, and mobile forms and remains bounded by the module capabilities and ECA primitives exposed by the kit.

contents.title: BreathVis: A Public Demonstration of Secondhand Smoke-Induced Lung Pathological Damage
contents.abstract: Tobacco and secondhand smoke (SHS) are the top preventable public health risk worldwide. In China, over 740 million non-smokers suffer long-term SHS exposure, yet invisible particulate pollutants and delayed lung lesions lead to severe public cognitive bias. Traditional tobacco control propaganda relies on static text and pictures, lacking participatory sensory experience to form deep health memory. This paper designs BreathVis, a desktop multi-modal interactive science device. During the demonstration, visitors can interact with the device by blowing air, triggering synchronized visual, auditory, and material responses. Supported by multi-sensor joint detection, atomization aerosol visualization and magnetofluid dynamic simulation, the device builds graded causal feedback between simulated smoking intensity and progressive lung damage metaphor. It converts invisible smoke diffusion and alveolar fibrosis into visible, audible physical phenomena, forming an embodied cognitive chain of “smoking behavior → physical damage”. Oriented at adolescents and adult citizens, the work fills the blank of physical experiential tobacco control education and provides immersive health intervention tools for schools, communities and public exhibitions.

contents.title: Collective Object Intelligence: Coordinating AI-Driven Household Objects with Large Language Models
contents.abstract: Current smart home systems largely rely on fixed automation, predefined triggers, and centralized control interfaces.  We present Collective Object Intelligence, a two-tier orchestration approach for coordinating AI-augmented household objects. A central agent generates a shared plan from live user and environmental context, while local object agents interpret and execute that plan through object-specific sensing and action. Our prototype connects a lamp, radio, mirror, and fruit bowl whose roles remain grounded in their physical affordances. This paper presents three core elements of the approach: an orchestration architecture for multi object coordination, an affordance role mapping that links object form and function to the intelligence it can express, and an analysis of failure modes. We implement this system and demonstrate four application scenarios. Our research suggests that in future domestic environments, intelligence may be expressed through the different modalities of collective objects themselves rather than through a centralized interface.

contents.title: Constance: Generative Re-rendering of Arbitrary Web Interfaces into a Persistent Personal UI
contents.abstract: Website authors determine how their interfaces are presented, leaving a person who needs larger text, less clutter, or a different layout without a general way to apply that preference. Constance re-renders arbitrary, uncooperative third-party websites in a layout the user specifies once, in natural language, and reuses across sites. A language model generates replacement HTML from a compressed page snapshot and annotates actionable elements with semantic intents rather than element references. When the user acts, a browsing agent grounds the intent against the current page and must observe a concrete postcondition before claiming success. Per-category prose templates project different sites into one personal layout, while source labels and routed actions allow several sites to be fused. A chat sidebar accepts free-text requests, elicits user decisions, and can add the pages it finds to the displayed layout. Demo attendees will restyle authenticated websites, inspect the agent's actions, compare products from two sites fused into one view, and delegate a request whose result appears alongside the original content.

contents.title: Demonstrating Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making
contents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly generate rationales to support human decision-making, yet these rationales are typically presented as dense linear text. We demonstrate Graphionale, a co-design-informed system that transforms LLM rationales into interactive argument graphs with compressed nodes, developed as a research prototype for generating design knowledge about when graphical rationales support AI-assisted decision making. In a controlled study (N = 204) reported in our accompanying paper, the effect of this design reversed across task modalities: argument graphs improved trust calibration in verbal reasoning but impaired it in visual reasoning; in each modality, the format that led to better decisions was not the one that felt better. The demo recreates all four study conditions. Attendees answer verbal and visual reasoning questions, inspect textual and graphical rationales, and try to catch trials where the AI’s answer is wrong, so they can directly experience when graphical rationales support calibrated decisions and when they merely feel helpful.

contents.title: Demonstrating AirForce: Personal Fabrication of Large-Scale, Load-Bearing Animatronics Structures from a Single Tube
contents.abstract: This UIST demo allows attendees to experience a fabrication system called AirForce [3] and two models we created using it. Air-Force allows users to create large-scale, load-bearing animated structures from a single inflatable tube. AirForce builds on the per-sonal fabrication of animated truss structures, based on which it replaces not only the static elements with tube, but also introduces tube-based actuators that integrate with that same tube. This ‘single-tube’ design affords efficient single-person assembly, excellent power-to-weight ratio, easy transport and setup, and near 100% material reuse. We show three variants of actuators: buckling actuators for pushing, muscle actuators for pulling, and telescoping actuators for large forces. Our blender plugin enables users to place actuators in structures and export instructions for efficient fabrication. The system allow making a 6DOF motion platform that lifts humans and an 8m high animatronic T-rex that animates with 3DOF, enabled by custom hardware components. In our technical evaluation, the three actuators delivered peak forces of 480N, 1420N, and 2330N, respectively.

contents.title: Demonstrating VisiPrint: Previewing 3D-Print Appearances from Real Material Samples
contents.abstract: We demonstrate VisiPrint, a tool for appearance-first previews of 3D-printed objects. Existing print preview slicers focus on toolpaths, not appearance, while pure rendering software are complex and cannot automatically reproduce slicing patterns. Prior work highlights persistent gaps between digital previews and printed results, such as color shifts, gloss/translucency changes, and layer-line highlights, motivating the creation of VisiPrint, an appearance-focused support tool. The VisiPrint algorithm combines slicer screenshots with filament photos via a custom diffusion-based synthesis pipeline. We present both a standalone user interface for VisiPrint compatible with any slicer and an Ultimaker Cura Plugin. In this demonstration, we present VisiPrint's user interface for print preview, real physical 3D-printed material exemplars that users can photograph to generate previews, and the corresponding 3D-printed objects produced with those materials for comparison.

contents.title: Demonstration of MANA: Multi-perspective Alignment of NPC Agents
contents.abstract: We present MANA (Multi-perspective Alignment of NPC Agents), an interactive approach for authoring NPC behavior through embodied demonstration. We show MANA in the context of Minecraft, where a developer aligns NPCs while playing the game itself. Activating MANA lets the developer dynamically switch into the point of view (POV) of any character and demonstrate, in-situ, how it would act given the surrounding context, through both movement and dialogue. MANA then distills each demonstration into a generalized policy that maps in-game context to actions. Finally, once the developer switches to another NPC or exits MANA mode, this generalized policy drives the NPC on its own. We demonstrate MANA by aligning two initially generic Minecraft NPCs: Fletcher and Farmer to act aggressively and cowardly, respectively. After roughly 2 minutes of in-game play, each character exhibits consistent and believable behaviors across new, unseen scenarios.

contents.title: Designing with Imperfection: Defect-aware Interactive Workbench to Support Upcycling Secondhand Wood
contents.abstract:
Secondhand wood is a sustainable material for craft, but its earlier lifecycle
leaves it with defects, such as embedded metal, chemical residues from coatings,
moisture, and structural cracks, that make designing and fabricating with it
risky. We present \textbf{UBench}, a projector-based interactive workbench
that supports assessing, interpreting, and adapting secondhand wood to a design.
UBench uses overhead scanning to detect visible defects, handheld sensing pens to
probe hidden conditions such as embedded metal and moisture, and projected
in-situ annotations that keep defect information spatially tied to the material.
It further provides contextual suggestions when design intent intersects defect
regions, helping users adapt cuts, joints, fills, and sanding to the wood. Attendees can pick up the instrumented pens and go through the full
workflow hands-on.

contents.title: Demonstration of ScoreSight: Real-time Piano Music Reading Support for People with Decreased Central Vision
contents.abstract: Reading sheet music during a piano performance requires musicians to continuously interpret musical information to maintain performance continuity. For musicians with decreased central vision, existing music-reading tools provide full-score magnification to improve readability and playback-based cursor guidance to indicate the current playing position. However, full-score magnification reduces the visible context of the score, making it difficult to preview upcoming passages, especially across line transitions. Additionally, playback-based cursors often fail to adapt to musicians' natural playing speeds during live performances. To address these challenges, we present ScoreSight, a music reading system that combines real-time score following with adaptive visual guidance to support score reading during live piano performance for musicians with decreased central vision.

contents.title: dear___: Ephemeral Reveal for Interactive Absence in Personal Photo Archives
contents.abstract: Personal photo archives preserve traces of people, places, and moments, but they often make memory access fast, flat, and fully visible. For emotionally charged memories, immediate visibility may not always be the desired mode of interaction. We present dear___, a mobile memory album that explores ephemeral reveal as an interaction pattern for TeleAbsence. In dear___, users compose personal photos with editable white masks, diary text, music, and temporal metadata. A user can erase the mask through touch to reveal the photograph and its associated layers; after a short interval, the mask gradually returns, making the encounter partial, temporary, and reversible. The system also supports computer-vision-assisted mask generation, manual cover editing, memory notifications, share cards, and consent-aware export. Rather than simulating an absent person, dear___ works with existing traces and lets users decide how presence should briefly appear, fade, and return to absence. This demo contributes a working mobile system and interaction concept for designing absence as an interactive material in personal photo archives.

contents.title: Demonstrating CityGaze: An Ambient Social Layer for Situated Sharing on Smart Glasses
contents.abstract: Smart glasses are entering everyday life, and research increasingly uses them to provide people with helpful information about their surroundings. People also mark the places they visit with reviews, tags, and messages, and notice the traces others leave behind. On phones, though, this content sits in an app, apart from the place itself. We built CityGaze on see-through glasses for leaving and finding short place-based notes, called Glimpses. To post, a user looks at something and speaks. To read, the glasses quietly show nearby notes that match what the user is looking at.

contents.title: Towards Finger-Mounted Wearable Device with Wide Bandwidth Haptic Feedback and Robust Gesture Sensing
contents.abstract: With AR/MR technologies and devices becoming more prevalent, there is growing demand for finger-mounted wearable haptic devices that provide rich tactile sensations and robust gesture sensing. We present a novel, lightweight finger-mounted device that combines wide-bandwidth haptic feedback with accurate gesture recognition. The haptic module integrates pneumatic and piezoelectric actuators to deliver tactile sensations ranging from static pressure to high-frequency vibration, enabling a wide range of experiences. The gesture-sensing module uses an IMU and neural-network recognition models to achieve low-latency, accurate finger-gesture detection, even under out-of-view conditions. Using an immersive AR/MR gaming application as an example, we demonstrate how our system enhances user experience by providing rich haptic feedback and instantaneous gesture recognition.

contents.title: Sketch Oversight: Drawing Decision Boundaries for Delegated AI Agent Actions
contents.abstract:
Users increasingly delegate tasks to agents that act on their behalf across their apps, accounts, files, and messages. Current interfaces support oversight by making intended actions visible–through step-by-step approvals or editable plans–but a user's concerns stay implicit, scattered across one-off approvals and low-level plan edits. We introduce Sketch Oversight, an interaction technique that lets users directly specify a decision boundary over proposed agent actions: which may proceed as proposed, and which need revision before execution. Drawing on a formative analysis of publicly documented agent failure cases, the system plots each proposed action on a visual map judgment dimensions-–monetary cost, sensitive-information exposure, reversibility, and others. 
Users draw their boundary directly on the map to approve actions, and refine the plan with per-action controls: check-marking, deleting, editing in text, or asking the agent to re-propose. We ask: what if users could draw the line for their agent?–turning implicit concerns and comfort into an explicit specification the agent can act on.

contents.title: Demo of NailSense: Unobtrusive Wireless Smart Nail Stickers for Whole-Hand Posture Tracking
contents.abstract: We present NailSense, an unobtrusive wireless smart nail system for whole-hand posture tracking. NailSense uses ultra-compact nail-mounted stickers, each integrating a 3-axis accelerometer, microcontroller, Bluetooth transmission, and a small battery, to capture finger movement directly at the distal fingers. By distributing sensors across multiple fingernails, NailSense provides a lightweight, low-profile, multi-point view of finger articulation for everyday interaction. Using gravity vectors measured by the accelerometers, NailSense estimates fingertip orientation and captures finger-specific movement patterns under anatomical hand constraints. In this demo, we showcase NailSense through real-time gesture interactions and illustrate its potential for continuous hand posture estimation, enabling applications such as natural input for wearables, VR/AR interaction, daily activity recognition, sign language recognition, motion capture, and rehabilitation.

contents.title: A Demonstration of Lightweight Generative UI Personalization
contents.abstract: Generative user interfaces are increasingly part of everyday interactive systems. Each interface is ephemeral, generated on demand for a task the user prompts for or built directly from a prompt as a bespoke interface. Users seldom get a persistent interface to configure or grow familiar with. A generator that matches a person's visual and interaction preferences can make these interfaces more satisfying and smoother to use, but a generic model knows nothing about the person it is generating for. We present an interactive, cross-platform demonstration that frames personalization as an anonymized, side-by-side comparison of generated interfaces. Attendees first describe their preferences from both end-user and creator perspectives, then complete eight onboarding comparisons that adapt to their earlier answers. For each task request that follows, they rank three anonymized interfaces: one from a non-personalized generator, one from a generator conditioned on their written profile, and one from an adaptive generator that combines the profile with their onboarding choices. Attendees repeat the ranking across various types of applications, and can also try a prompt of their own. The demonstration lets attendees see directly which personalization method comes closest to their taste.

contents.title: Demonstration of TeethMark: Enabling Tongue–Tooth Interaction with Capacitive Sensing and Electrotactile Feedback using an Intraoral Wearable
contents.abstract: We present TeethMark, an intraoral interface that enables tongue-tooth interaction by leveraging the tongue as the active medium for gesture input and electro-tactile feedback, while utilizing teeth as positional cues for localization. By applying a flexible PCB on a 3D-printed brace, TeethMark can recognize tapping, sliding, and area-touch gestures, and deliver two forms of electrotactile feedback: co-located feedback when the tongue touches the inner side of the teeth, and always-available feedback on the lip-facing side.

contents.title: Demonstration of Sona: Personalizable Real-Time Soundscape Mediation for People With Sound Sensitivity
contents.abstract: For people with sound sensitivity, everyday soundscapes can be overwhelming. Existing noise-management tools, such as active noise cancellation, typically apply broad suppression across the entire environment, easing discomfort at the expense of situational awareness and participation. We present the demonstration of Sona, a personalizable soundscape mediation system that attenuates triggering sounds in real time while preserving the ambient sounds users may want to hear. Sona combines on-device neural attenuation of multiple simultaneous target sounds, context-aware suggestions that reduce interaction effort during moments of sensory overload, and end-user personalization that extends filtering beyond fixed sound taxonomies using short recordings from users' own environments. In this demo abstract, we describe Sona's system design and implementation.

contents.title: EKPHRASIS Chess: A Turn-Taking AI Canvas for Graphic Design Concept Learning
contents.abstract: Graphic design education often relies on examples and critique to teach abstract visual concepts such as balance and hierarchy. However, novices may struggle to translate these vague concepts into concrete visual actions, especially because the reasoning behind visual decisions is often tacit. We present a demonstration of EKPHRASIS Chess, an interactive design learning system that uses a simplified shared canvas to help learners explore the relationship between visual concepts and compositional changes. A user first places a basic visual element, such as a block, and an AI agent responds by adding another element according to a selected target concept. The system supports three response modes: Help, in which the AI moves the composition toward the concept; Oppose, in which the AI acts as a contrastive opponent that tries to destabilize the target concept while the learner attempts to maintain or recover it; and Random, in which it produces an unrelated alternative. By comparing these contrasting responses, learners can observe how specific changes in position, scale, color, and visual relation affect the expression of an abstract design concept. This demonstration invites attendees to explore how human-AI turn-taking can make tacit design knowledge visible and support reflection, experimentation, and concept learning in graphic design education.

contents.title: FactNudger: An AI-Powered Wearable Fact-Checker for Everyday Conversations
contents.abstract: Misinformation is often encountered through speech, where claims are fleeting and verification requires leaving the interaction. We present FactNudger, a wearable system that fact-checks everyday speech and selectively alerts users through a smartwatch. FactNudger transcribes conversation, interprets claims in context, retrieves web evidence, and decides whether to wait for more speech, remain silent, or deliver a haptic nudge. The watch presents a concise rationale, while a companion phone provides supporting sources. FactNudger achieved 77% binary verdict accuracy on 125 sampled AVeriTeC claims and selected the intended action for 40 of 50 conversational edge cases. The demonstration lets attendees experience and inspect real-time fact-checking across false claims, incomplete statements, corrections, repetitions, and context-dependent speech.

contents.title: Demonstrating SustainaPrint: Making the Most of Eco-Friendly Filaments
contents.abstract: We demonstrate SustainaPrint, a system for integrating eco-friendly filaments into 3D printing without compromising structural integrity. While biodegradable and recycled 3D printing filaments offer environmental benefits, there is a trade-off in using them, as they may suffer from degraded or unpredictable mechanical properties. SustainaPrint addresses this by strategically assigning eco-friendly and standard filaments to different regions of a multi-material print—reinforcing the areas that are most likely to break with stronger material while maximizing the use of sustainable filament elsewhere. As eco-friendly filaments often do not come with technical datasheets, we also introduce a low-cost, at-home mechanical testing toolkit that enables users to evaluate filament strength before deciding if they want to use that filament in our pipeline. In this demonstration, users will interact with SustainaPrint's user interface for the creation of sustainable printed objects and five applications of SustainaPrint with physical 3D-printed models.

contents.title: ReadGaze: Query the Gaze, Shape the Debrief
contents.abstract: Post-simulation video-assisted debriefing helps instructors reflect on team performance, yet video replay alone makes it difficult to recover what learners attended to in the moment. Raw gaze offers a dense signal of visual attention, but existing debriefing tools typically present gaze as passive and aggregated heatmaps or scanpaths that instructors cannot easily query, verify, or translate into debriefing prompts. We demonstrate ReadGaze, an interactive debriefing system that transforms gaze traces into four temporally aligned attention states---broad scanning, targeted checking, anchored targets with shifts, and sustained fixation---and exposes them as interactive primitives linked to replay, clinical context, and structured debriefing scaffolds. Clinical instructors will explore preloaded VR cardiac-arrest simulation sessions, inspect candidate teachable moments along the attention timeline, verify them against synchronized replay, and assemble debriefing-ready evidence and inquiry prompts. An expert evaluation with seven clinical simulation instructors showed that ReadGaze supports evidence-grounded debriefing preparation beyond conventional video review.

contents.title: Demonstration of AVA: Smartglasses-Integrated Adaptive Vision Assistant for Blind and Visually Impaired Individuals
contents.abstract: We present AVA (Adaptive Vision Assistant), a smartglasses-based software and hardware system for exploring adaptive, situated visual assistance for blind and visually impaired (BVI) individuals. Through co-design workshops with BVI individuals around AVA, we investigate how wearable sensing, on-device perception, voice control, audio guidance, directional haptics, and human-assistance fallback can be combined into a hands-free interaction model.

contents.title: Step into My Agent's Shoes: Augmenting Processual Experiences via  Interactive Narrative Game Generation
contents.abstract: Advanced agentic AI lets users delegate everyday tasks through a simple natural-language command, yet typically returns only a summarized outcome---causing users to miss the processual experiences embedded in execution, such as the moment-to-moment deliberation and decision-making, and risking the accumulation of cognitive debt. To convey these experiences, we turn to narrative, one of the most established ways of conveying others' experience. We present AgentShoes, a chat-based agentic AI system that transforms an agent's task execution into an interactive narrative game. AgentShoes extracts key decision points from the agent's reasoning and recasts them as narrative branches, letting users deliberate, choose, and observe the outcome---experiencing not merely what the agent produced, but how the task unfolded.

contents.title: VersaFunc: A Self-Networked Shape-Reconfigurable Interface with VLM-Based Shape-to-Function Mapping
contents.abstract: We present VersaFunc, a self-networked shape-reconfigurable interface that turns user-rearranged module layouts into context-aware input devices. VersaFunc consists of square touch-sensitive modules that communicate with adjacent modules through local wireless communication, allowing the system to recognize its overall shape and shape changes without external sensing. The recognized shape is interpreted by a vision-language model (VLM) together with the current application context, enabling the system to dynamically assign functions to improvised shapes without predefined rules for individual shapes. Through representative examples, we demonstrate how user-created physical shapes become input functions such as trackpads for pointing, sliders for media control or scrolling, keys, and application commands.

contents.title: Inferring an Elephant: An LLM-Driven Tangible Interface for Human-AI Co-Hallucination
contents.abstract: Computer vision and generative AI increasingly shape how people interpret ambiguous visual evidence. Yet machine misclassification is often treated only as an error to be corrected, leaving less attention to how interfaces combine uncertain machine outputs with human judgment. We present Inferring an Elephant, an LLM-driven tangible interface inspired by the blind men and the elephant. A participant examines an elephant fragment, forms an initial guess, scans the NFC-tagged piece, and receives ten candidate species without confidence scores. The participant selects an Anchor and a Challenger, adjusts their relative dominance, and receives a printed hybrid specimen generated from these choices. We describe this process as human-AI co-hallucination, a situated form of knowledge-making in which human expectations, faulty machine classifications, and choices made through the interface form a provisional interpretation. This demo contributes 1) a working tangible system for staging co-hallucination and 2) an interaction approach that makes human judgment, machine suggestion, and generative transformation visible for reflection.

contents.title: Demonstration of ProgramAT: Agentic Coding for Bespoke Visual Assistance
contents.abstract: AI-powered assistive technologies (AT) support blind and low vision (BLV) people in everyday tasks but are often too general-purpose to address individualized, in-situ accessibility needs, leading many users to prefer bespoke solutions. However, creating bespoke AT often requires collaboration with expert designers, limiting scalability. Code agents offer to lower these barriers by enabling end users to build AT through natural language. We present ProgramAT, an agentic programming system enabling BLV users to author camera-based AT by describing desired behavior and iteratively refining executable artifacts. Building on insights from a formative co-design study (to appear at ASSETS 2026), ProgramAT supports intent specification through a brainstorming agent and video-based programming by example, while intelligent model routing and task decomposition support balancing latency and accuracy. We demonstrate ProgramAT with three example tools: a plug point finder, a playing card reader, and a UIST demo navigator.

contents.title: Toward a Formally Verified Co-Reasoning Interface for Natural-Language Proof Tutoring
contents.abstract: In math tutoring, students often need feedback on whether their reasoning is correct. Large language models can give natural-language feedback, but the output may hallucinate or fail to follow the student's argument. Formal proof assistants such as Lean can verify reasoning, but require users to write precise formal code. We explore how an interface can combine these strengths: letting students write and revise proofs in natural language while a verified backend checks the reasoning and returns natural-language feedback. We present LeanTutor, a proof-tutoring interface that uses auto-formalization to translate student reasoning into Lean and informalization to translate verifier output back into readable feedback. We identify design goals for this interaction and assess the interface in a preliminary study.

contents.title: TranslateAR: Towards Style-Preserving In-Situ Text Translation in Augmented Reality
contents.abstract: Foreign-language texts are all around us—on signs, menus, labels, and packaging—and camera-based translation tools now let us read it. However, these tools render translations as plain overlays: the cursive on a cafe menu and the neon of a storefront sign both arrive in the same dull, default font. Typography, color, and layout carry a message’s formality, tone, and identity—and sometimes a bit of delight worth saving. We introduce TranslateAR, a mobile AR prototype that translates text in the scene while preserving its style, regenerating the surface itself so the translation keeps the look of the original. Doing this in a live camera view is non-trivial: text must be detected and stabilized across frames, localized on a physical surface in 3D, and rectified before it can be convincingly regenerated. And because a faithful patch takes seconds to produce, we pair an immediate on-device translation with a slower generative pass. In this demo paper, we describe our initial prototype and the questions it raises for situated, visually faithful translation.

contents.title: Demo: Responsive XR Rehabilitation Applications with Network Latency Mitigation
contents.abstract: Multi-player extended reality (XR) can make users in different places feel as if they are interacting in the same shared space, but maintaining the shared experience is challenging: differences in network delay across players can cause their local views to diverge. Current games mainly hide network delay at the application layer; we instead make the network an active part of the experience, selecting the cloud server that best serves a set of geographically distributed players and exposing multiple distinct routes over the Internet, so the best-performing route can be chosen and switched as conditions change. We demonstrate this with a networked version of iGYM, an exergame designed to support rehabilitation and inclusive play on a projected AR playfield. In our demo, traffic from two miniature play fields is routed over the public Internet to a game server in the cloud, letting attendees play two-on-two and experience our network latency mitigation techniques compared to existing baselines. Players and spectators can observe how network decisions change the shared user experience in real time.

contents.title: Finding Trees in Names: Planting Personal Data into an Infinite Collective Landscape
contents.abstract: We present an interactive demo in which visitors transform names into deterministic tree drawings, plant those trees into an infinite procedural landscape, and print a sticker as a physical trace of participation. The system combines Name2Tree, a text-to-tree generator; APack, a stamp-like authorship mark inspired by seal traditions in Chinese painting; and {Mountains, Trees, Names}*, a zoomable landscape where personal artifacts become part of a collective visual world. The same input always grows the same tree, allowing visitors to recognize, revisit, and share their contribution. The landscape has been deployed publicly, with more than 1,700 online participants planting trees after release on Hacker News, and the interaction has been tested in prior public installation settings. At UIST, attendees will type a name, watch a tree grow, plant it into the shared terrain, explore the landscape, and print a sticker to keep or place on a shared board.

contents.title: Demonstration of VisiAgent: A Mixed Reality Agent with Visual Reference and Guidance for People with Low Vision
contents.abstract: While recent assistive technologies based on vision-language models (VLM) for blind people have enabled conversational audio descriptions of surrounding scenes, they often do not leverage the residual vision of people with low vision (PLV) to directly reference visual targets or provide accessible visual feedback. To address these gaps, we designed and implemented VisiAgent, an MR agent that provides visual-reference grounding and multimodal feedback coordination for PLV. VisiAgent indicates the user's attention with a cursor and marks swept objects as visually accessible candidate references for PLV using semi-transparent overlays. A VLM-powered backend interprets user requests and coordinates visual augmentations with synchronized audio narration. Beyond user-initiated visual inquiries, VisiAgent also supports system-initiated interventions when timely feedback is needed for safety or task support. We demonstrate VisiAgent across challenging daily tasks for PLV, including reading text, searching for objects, and manipulating objects.

contents.title: PreView: Rehearsing Real Routes in VR to Support Independent Navigation with Low-Vision
contents.abstract: Low-vision individuals (LVI) must focus on their immediate surroundings while walking, a rational response to the risk of unseen curbs and obstacles. This protective attention leaves the landmarks that anchor cognitive maps unattended, and most navigation support concentrates on the walk itself, when attention is scarcest. We present PreView, a system that turns real 360-degree route imagery into a VR rehearsal of a route that a LVI plans to walk: realistic enough to learn from, safe enough to look up in. PreView highlights salient, permanent landmarks, layers an imagery-derived soundscape with surface-matched footsteps, and answers questions through an AI agent grounded in the user's current view. Rehearsing a route in PreView lets LVI form a cognitive map in advance and navigate it more independently. In this demo, attendees freely explore real captured routes and experience how multimodal AI augmentation turns commodity imagery into route knowledge that LVI could acquire safely before ever walking the street.

contents.title: Interactive Demonstration of Active Bed-Frame Vibration Sensing for Respiratory Airflow Monitoring
contents.abstract: Respiratory airflow waveform monitoring is a crucial physiological signal for sleep disorders and critical care monitoring. However, current clinical approaches often require cumbersome instrumentation, which limits their practicality for everyday use. We present a non-invasive system that reconstructs an airflow-correlated respiratory waveform across unconstrained sleep postures. Our system injects an imperceptible single-tone vibration into an ordinary bed frame and measures how respiration-induced body-load redistribution modulates the frame's structural vibration response. A co-designed L-shaped sensor bracket and resonance-aligned excitation enhance sensitivity to these subtle respiratory effects, while a real-time signal-processing pipeline demodulates the measured response into a continuous respiratory waveform.

contents.title: AgentCube: AI-Assisted In-Situ Authoring for Physical Computing
contents.abstract: Physical computing kits introduce novices to hardware programming, but the creation process is often separated from the environment where the resulting artifacts will be tested and used --- such as building an interactive nightlight in a well-lit classroom. Every tweak typically requires a back-and-forth trip to the workbench. We present AgentCube, a portable, AI-agent-powered platform enabling novices to program interactive and context-aware hardware artifacts using voice, directly at the deployment site. AgentCube employs a human-agent workflow that translates a novice's spoken concepts into executable behaviors grounded in hardware states and, optionally, the environmental context. By eliminating the need for keyboards and screen-based programming interfaces, AgentCube allows users to author, test, and refine their creations in situ. In this demo, we present AgentCube's all-in-one architecture, its hardware-aware agent harness, and example artifacts enabled by AgentCube's in-situ authoring capability.
